title: Jason La Canfora talks C.J. Stroud with NFL insiders
summary: Jason La Canfora is in a very small group of journalists who sit at the tip of the NFL news cycle spear. Along with Adam Schefter and 1 or 2 others, if these guys are unavailable, a ridiculously high percentage of NFL breaking news comes through him, usually via X (Twitter). So, when I’m alerted […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - JANUARY 11: C.J. Stroud #7 and Davis Mills #10 of the Houston Texans embrace on the field after defeating the Los Angeles Chargers 32-12 during the AFC Wild Card Playoffs at NRG Stadium on January 11, 2025 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Jason La Canfora is in a very small group of journalists who sit at the tip of the NFL news cycle spear. Along with Adam Schefter and 1 or 2 others, if these guys are unavailable, a ridiculously high percentage of NFL breaking news comes through him, usually via X (Twitter). So, when I’m alerted that La Canfora did an exclusive piece for the Canadian website Casino.ca, focused on Houston Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud (and Baker Mayfield & Lamar Jackson), I sit up and take notice. For the piece, La Canfora discussed the 3 field generals with a wide range of NFL folks from scouts, to executives to general managers. While there’s no “hidden truth” any of them have that predicts the future, it does come with some solid legitimacy since these are smart, successful people paid to be smart and successful when it comes to NFL quarterbacks. Right out of the gate, one of them kicks Stroud when he’s down. An advance scout who does a lot of work in the AFC South told La Canfora, regarding CJ Stroud’s playoff performance v New England, “Houston wins that game if Davis Mills starts”. It’s hard to know for sure if Mills would have won that game due to a variety of factors that we’ll never see play out. Does Vrabel dial up a different defense based on Mills vs Stroud? Are there 1 or more Patriot defenders who have a banner game due to matching up better against Mills’ style than Strouds’? Does the Houston O-Line respond worse to Mills than Stroud? Is the stage too big for Mills the same way many feel it may have been too big for Stroud? Certainly a lot to crunch through on that one… Another interesting tidbit: It stands to reason that at least one of them [Jackson, Mayfield, Stroud] won’t be back with their current team by 2027, and possibly more. Front office executives around the NFL are watching closely to see if they might be able to land one of these accomplished passers next season, as supply never meets demand with the most important position in all of professional sports. It’s hard to argue the possibility that Stroud is no longer in H-Town if this season doesn’t bear better results than last. Especially if the fault lands at C.J.’s cleats. But it also shows the value of all 3 signal callers – if any was “trash” other teams wouldn’t be watching, hoping, praying for a chance to grab 1 of them should they land in the unemployment line after the 2026 season. Here’s where La Canfora focuses in on Stroud: Stroud, also a first-round pick, is three years into his career, they have a fifth-year option on him and they could apply franchise tags after that. The Texans were never going to make a real push to sign him this year after some dramatic declines from his rookie season, and general manager Nick Caserio is a product of Bill Belichick in New England – even Tom Brady took less to be a part of that dynasty and there was no dynasty without Brady. “Nick is no pushover,” another general manager told me this offseason. “Stroud is going to have to earn it.” The notion that Caserio and the Texans have to give Stroud a big paycheck at the end of this year isn’t necessarily rooted in fact. The option and tags could buy them time to get Stroud onboard and/or replaced. La Canfora’s hot take on how this plays out: Prediction: Stroud heads into 2027 without a new deal There are 17 games in the 2026 Houston Texans schedule – and hopefully, at least 3 more after those. If they win the last 3-4, Stroud will likely get paid. If not, La Canfora may seem prophetic. A lot of folks familiar with Stroud’s days at Ohio State were somewhat shocked at his early, elite-adjacent performances in the NFL. Most of those same folks are buying the current Stroud as the guy they knew all along who couldn’t get it done. On the flipside, Stroud does hold the Rose Bowl record for most passing touchdowns in a game – in a stadium that holds 100k+ people. Hard to think of a college-level game that could feel bigger than 100,000+ screaming fans within 200 yards of you at all times. Personally, I think Stroud gets it done this year and we’re all looking back saying “remember when so many people didn’t believe in him?” But, I also thought Jadeveon Clowney and J.J. Watt were going to be the best DE tandem in the NFL for the better part of a decade. In reference to the AFC South scout’s quote above, if the scout works for the Glitter Kitties or the Baby Horses, the opinion is immediately sus. If employed by the Not-The-Oilers, it’s almost impossible to take seriously. What do you think?

title: Colts announce Jonathan Taylor’s extension as backfield duo stays ‘on fire’ in lone night practice
summary: WESTFIELD, Ind. — Under the lights at Droplight Grand Park Sports Campus, the Indianapolis Colts turned up the intensity for the lone night practice of training camp.  What started off as a special announcement became a celebration for the stampede of fans and evolved into the most competitive practice of camp. The festivities began with Colts […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, Ind. — Under the lights at Droplight Grand Park Sports Campus, the Indianapolis Colts turned up the intensity for the lone night practice of training camp. What started off as a special announcement became a celebration for the stampede of fans and evolved into the most competitive practice of camp. The festivities began with Colts principal owner Carly Irsay-Gordon declaring running back Jonathan Taylor is “here to stay” after the 27-year-old tailback agreed to a two-year, $44 million contract extension. The announcement earned an emphatic roar from the crowd, which was followed by Irsay-Gordon treating fans at least 21-years-old with a free Bud Light can. It set the tone for an electric atmosphere that carried throughout the two-hour workout. for the best fans.💙 @budlight pic.twitter.com/KDEDXrSRNj — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) August 7, 2026 Quarterback Daniel Jones continued his impressive stretch of camp, looking more comfortable while operating the offense both inside and outside the pocket. Jones ignited the initial team drills and got loose with a pair of scrambles before settling into a rhythm through the air. He orchestrated the run-pass-option scheme, using play-action to throw a dig route to receiver Nick Westbrook-Ikhene for roughly 20 yards, then later connected with the veteran receiver again on a post route. The first-team offense was tasked to sustain a drive while backed up inside its own 10-yard line during a live period. Jones escaped the incoming pressure before delivering a strike to receiver Ashton Dulin up the seam for a 25-yard gain that flipped field position. Perhaps his best throw of the evening was a perfectly placed wheel route 30 yards downfield to tight end Tyler Warren, placing the football between cornerback Sauce Gardner and safety AJ Haulcy. The Colts capped the night practice inside the red zone and Jones fired a laser to find Dulin in the back of the end zone for a touchdown. DUUUUUUULIN 🗣️ pic.twitter.com/mXM3yWxEmG — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) August 7, 2026 For the third consecutive practice, Taylor took a slip screen the distance for what would have been another explosive touchdown. By design and perfect execution, the Colts have repeatedly found ways to get the ball to their All-Pro running back into open space during camp. The rookies on the defense answered with several standout moments of their own. Rookie edge rusher Caden Curry recorded what could have been a sack during the live tackling period, while rookie linebacker Bryce Boettcher burst through untouched on a blitz for another sack. Fellow rookie George Gumbs Jr. delivered one of the loudest hits of the night after dropping back in coverage to lay a significant strike. Third-year edge rusher Laiatu Latu also flashed his instincts by blowing up a Taylor zone run before later dropping into coverage to break up a quick slant intended for Taylor inside the red zone. Anthony Richardson Sr.‘s turbulent training camp continued. The fourth-year quarterback again struggled again with ball security, dropping another snap with the second unit. Richardson was later picked off after forcing a throw over the middle that sailed high. Cornerback Mekhi Blackmon capitalized after rookie receiver Deion Burks tipped the pass into the air and Blackmon hauled it in for an interception. Linebacker Austin Ajiake also secured his second interception of Riley Leonard during Thursday’s workout. Special teams was a major emphasis as Thursday’s practice featured an extended kicking session. Blake Grupe converted 4-of-5 attempts, connecting from 33, 41, 49 and 57 yards before coming up short on a 61-yard try. Spencer Shrader finished 3-for-5, delivering successful kicks from 33, 49 and 57 yards, while missing from 41 and 47 yards. The Colts host two morning practices this weekend at 10 a.m. before traveling for the first preseason game against the New England Patriots.

title: Josh Downs looks ready for a bigger role in the Colts offense
summary: “A guy that can play inside and outside now for us, and his role is going to improve this season.“ That was Shane Steichen on Josh Downs, and it feels like one of the more important offensive developments of Colts training camp. Downs has already proven he can play in this league, and now the […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - JUNE 11: Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Josh Downs (2) runs through a drill during the Indianapolis Colts Minicamp on June 11, 2026 at the Indiana Farm Bureau Football Center in Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images “A guy that can play inside and outside now for us, and his role is going to improve this season.“ That was Shane Steichen on Josh Downs, and it feels like one of the more important offensive developments of Colts training camp. Downs has already proven he can play in this league, and now the conversation is shifting from whether he belongs to how much more Indianapolis can put on his plate. That is where this season gets interesting, because Downs does not need to become a traditional No. 1 receiver to become one of the most important players in the Colts’ passing game. The role was always likely to grow. Michael Pittman Jr. is gone, Alec Pierce has a different job as the vertical outside receiver, and Tyler Warren is a major piece at tight end, which leaves Downs in a spot where his weekly target share could climb quickly. He may not be the primary read on every concept, and he does not have to be used the same way Pierce is, but Downs is the type of receiver who can end up with the most targets in a lot of games simply because of how he wins. He separates quickly, works well underneath and intermediate, and gives the quarterback answers on the downs that usually decide drives. That has been the most impressive part of Downs since he got to Indianapolis. Even with inconsistent quarterback play, he has found ways to be productive and reliable. The Colts have not exactly given him a stable offensive environment, yet his skill set has translated because separation travels. Quarterbacks trust receivers who get open on time, and Downs does that about as well as anyone on the roster. He is especially valuable on third down, where timing, leverage and route detail matter more than size or straight-line speed. The outside part of Steichen’s quote is important too. Downs’ best work still comes from the slot, and that should remain the foundation of his role, but he is not limited to only being a slot receiver. If the Colts can move him outside in certain looks, use him in motion and make defenses declare how they want to match him, the offense becomes less predictable. That does not mean forcing him into a role that does not fit. It means expanding the menu so defenses cannot treat him like a static inside option. He can become a 100-catch receiver and the idea is not ridiculous. That does not mean he has to turn into a superstar overnight, and it does not mean he needs to be force-fed empty targets. It means the opportunity is there if the Colts build the passing game correctly. Downs is the kind of player who can catch six balls in a game without it feeling like the offense was designed around him, because so much of his production can come naturally through option routes, quick-game concepts, third-down throws and answers against pressure. For the Colts, that kind of player is extremely valuable. This offense still begins with Jonathan Taylor, and Warren may become the most dangerous matchup piece, but Downs can be the receiver who keeps the passing game on schedule. That role is not always flashy, yet it is often the difference between an offense that has to survive on explosives and one that can consistently move the chains. Training camp buzz always needs to be handled carefully, because every summer has players who look ready for a leap and then settle back into what they were. Downs feels different because this is not random hype attached to an unknown player. This is the next logical step for someone who has already shown he can win in the NFL, now entering a season where the depth chart and coaching staff are pointing toward more responsibility. The Colts do not need Downs to become something he is not. They need to lean into what he already does well and give him more chances to do it from different spots. If that happens, his expanded role could end up being one of the biggest reasons the passing game takes a needed step forward.
author: Andrew Aziz

title: Rapid Reaction: Colts agree to new multi-year contract extension with star RB Jonathan Taylor
summary: According to multiple league reports, the Indianapolis Colts reached a 2-year, $44 million contract extension (featuring $39 million guaranteed) with star running back Jonathan Taylor: The 27-year-old running back had been entering the last year of a 3-year, $42 million contract extension that he had inked back in October of 2023 following a contentious and […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - DECEMBER 28: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts rushes for yards during the first half of the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Lucas Oil Stadium on December 28, 2025 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to multiple league reports, the Indianapolis Colts reached a 2-year, $44 million contract extension (featuring $39 million guaranteed) with star running back Jonathan Taylor: Another big running back deal: three-time Pro-Bowl RB Jonathan Taylor and the Colts reached agreement today on a two-year, $44 million extension worth up to $47 million that includes $39 million guaranteed, per @rapsheet and me. Taylor’s agent Malki Kawa of @FirstRoundMgmt and… pic.twitter.com/8DsowuNjG0 — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) August 6, 2026 The 27-year-old running back had been entering the last year of a 3-year, $42 million contract extension that he had inked back in October of 2023 following a contentious and highly public summer hold-out with the team. This latest contract extension will keep him as an Indianapolis Colt for arguably the remaining prime of his playing career and through the 2028 season. It was seemingly a domino effect, after Atlanta Falcons’ 24-year-old reigning NFL First-Team All-Pro running back Bijan Robinson signed a 3-year deal with his club, worth up to $75 million (with $51M guaranteed). After hearing that breaking news earlier this week, Taylor indicated firsthand that he’d have to ‘tap in’ to his agent, and just days later, he signed the 3rd largest deal for a running back ever in NFL history. Earlier this offseason, while it’s a business, Taylor indicated his preference to “retire a Colt,” and team owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon seemed to have a fresh perspective when asked just a few weeks ago on re-signing one of the greatest running backs in Indianapolis franchise history and a potential future Hall of Famer, saying, “I would love if he would be a Colt for life.” Those comments were quite a contrast to her late father Jim Irsay’s comments in the summer of 2023, regarding the ongoing contentious contract negotiation with Taylor, when he stated, “If I die tonight and Jonathan Taylor is out of the league, no one’s gonna miss us. The league goes on. We know that. The National Football (League) rolls on. It doesn’t matter who comes and who goes, and it’s a privilege to be a part of it.” Given that Robinson’s new deal set the elite running back market, and provided the Colts a reasonable measuring stick for Taylor’s fair market value, and the two sides made quick work to keep him in Indianapolis for at least the next three seasons (including this one where he was already under contract). Even with the uncertainty of the Colts leadership at general manager and head coach going forward, Taylor projects to have at least three more elite seasons left in him. He keeps himself in tip-top shape, and is coming off another highly productive 2025 season in which he rushed for 1,585 total rushing yards and 18 rushing touchdowns on 323 total carries (4.9 ypc. avg.) during all 17 starts—earning Pro Bowl honors again.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Jonathan Taylor made the Colts pay
summary: The NFL is a copycat league. When one team finds success with a certain style or play, you can bet other teams will follow suit. The same goes for players. See success, chase that same success. Bijan Robinson just became the highest paid running back in the league. Jonathan Taylor was well aware of that […]
full_text: The NFL is a copycat league. When one team finds success with a certain style or play, you can bet other teams will follow suit. The same goes for players. See success, chase that same success. Bijan Robinson just became the highest paid running back in the league. Jonathan Taylor was well aware of that new deal and made the Indianapolis Colts pay. Taylor signed a two-year extension worth $44 million worth up to $47 million and includes $39 million guaranteed, per a report from ESPN’s Adam Schefter and Ian Rapaport on Thursday monring . Taylor was informed of Robinson’s 3-year, $75 million deal during training camp earlier this week. With $51 million in guarantees, it’s a whopper. Said tongue in cheek, Taylor was looking for the Colts to pony up, which played out with an ensuing contract extension. Colts running back Jonathan Taylor, after hearing about Bijan Robinson’s extension in Atlanta, says he’s going to “tap in” with his agent “now that you guys broke the news to me.” pic.twitter.com/FTsLpM9GjI — Stephen Holder (@HolderStephen) August 4, 2026 Yes, he was joking, but then again, he was dead serious and should be. Rewind three years ago and running backs were a dime a dozen. At least that’s how the league saw them. After a zoom call, Taylor became the poster child for “running backs for better rights” and held out on the Colts. That produced a nice contract and helped reset the running back market. Robinson’s contract is a reflection of Taylor’s effort. Why shouldn’t Taylor reap the ultimate rewards himself? He was a dark horse candidate for MVP over the first ten weeks of last season. He broke huge runs, set franchise records, and carried the Colts at times. There is a lot of distance between that unfortunate offseason and the accompanying ankle injury. Time has passed but the results live on. Luckily for Taylor, he was able to cash in one more time. The Colts paid handsomely to keep Jonathan Taylor. Based on last season’s production that should be no problem. Editor’s note: This article was originally written before Taylor agreed to his contract extension and has been updated to reflect the signing.
author: Jon Spradley

title: Parker Washington is ‘feared across the league’ as a punt returner: Can he become the same as a receiver?
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars believe they have the luxury of rostering the best kicker, punter, and long snapper in the NFL. “I’m very fortunate,” special teams coordinator and associate head coach Heath Farwell said Thursday after Day 7 of training camp. “There’s no question. Those guys are fantastic. They’re the best in the game at their […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - JULY 30: Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Parker Washington (11) catches a pass during training camp on July 30, 2026 at the Miller Electric Center in Jacksonville, Fl. (Photo by David Rosenblum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Jacksonville Jaguars believe they have the luxury of rostering the best kicker, punter, and long snapper in the NFL. “I’m very fortunate,” special teams coordinator and associate head coach Heath Farwell said Thursday after Day 7 of training camp. “There’s no question. Those guys are fantastic. They’re the best in the game at their positions. “And then throw Parker Washington into that as well.” “He’s a fantastic receiver,” Farwell allowed, “but he’s an elite returner. He’s a game changer. He’s feared across the league. He’s the best returner in the National Football League as far as I’m concerned.” Indeed, part of Washington’s recent breakout season was being a return man on special teams. In 2024, he became the first NFL player to score an international special teams touchdown with a franchise-record 96-yard punt return . Last season, he was promoted to primary punter returner and became the first Jaguar to house multiple returns in a single season. He finished first in touchdowns, fifth in yards (341), and sixth in yards per return (13.6) among all NFL punt returners. Washington’s career average of 14.2 yards per punt return ranks first in franchise history and fourth among active NFL players (min. 20 returns). For the first time in his young career, Washington is expecting a full-time workload on offense, but it sounds like he’ll continue to give the offense a boost as the punt returner. “He says that he wants to play, wants to be back there, help the team win,” Farwell said. “That’s the culture Coach Liam [Coen] brought in, and he’s part of it. He wants to win. And how is he going to help us? It’s part of being a punt returner.” Washington also spoke after Thursday’s practice. When asked about return duties, he said, “I’m just open to the opportunity, whatever it is. Obviously, we’ll get some more receiver play, but as I said, I want to come out here and be my best self. If that happens to be on return, shoot. I feel like I’ve been studying that for a while now. Let’s see if we can make some more plays.” Washington’s unique drive was instilled by his family at a young age. “One day going into middle school, I was like, ‘I’ve got to make my parents proud.’ Whatever I’m doing, I’m going to make sure I give my absolute best … I couldn’t tell you what clicked. Something just in me just was like, I want to do something different. I want to be special.” It seems like Washington couldn’t have made his special teams coordinator any prouder — but now, the person he’s most looking to prove himself to is his quarterback. “The trust [Trevor Lawrence is] having in me on some of these passes is really cool. I know a couple years ago, he probably wouldn’t throw some of the passes he’s throwing now to me, so it’s just really cool for him to have that trust in me and I’m going to continue to make sure that he has that, and I’m going to make those plays for him.” When asked about his reaction to Zay Flowers’ record-breaking contract extension, Washington — entering the final year of his rookie deal — said, “My focus is just coming out here. I need to make plays for Trevor.” Given the option to fair catch the ball, punt returners don’t see enough action to really stress about extra hits. Washington should continue to trot onto the field when the Jaguars force a fourth down. But the days of his game-changing, fear-inducing abilities being limited to special teams snaps only are far from over. Notes & Quotes Farwell anticipates Caleb Ransaw joining Rayuan Lane III as the team’s starting gunners on special teams. “Ransaw has been a fantastic gunner … between those two guys, I think we have two of the better gunners in the National Football League.” Usually, rookie receivers look like rookie receivers, but CJ Williams and Josh Cameron genuinely seem like veteran additions to the room. “CJ contacted me more this summer than anybody. And it’s a reflection of how much he cares,” Farwell said. “He’s done a great job for us.” And Cameron, who snatches a contested ball over defenders seemingly every practice, appears to be on track for a role on kick returns. “Cameron is a dynamic returner. I’ve been super impressed with him back here at training camp in practice,” Farwell said. “We have a bunch of guys that can do it. I think we’ve just got to kind of see how this thing all plays out with the roster, active on game days and playing times.” Yesterday, I mentioned on the Prowler Podcast that Jabbar Muhammad has carried over his standout play from OTAs in such a way that makes me think he could earn a role in dime/nickel packages — with the caveat that his frame could cause natural limitations as a full-time perimeter player. Muhammad shut me up today by breaking up a pass to Brian Thomas Jr. on a dig route. His arrow continues to point up. The play of the day belonged to Ventrell Miller, who’s competing with Branson Combs to fill a Devin Lloyd-sized hole at linebacker. Get the ball out, 5-1 🥊 @Dream_Finders | #DUUUVAL pic.twitter.com/jLTyuwDFx2 — Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) August 6, 2026 Jags fans, let us know your thoughts in the comments below!

title: Which Jaguars rookies have impressed early in Training Camp?
summary: Training camp optimism is a rite of passage across the NFL, but genuine buzz is much harder to come by. Every summer produces a handful of rookies who force coaches, teammates and beat writers to sit up and take notice long before the preseason begins. In Jacksonville, the headlines have understandably centred on established stars […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - JULY 29: Josh Cameron #19 of the Jacksonville Jaguars runs with the ball during Training Camp at The Miller Electric Center on July 29, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by James Gilbert/Getty Images) | Getty Images Training camp optimism is a rite of passage across the NFL, but genuine buzz is much harder to come by. Every summer produces a handful of rookies who force coaches, teammates and beat writers to sit up and take notice long before the preseason begins. In Jacksonville, the headlines have understandably centred on established stars and the continued evolution of Liam Coen’s offense. Yet behind the scenes, several first-year players are quietly making compelling cases for increased roles through the first seven days of training camp. From spectacular catches to valuable first-team reps, these are the Jaguars rookies who have wasted little time making an impression at the Miller Electric Center: Josh Cameron, WR Rookie vibesss Grab free tickets to Friday’s mock game: https://t.co/fhVdfYSB9O @Dream_Finders | #DUUUVAL pic.twitter.com/mvNFRhAdL4 — Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) August 4, 2026 If one rookie has emerged as the surprise package of Jaguars training camp so far, it’s sixth-round wide receiver Josh Cameron. The former Baylor walk-on arrived in Jacksonville with a reputation for doing things the hard way. After developing into one of the Big 12’s most productive receivers during his final collegiate seasons, Cameron entered camp needing to prove he belonged in one of the deepest receiver rooms in football. So far, he’s done exactly that. While plenty of rookies flash during individual drills, Cameron has repeatedly produced when the intensity has increased. His spectacular diving reception during an early team session immediately caught the attention of those watching practice, but perhaps more impressive has been the consistency that followed. Rather than disappearing after one highlight, Cameron has continued stacking positive days together, showing reliable hands, crisp routes and an ability to create separation against NFL defensive backs. With Brian Thomas Jr., Jakobi Meyers, Travis Hunter and Parker Washington ahead of him, opportunities won’t come easily. That’s precisely why every rep matters. Cameron has made the most of virtually all of them. The Jaguars didn’t draft Cameron expecting immediate headlines. They drafted an intelligent, dependable receiver with a history of outperforming expectations. Through the opening stretch of camp, he’s doing exactly that again. His biggest challenge now is sustaining the momentum once preseason games begin. If he can translate these practice performances into live action, Jacksonville may have found one of the steals of the later rounds. And if you’re looking for the rookie who has generated the most genuine excitement through the opening week of camp, Cameron sits comfortably at the top of the list. Emmanuel Pregnon, G #Jaguars OG Emmanuel Pregnon getting coached up then getting the reach block rep ✅️ Earned the dap from OL Coach Shaun Sarrett before Day 4 of 2026 Training Camp pic.twitter.com/oTidTimgO7 — 𝕋𝕣𝕒𝕧𝕚𝕤 🅓. ℍ𝕠𝕝𝕞𝕖𝕤 (@TravisDHolmes) August 2, 2026 Offensive linemen rarely generate highlight reels during training camp, but Emmanuel Pregnon has quietly enjoyed one of the more encouraging starts among Jacksonville’s rookie class. With injuries causing the Jaguars to juggle things around on the o-line, the third-round selection has been given valuable work alongside experienced offensive linemen, with coaches clearly eager to evaluate his versatility across the interior. Those opportunities alone speak volumes about how highly the Jaguars view his long-term potential. Camp hasn’t been without its welcome-to-the-NFL moments. Veteran defensive tackle Arik Armstead produced one of the practice highlights when he powered through Pregnon to disrupt a running play. Rather than hurting the rookie’s stock, however, it served as another reminder that Jacksonville is deliberately throwing him into meaningful situations against elite competition. For a rookie offensive lineman, development often comes through difficult reps rather than dominant ones. Pregnon appears to be embracing exactly that challenge, and every additional snap with the first-team offense will only accelerate his progress. CJ Williams, WR CJ Williams is off to a strong start to camp he has turned a lot of heads pic.twitter.com/1zF5QTigoH — Jamal St. Cyr (@JStCyrTV) August 2, 2026 Josh Cameron may have stolen the spotlight, but fellow sixth-round receiver CJ Williams has quietly put together a solid start to his own NFL career. Williams entered camp facing the same uphill battle as Cameron, attempting to carve out a place in an exceptionally competitive receiver room. Rather than forcing spectacular plays, he’s impressed through consistency, clean route running and dependable hands whenever his number has been called. That approach may not produce viral social media clips every day, but it’s exactly the type of reliability coaching staffs value during the early stages of training camp. Every clean route and routine catch builds confidence, particularly for young receivers hoping to earn preseason opportunities. If Williams can continue producing steady performances while others chase highlight moments, he’ll give himself every chance of remaining firmly in the fight for a roster spot as camp progresses. Tanner Koziol, TE Can Tanner Koziol block, if so he’s going to be dangerous. Has shown great receiving skills pic.twitter.com/prphaYvUuP — Rick Ballou (@Ballou1010xl) August 4, 2026 Tanner Koziol hasn’t dominated headlines, but the rookie tight end has quietly gone about the business of showing why Jacksonville invested a fifth-round pick in him. The former Houston standout brings versatility to the Jaguars’ offense, offering value both as a receiver and as a developing blocker. Early camp sessions have reflected that flexibility, with Koziol seeing opportunities in a variety of personnel groupings as coaches assess how best to utilise his skill set. Behind established options on the depth chart, Koziol isn’t under pressure to become an instant starter. Instead, every practice is another opportunity to prove he can contribute sooner rather than later. Tight ends often require patience at the professional level, but Koziol’s encouraging start suggests Jacksonville believes there’s enough upside to begin expanding his responsibilities as camp unfolds. title: Chiefs training camp: 53-man roster prediction after one week
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs have gone through eight practices at training camp so far. The Arrowhead Pride staff has been on hand for each session and has listened to each press conference, building the knowledge that went into my personal 53-man roster prediction as things currently stand. Here we go: Offense (25) Quarterbacks (3): Patrick […]
full_text: Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid observes players during practice at training camp on Friday, July 31, 2026, in St. Joseph. (Emily Curiel/Kansas City Star/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) The Kansas City Chiefs have gone through eight practices at training camp so far. The Arrowhead Pride staff has been on hand for each session and has listened to each press conference, building the knowledge that went into my personal 53-man roster prediction as things currently stand. Here we go: Offense (25) Quarterbacks (3): Patrick Mahomes, Justin Fields and Garrett Nussmeier Fields is signed to a one-year contract as the backup quarterback, but seventh-round pick Garrett Nussmeier has put together an impressive enough camp to warrant a spot on an NFL team’s 53-man roster come September. It feels like he could put together some notable film against third-team defenses in the preseason. If the Chiefs are serious about him being the immediate understudy to Mahomes next season and beyond, he will likely need to be on the active roster. Running backs (4): Kenneth Walker, Brashard Smith, Emari Demercado and Emmett Johnson This group feels pretty set in stone as the team’s backfield for this season. Walker’s the lead back, Smith is the change-of-pace, versatile weapon, Demercado will settle in as the pass-down back, and Johnson is the hungry rookie who is ready to make a splash if given the opportunity. Wide receivers (6): Rashee Rice, Xavier Worthy, Tyquan Thornton, Cyrus Allen, Jalen Royals and Andrew Armstrong CLOSE CALL: Armstrong over Nikko Remigio The competition at the receiver position, in terms of who will make the active roster, begins at No. 5. With the uncertainty at the top of the depth chart, it seems like the team needs to keep more than five receivers. There’s more to find out about Royals and Armstrong, but that’s more than can be said about Remigio. He has maximized his role in Kansas City, and the return job should be handed off to Brashard Smith. Allen has lined up and caught punts and kicks as well. Special teams coordinator Dave Toub noted Armstrong as someone he is excited about “as a cover guy” on Monday. He has also stepped up in the place of injured starting receivers this camp and has seen plenty of throws from Mahomes at practice. He appears to be more than the big-bodied, jumpball player that can fool Chiefs Kingdom at training camp. Tight ends (3): Travis Kelce, Noah Gray and Jared Wiley CLOSE CALL: Jake Briningstool left off There is an urge to find room for second-year tight end Jake Briningstool on the roster, but at this point, the trio of starters has taken care of business for the first-team offense, and it feels as if Briningstool — or another potential practice-squad member — could be called up midseason if the team happens to suffer an injury. If Briningstool, who racked up 1,380 receiving yards and 17 touchdowns in his college career at Clemson, has an impressive preseason, he could force the team to make room for his skill set. Offensive linemen (9): LT Joshua Simmons, LG Kingsley Suamataia, C Creed Humphrey, RG Trey Smith, RT Kahlil Benson, Jaylon Moore, Esa Pole, Hunter Nourzad and Mike Caliendo CLOSE CALL: Caliendo over Ethan Driskell We don’t know who will start at right tackle in Week 1, but it feels like we know Benson and Moore will be on the roster. To me, Pole and Nourzad appear to be the highest on the depth chart among the rest. Nourzad has played backup center in camp, but has played guard in his career and has also lined up as an eligible-reporting sixth offensive lineman with the starting offense in camp and towards the end of last season. He is more athletic than strong, and is obviously battling to stave off veteran Mike Caliendo as the first backup to the interior positions. If Benson, Moore, Pole or third-year tackle Ethan Driskell show any guard versatility during the preseason, one of Nourzad or Caliendo could be outed to maintain two reserves on the inside. Give me Nourzad as of now. Defense (25) Defensive tackles (4): Chris Jones, Khyiris Tonga, Peter Woods and Omarr Norman-Lott There’s not a lot of debate here, although second-year player Marcus Harris from Auburn has shown off at times in camp. With the starting defense in a goal-to-go period, he tipped up a pass that led to an interception by safety Chamarri Conner. He will push with the fifth defensive end below to round out the defensive line room as a whole. Defensive ends (5): George Karlaftis, Ashton Gillotte, Felix Anudike-Uzomah, R Mason Thomas and Tyreke Smith With an injury to Gillotte and so much unknown between Anudike-Uzomah and the rookie Thomas, there should be a fifth player in the room. Smith would likely be a game-day inactive. Linebackers (5): Nick Bolton, Drue Tranquill, Jeffrey Bassa, Cole McDonald and Jack Cochrane It’s good to see more of Bassa with the starting defense in camp, solidifying his roster spot, but the veteran Cochrane has reminded spectators of his value as reliable depth in case of injury. It’s hard to imagine the coaching staff signing off on cutting the fifth-year linebacker as things stand. Cornerbacks (6): Mansoor Delane, Nohl Williams, L’Jarius Sneed, Kristian Fulton, Kader Kohou and Jadon Canady CLOSE CALL: Kohou over Kevin Knowles Kohou’s fully-guaranteed $1.8 million salary, along with his veteran experience in a young secondary, will likely keep him on the roster. He has worked with the starters plenty, but there has been quite the rotation in the slot at camp. Kevin Knowles flashed last year on defense and special teams; he feels hard to cut, but he could still sneak onto the team’s practice squad. Now, Fulton has worked nearly exclusively with the second-team defense in camp. He got some time with the starters this week before injuring his hip flexor. He has an $8 million dead cap hit . If he recovers quickly and shows enough to garner interest from a cornerback-desperate team, the team might feel as if it’s in position to move forward without him in the picture if it was unwilling to sacrifice a younger player. Safeties (5): Alohi Gilman, Chamarri Conner, Christian Roland-Wallace, Jaden Hicks and Xavier Nwankpa Hicks has not seen any work with the starting defense, seemingly needing to do more work to impress defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo. He’ll get that opportunity, and so will former Iowa safety and special-teams ace Xavier Nwankpa. He is comfortably on the roster right now and looks the part on defense and all four phases of special teams. Specialists (3) Placekicker Harrison Butker, punter Matt Araiza and long snapper James Winchester The usual suspects.

title: Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker talks about tweaking routine this season
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs as a whole are seeking a bounce-back season in 2026, but kicker Harrison Butker is especially. The Arrowhead Pride staff identified Butker as one of the players with the most at stake this year in terms of his NFL career. After a total of nine missed kicks last year, with a […]
full_text: ST. JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: Kicker Harrison Butker #7 and punter Matt Araiza #14 walk to the field before practice during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on July 29, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs as a whole are seeking a bounce-back season in 2026, but kicker Harrison Butker is especially. The Arrowhead Pride staff identified Butker as one of the players with the most at stake this year in terms of his NFL career. After a total of nine missed kicks last year, with a career-low percentage on point-after attempts, Butker is looking to improve by making sure his preparation is as effective as possible. That starts with his practice routine, which he has tweaked to better mimic a game day. He told local media after practice on Wednesday. “In a game, what a kicker is asked to do is to execute one kick every 15-20 minutes,” Butker explained. “I’ve been trying to gain confidence in waiting 15-20 minutes, then having to have a field goal that matters… however well I do, that’s the end result. “In the past, it’s easy for practice; you kick a bunch of balls before the field-goal period, and then you’re kind of done for the day,” Butker went on. “But I’m trying to take advantage of these longer practices, treat it like a game and do what I’m going to be asked to do in a game, which is just one kick every 20 minutes or so.” He clearly put a lot of thought into sharpening his routine in St. Joe, but he believes his entire process is requiring less thinking, acknowledging the kicker position as one where mental toughness is especially key. “Last year, I wasn’t dropping down to that plant-foot knee, but I was having to think about it a lot,” Butker said. “Especially during training camp. Now I don’t have to focus on that, so I’m hoping I can just focus on things that matter more, smooth swing thoughts, and I think that’s been helpful for me to keep it simple and just focus on good ball contact instead of really focusing in on not dropping down on that knee.” Butker’s narrowed focus includes disregarding a different kicking strategy when kicking off. He believes streamlining his technique was an important part of finishing strong in a tough season last year. “Obviously, the place kicking and field goals matter the most. I think, maybe trying to hit those knuckle balls and the funny kickoffs maybe affected the field goals a little bit,” Butker shared. “I’m just going to hit a high hangtime ball, good rotation, just focus on the location,” Butker continued. “I’m not going to try to hit a low, line-drive knuckle ball and I think that has helped my field goals. It’s kind of the same foot-to-ball contact… rather than having two different swings. That helped me the second half of the season, and I’m kind of sticking with that for training camp and this season.” Cleaning up the practice routine for the Chiefs’ place-kicking team includes eliminating unrealistic or less-important distanced attempts. “Throughout my entire career here, I feel like the only time I’ve ever hit a field goal longer than 58 yards was the end of the half or the end of the game,” Butker said. “Even when the wind is at my back, if we get the ball to the 40-yard line, it’s a 58-yarder; that’s what I’m expected to make. The other stuff is very rare; I need to be able to dial that up, but the majority of my kicks need to be 58 and in.” Butker did the math, eliminating chip shots to further understand what range he should be most focused on. “If you take those field goals out, the average field-goal distance is like 45 yards; I’m really trying to focus in on that number. Let me hit 40- to 50-yard field goals consistently.” Butker, who is scheduled at the podium today, with a 10/10 during FG period. — Harold R. Kuntz (@HaroldRKuntz3) August 5, 2026 On Wednesday, Butker followed up a strong day — according to Harold Kuntz of FOX4 — with a shanked attempt that went far left. He was asked about his only blemish of practice. “I just destroyed the ground,” Butker smiled. “Coach Reid was reminding me that the footballs are brown, not green, because I hit so much of the ground.” Whether or not Butker’s changed process results in a stronger season will be found out soon enough, and will be vital to the team’s success this year.

title: Chiefs training camp notebook Day 8: The defense has ‘long way to go’
summary: The eighth practice of Kansas City Chiefs training camp was a mild one in comparison to the other seven. After three consecutive days in full pads, the team was mandated to have a lightened practice on Thursday ahead of donning the pads again Friday and Saturday. By all accounts, most of the work done on […]
full_text: Jul 29, 2026; St. Joseph, MO, USA; Kansas City Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo walks down the hill to the fields prior to training camp at Missouri Western State University. Mandatory Credit: Denny Medley-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The eighth practice of Kansas City Chiefs training camp was a mild one in comparison to the other seven. After three consecutive days in full pads, the team was mandated to have a lightened practice on Thursday ahead of donning the pads again Friday and Saturday. By all accounts, most of the work done on the field was basically a sped-up walkthrough, working on timing and the details of plays without full-speed contact to disrupt things. After practice, defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo was able to share a state of the defense after a week of camp. Spags needs to see ‘a lot’ from Mansoor Delane before Week 1 Still wearing a yellow, non-contact jersey, rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane has been unable to show Spagnuolo the full extent of his abilities so far. “We’re trying to be a little cautious with the shoulder, the shoulder blade,” Spagnuolo told reporters. “He was out there today because we only had shells on so he could protect himself. The other three days, with the shoulder pads, it was just really being safe, protecting him from himself because we don’t want to set him back.” “He did a good job,” Spaguolo noted. “You saw him in and out of huddles, getting everything mentally, trying to keep the conditioning up. We’ll see where we are tomorrow, because we put the pads back on.” The defensive coach was asked what he needs to see from Delane before the team takes the field against the Denver Broncos in Week 1. “A lot,” Spagnuolo said. “We just haven’t had the work; you go through OTAs, and it’s just helmets. The thing he’s missing right now is the continuity with a bunch of guys that are new to him; everybody’s new, so we’re going to have to fight through that; before you know, we’re going to be lining up against Denver. Hopefully we can get him back quicker than we thought.” Peter Woods has ‘a ways to go’ When asked about rookie defensive tackle Peter Woods, Spagnuolo excitedly tried to describe the good things he has put on display at camp. “That’s the way they’re supposed to look, right?” Spagnuolo asked the media. “I think he has a ways to go,” he continued. “Some of these younger guys aren’t really used to the way we do things, and that’s for all the rookies. Pete’s right in there with that crew, but when he does get his feet right, he does keep his pad level low; he’s a pretty good football player. It’s our job to get him to do that every down, and he’s a willing guy. I like him; he’s a smart, good football player.” Regardless of how much Woods still has to pick up as an NFL player, Spagnuolo admits that the interior positions may be better set up for a young, learning player to make an impact. “It’s pretty well defined as what an inside guy does as a three-technique or an A-gap tackle,” Spaguolo acknowledged. “We’ve got a few multiple things we’re looking at, so I think Pete’s learning some things that maybe he didn’t do before, and we’d like to find out what he can do. I believe in having as many versatile players as we can, so he’ll be thrown in that same category.” Spags needs to see more physicality and violence When prompted to summarize his unit’s performance throughout camp, a negative day in “goal-line” work stood out in Spagnuolo’s head. It’s clear that Kansas City’s defensive coordinator needs to see more of his defense in live action. “If I’m assessing the three days in pads, I would say we have a long way to go with our physicality and our violent play,” Spagnuolo said. “Yet, you’re going against your own team, so you have to play that game, but hopefully we can get enough of those snaps in the preseason games to see where we are.” When zoning in on the defensive backfield, Spags talked through the lack of vocal leadership compared to previous seasons. He mentioned the loud communication of former Chiefs safety Bryan Cook while also pointing to cornerback Trent McDuffie stirring the pot. “It’s going to take a little while before this group gets comfortable together,” Spagnuolo admitted. “Hopefully sooner rather than later… I think Alohi will be that kind of guy; he’s just still learning the defense, too.” Ending on a positive note: Felix Anudike-Uzomah One day after head coach Andy Reid emphasized improvement in the get-off of defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah, Spagnuolo doubled down on a growing narrative from the week of practices: Anudike-Uzomah is playing well. “I think he’s had a really good camp,” Spagnuolo said. “He’s fought these injuries all the way through; even when he was playing, I think he was hampered by it… When I’ve had my brief conversations, it feels like it’s the healthiest he has been.” “He has been in the system now for the fourth year, so he should know it,” Spagnuolo pointed out. “I think he has had some pretty effective, productive plays, and I’m hoping that continues… Ashton [Gillotte], we need him out there too, but the blessing in disguise for Felix is he gets more reps, so hopefully it keeps being positive.” The Chiefs will be back on the practice field in pads on Friday morning, starting at 9:15 a.m.

title: In Cyrus Allen, Chiefs reportedly see ‘similarities’ to Stefon Diggs
summary: We are over a week into Kansas City Chiefs training camp, which has given the national media time to make stops in St. Joe to take in practice. Albert Breer, senior NFL reporter for Sports Illustrated, visited practices this week and shared insight in an article from earlier this week, emptying out his notebook with […]
full_text: ST. JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: Cyrus Allen #13 runs with the ball during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on July 29, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images We are over a week into Kansas City Chiefs training camp, which has given the national media time to make stops in St. Joe to take in practice. Albert Breer, senior NFL reporter for Sports Illustrated , visited practices this week and shared insight in an article from earlier this week , emptying out his notebook with plenty about the team heading into the 2026 season. One particular note about rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allen, currently recovering from a bone bruise on his shin, stood out: The bigger questions lingering are elsewhere in the skill group, particularly at receiver. Rashee Rice, coming off injury, needs to be more dependable—he’s still working his way back. Third-year man Xavier Worthy has had a really solid camp, and looks ready to take a step. And rookie Cyrus Allen, a fifth-rounder out of Cincinnati, might’ve been the best receiver in camp before bruising his shin; he’s expected back soon. The Chiefs see some similarities to Stefon Diggs in physical profile and play style in Allen, and he’s very much part of the offensive plan. The stylistic comparison to veteran free agent Stefon Diggs is interesting, but it’s also noteworthy to me that Diggs is a former fifth-round pick (146th overall), just like Allen (176th overall). With the talent Allen has flashed so far in camp, is it possible the Chiefs struck gold late in the draft with a Pro Bowl-level wideout? Diggs didn’t reach 1,000 single-season receiving yards until his fourth year in the NFL, but in the prime of his career, he ripped off four consecutive Pro Bowl seasons, including a 2020 campaign that featured him as the NFL leader in receptions (127) and receiving yards (1,535). If the excitement for Allen wasn’t already boiling over, it’s overwhelming to consider Allen as the breakout Day 3 offensive playmaker of this year’s draft. Whether it was Diggs in 2015 or Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua a few years ago, these underrated pass catchers come around every once in a while, and signs are pointing to Allen being next in line.

title: Emari Demarcado is embracing his ‘niche in the league’ with the Chiefs
summary: If you come into the league as an undrafted free agent who is hoping to stick, you have to learn how to do the little things right and make yourself valuable. And aside from one glaring mistake he made against the Tennessee Titans in Week 5 of last season, one of the Kansas City Chiefs‘ […]
full_text: ST. JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: Emari Demercado #25 smiles as he walks to the field before practice during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on July 29, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images If you come into the league as an undrafted free agent who is hoping to stick, you have to learn how to do the little things right and make yourself valuable. And aside from one glaring mistake he made against the Tennessee Titans in Week 5 of last season, one of the Kansas City Chiefs ‘ newest additions to the running back room has done just that. Genuinely curious, why do players do this? Emari Demarcado must have seen Adonai Mitchell do this JUST LAST WEEK and yet…. pic.twitter.com/KiBkQwoeSz — James D Koh (@JamesDKoh) October 5, 2025 If you haven’t seen Demarcado’s infamous highlight, this is the mistake I’m referring to. But even when it happened, Demarcado didn’t make any excuses for himself. “I can’t expect myself to be perfect,” Demercado said. “No one is. I had to let (the incident) go. That’s not who I am. Everybody messes up. Unfortunately, mine was that. “I’ve seen the replay. Bonehead play. You look at it, you shake your head. … I definitely thought I was in. But emotions, I let them get the best of me.” Instead, in the following weeks, he started trying to make a new name for himself. Fans wanted Demercado to be released, lashing out in anger over social media. But the one-time undrafted rookie was on the roster for a reason. The Cardinals needed him. And that was emphasized again Monday in the win over the Cowboys, when Demercado rushed for a team-best 79 yards on only 14 carries and provided QB Jacoby Brissett with a number of key blocks that helped make the passing game go. “I put who I am back on tape,” the understated Demercado said. “You make one mistake and the whole world kind of flames you for it. (Monday was) to set the record straight.” It was Demarcado’s pass blocking that caught the eye of the media covering the Arizona Cardinals , and it’s what’s caught the eye of Kansas City’s coaching staff as well. “I like the pass protection,” Chiefs head coach Andy Reid described Demarcado after practice on Wednesday. “He’s not going to bounce anything; he sees it, he lowers it, and he hits it in the run game; I think that’s important. Pass routes are pretty good. He’s played; he has experience; it’s just pushing yourself through this workload, and I like what I’ve seen the last couple of days.” For everyone wondering why the Cardinals like Emari Demercado so much: pic.twitter.com/8srL6gthUQ — Theo Mackie (@theo_mackie) October 29, 2024 Pass protection isn’t something that came naturally to Demarcado, or as he once put it to a reporter while he was in Arizona: “I sucked at it in college.” But he worked at it, and now, as he battles to carve out a role for himself as the third-down back on Kansas City’s offense, it’s once again begun to pay dividends for Demarcado. “I take a lot of pride [in pass protection],” Demarcado told the media after practice on Wednesday. “I think that’s just where I found my niche in the league.” Especially when you consider who he is tasked with protecting this time around. And that’s not a knock on Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett, but not all signal callers are created the same. Some players are more valuable to their team than others, and you’ll be hard-pressed to find a player more important to the fortunes of their franchise than quarterback Patrick Mahomes. It’s not something Demarcado takes lightly. “To stay on top of that and protect somebody like Pat, that’s a big deal,” Demarcado emphasized. “So I take a lot of pride in that.” Some lessons can only be taught through taking reps and learning from your experiences. And it’s this experience that Demarcado has gained through his successes and failures that so far is giving him a hand up in the battle to be the third-down back, against younger and less experienced players like rookie Emmett Johnson, who, as Andy Reid noted on Wednesday, is “learning as he goes…” “He’s pushing himself,” continued Reid, speaking about Johnson. “You saw a couple of these where he has to drop that pad level down. You go in high at this level, you’re going to get rearranged, and you don’t want that to happen.” At the end of the day, I don’t care if it’s Demarcado, Johnson, or Gandalf standing in the backfield shouting, “You shall not pass!” to oncoming defensive tackles and Balrogs. As long as Patrick Mahomes stays upright, that’s all I care about. And right now, it seems Demarcado has the inside track to be that guy.

title: Chiefs News: Chiefs drop ‘GEHA’ from Arrowhead Stadium name
summary: The latest The home of the Kansas City Chiefs is once again Arrowhead Stadium. Not GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium. No, just Arrowhead Stadium. It has been that way since 1972, so the team “shedding” the sponsorship is not only welcome, but a nice way to pay tribute to a legendary stadium before the team […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - AUGUST 22: Kansas City Chiefs flag team after a score against the Chicago Bears on August 22nd, 2025 at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri (Photo by William Purnell/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The latest The home of the Kansas City Chiefs is once again Arrowhead Stadium. Not GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium. No, just Arrowhead Stadium. It has been that way since 1972, so the team “shedding” the sponsorship is not only welcome, but a nice way to pay tribute to a legendary stadium before the team moves across the state line in 2031. Kansas City Chiefs drop GEHA Field from stadium, return to simply Arrowhead Stadium | Associated Press The Chiefs and GEHA signed a naming rights deal in 2021 that resulted in the name change. But it never stuck among fans, and even players and coaches often forgot to use the official moniker, instead using the name it was christened with upon opening in 1972. In fact, Arrowhead Stadium has become such a well-known brand that just about everybody in Kansas City and beyond continued to refer to it that way during the recent World Cup, when FIFA renamed it “Kansas City Stadium” for the six matches played there. Eight observations from Day 7 of Chiefs camp: Kahlil Benson takes control at RT | The Kansas City Star In 11-on-11 near the 25-yard line, Mahomes drew the defense in to set up a screen for Kenneth Walker, who likely would have taken it for a touchdown in a game setting. Closer to the goal line, Mahomes nearly had a touchdown pass to Travis Kelce, but Kelce couldn’t keep his feet in bounds from my vantage point. From the 10-yard line, wide receiver Tyquan Thornton high-pointed a pass from Mahomes along the left sideline and, despite being elevated, found a way to toe-tap in bounds to complete the reception. A few plays later, the quarterback threw a quick pass to tight end Noah Gray, who scored the first of four touchdowns during team periods on the day. As the Chiefs experiment with heavier looks, especially in scoring areas, Gray remains a target to watch. Jake Briningstool and 4 more Kansas City Chiefs players with stock on the rise after first week of training camp practices | A to Z Sports S Xavier Nwankpa Dave Toub put Nwankpa on everyone’s radar back in June. Now, Nwankpa is putting himself squarely on the radar through his play during practice. He’s primarily worked with the second-team defense at safety, along with special teams. On defense, he’s flashed numerous times. His interception and return against Justin Fields on the first day of pads stood out most. Nick Jacobs’ Chiefs Camp Notebook: It’s Noah Gray Day in St. Joseph | KSHB Quarterback Patrick Mahomes and tight end Noah Gray connected on multiple touchdown throws during red zone work. The first touchdown Mahomes was able to bullet between two defenders. The second one, Gray was able to keep the defender at bay and catch the far-shoulder throw. Rookie quarterback Garrett Nussmeier made an impressive throw on the run and placed it in a spot where only wide receiver Omari Evans could reach for a sliding touchdown. Kansas City Chiefs reveal limited-edition Red Thursday flag for 2026 | KMBC Similar to last year, the 13th edition of the flag displays head coach Andy Reid’s iconic phrase, “How ‘Bout Those Chiefs,” this time on a red background with white and gold lettering. Flags are available for presale here starting at 10 a.m. Thursday, Aug. 6. Fans can snag a flag for a $10 donation, with proceeds going toward the Ronald McDonald House Kansas City. Around the NFL Sources: WR Stefon Diggs set to sign with Commanders | ESPN Diggs strengthens a receiver group whose depth had improved from 2025 but was still facing questions at the top, aside from McLaurin. Diggs, who was born in suburban Washington and played collegiately at Maryland, had made his desire to play for the Commanders known. Diggs attended Maryland’s first fall practice Wednesday and the university shared a video message on Instagram from the former Terrapins wide receiver. “Shout out to my Terps and go Commanders,” he said in the video. “Let’s go!” Sean McVay on Aaron Donald’s Rams tryout: ‘I think he can make the team’ | The Athletic Labeling the workout at the Rams’ facility as a “tryout” was a formality to comply with league rules and processes, head coach Sean McVay later said in an interview with NFL Daily, which is why it appeared on the league’s official transaction wire. “Best tryout that we’ve ever had,” a grinning McVay said. “I think he can make the team.” D.J. Jones says Broncos can break ‘84 Bears’ sack record: ‘We’re about to eat again’ | NFL.com “We can break it. We can break the record,” the veteran defensive tackle said Wednesday when asked about the Broncos’ sack goals in 2026. “What is that, 72? We can break it.” Those 72 sacks were compiled by the 1984 Bears, one of the best defenses in the history of the game. And Chicago set that mark in just 16 games, as compared to the 17 that the current Broncos have to work with. The ’25 Broncos’ 68 quarterback takedowns are tied for fifth-most all time behind the ’84 Bears, ’89 Vikings (71), ’22 Eagles (70) and ’87 Bears (70). Jones isn’t the only Denver defender who’s been confident this offseason about snapping Chicago’s record. Pass rush mate Zach Allen said in early July that the Broncos “fully expect to break it” in 2026. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Khyiris Tonga: ‘Peter Woods is a little pitbull’ “P-Woods, he’s a little pitbull,” defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga said after Tuesday’s practice. “He’s nasty. He’s got something to him, and he’s got a chip on his shoulder. [He’s] eager to learn — just a sponge. Just taking everything in and just learning and growing, it’s cool to see that. Really, all the rookies too. full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 30: Tuli Tuipulotu #45 of the Los Angeles Chargers warms up prior to an NFL football game against the Las Vegas Raiders at SoFi Stadium on November 30, 2025 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Chargers pass rusher Tuli Tuipulotu has had a slow ramp-up period to begin training camp. He has mainly partook in individual drills before working off to the side with trainers. It has been everyone’s guess on whether or not this was due to a physical ailment or if Tuli has not been comfortable with putting his body on the line just ahead of his presumed upcoming extension. Those questions may not be put bed — at least somewhat — after Tuipulotu took the field with his teammates on Thursday in full pads. But Tuli didn’t just take the field, he has been a participant in every phase, including team drills where he made one of the first big splash plays of the day for the defense. Per ESPN’s Kris Rhim, Tuli blew up a run by Omarion Hampton and was rewarded with massive cheers from the crowd in attendance. Chargers are in full pads for the first time today and Tuli Tuipulotu is participating in team drills again. He just blew up an Omarion Hampton run that drew roars from the defense. — Kris Rhim (@krisrhim1) August 6, 2026 Tuipulotu is coming off a breakout season that saw him rack up 13 sacks and 20 tackles for loss, both of which topped his previous career highs of 8.5 and 11, respectively. Entering his fourth season, expectations remain high as the team’s top pass rusher who will now be joined by first-round pick Akheem Mesidor to create one heck of a trio with Khalil Mack.

title: Latest RB deals will have drastic effect on Omarion Hampton’s future extension
summary: This week in the NFL has been stuffed with new contracts being handed out to the league’s best. Specifically, the running back position has been getting PAID. Early Thursday morning, it was reported that the Colts and Jonathan Taylor agreed to a new two-year, $44 million extension. This came on the heels of the Falcons […]
full_text: EL SEGUNDO, CALIFORNIA - JUNE 18: Omarion Hampton #8 of the Los Angeles Chargers runs the football during Mandatory Minicamp at The Bolt on June 18, 2026 in El Segundo, California. (Photo by Kevin Terrell/Getty Images) | Getty Images This week in the NFL has been stuffed with new contracts being handed out to the league’s best. Specifically, the running back position has been getting PAID. Early Thursday morning, it was reported that the Colts and Jonathan Taylor agreed to a new two-year, $44 million extension. This came on the heels of the Falcons and Bijan Robinson coming to terms on a massive three-year, $75 million extension which made him the highest-paid player at the position in NFL history. After a promising rookie season from Hampton despite the injuries, the future looks extremely bright and that feeling only amplified with the addition of Mike McDaniel as offensive coordinator. Hampton’s rookie season, from an efficiency standpoint, was very similar to Robinson. On a per-game basis, Robinson averaged 86 yards of total offense and scored .47 touchdowns. Hampton was right behind him with 82 yards of offense and .55 touchdowns. Robinson exploded for 1,887 yards of total offense and 15 touchdowns in his second season which was the springboard that sent him into the stratosphere of NFL backs. But things got even better in year three as he took it (somehow) to another level with 2,298 yards of offense but regressed a bit with 11 total scores. Now it would be foolish to believe Hampton will have a similar jump from year one to two, but it also wouldn’t be the craziest prediction given the circumstances. His full 17-game pace under Greg Roman and that abysmal offensive line was 1,394 yards of offense and nine touchdowns. Now imagine an full year with Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt at tackle on top of the new system. Omarion Hampton explosive runs (gain of 12+ yards) in the 2025 season. pic.twitter.com/FmQ2HdiXle — Nate Tice (@Nate_Tice) June 11, 2026 Is 1,600+ yards of total offense and 12+ touchdowns all that out of the question? I truly don’t think it is. If Hampton follows the type of path every single Chargers fan wants him to over the next two seasons, the team will be in a situation where they may have to make a massive extension work all while navigating a potential extension for Alt and the latter (and expensive) years on the contracts for Justin Herbert and Slater. It’s good to see the running back market back up and running in time for these deserving players to get their bag, but that doesn’t mean it won’t have its drawbacks for the Chargers when they’re looking to build their team for the latter half of Herbert’s career.
author: Michael Peterson

full_text: LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - JULY 31: Ty Simpson #15 of the Los Angeles Rams calls out a play during the Los Angeles Rams Training Camp at Loyola Marymount University on July 31, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Katelyn Mulcahy/Getty Images) | Getty Images Carson Beck was stellar in his preseason debut in the NFL Hall of Fame Game for the Arizona Cardinals. The rookie third-round pick completed 15 of 19 passes for 188 yards with a score. He also added two rushes for three yards on the ground. His most impressive moment was leading a 13-play, 96-yard touchdown drive. Carson Beck to Jalen Brooks. WOW. @ProFootballHOF Game on NBC Stream on @NFLPlus + Peacock pic.twitter.com/VjnMEP2mIQ — NFL (@NFL) August 7, 2026 Many felt Beck would be a throwaway pick with Jacoby Brissett set to start in a bridge year. The Cardinals will likely be returning to the quarterback market next offseason, especially if they again find themselves picking early in the draft. This was Beck’s first opportunity to say “what about me” and he passed the test. But Beck—Stetson Bennett’s backup at Georgia—was drafted two rounds after Los Angeles Rams quarterback Ty Simpson. Beck’s preseason success applies pressure to his fellow rookie. If Beck can play well, there are no excuses for Simpson. Sean McVay has not yet discussed his plan for which quarterbacks will take the field in the exhibition games for the Rams. Matthew Stafford is resting for roughly 50% of the team’s practices. Bennett has led the first team during the MVP’s off days. We know the Rams usually do not play starters or key contributors in the preseason. Bennett may fall into the key contributor category now, even though he has played a lot of football this time of year for Los Angeles. And should Bennett earn the safety of the sidelines—indicating that he’s likely going to make the 53-man roster—we will likely see a lot of Simpson. Beck played a full half for Arizona, and we should expect a similar (if not larger) workload from the Rams’ rookie. Look at Carson Beck, man!! pic.twitter.com/A6xxh5xn5u — Jon Gruden (@BarstoolGruden) August 7, 2026 Beck set the bar high. Simpson must meet the moment. He needs to prove that he can be trusted with the keys to a high-flying offense if Stafford decides to call it a career as soon as next season. Does Simpson need to be perfect? No, that is never a fair expectation. We simply need to see glimpses of the potential that made him the thirteenth pick in this spring’s draft. It would be nice to see a Rams quarterback with mobility and a sign that a modern prototype could soon lead the LA offense. The pressure is on for Ty Simpson.
author: JB Scott

title: Seahawks rookie vocal about disliking the Rams
summary: The Seattle Seahawks lost a few notable free agents this year, but one of their new replacements from the draft isn’t afraid to say that he already hates the Rams and 49ers despite not even playing his first game in the NFL yet. Rookie safety Bud Clark told Seattle Sports radio this week that just […]
full_text: RENTON, WASHINGTON - JUNE 11: Bud Clark #9 of the Seattle Seahawks stretches during practice at Virginia Mason Athletic Center on June 11, 2026 in Renton, Washington. (Photo by Jack Compton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks lost a few notable free agents this year, but one of their new replacements from the draft isn’t afraid to say that he already hates the Rams and 49ers despite not even playing his first game in the NFL yet. Rookie safety Bud Clark told Seattle Sports radio this week that just by being drafted to the Seahawks, he already has a dislike for the team’s in-division rivals. He’s just not sure which teams he hates more yet, the Rams or the 49ers. Just being able to play the ‘9ers and the Rams, I feel like it’s a big rivalry here and I love rivalries.” “I’m ready to kick their butt and keep kicking.” “I’ve been trying to figure it (who I dislike more) out, I’ve been trying to weight it but right now it’s kind of even,” Clark said jokingly. Yet another day when the Arizona Cardinals are irrelevant. While speaking on Seattle Sports' Wyman and Bob, #Seahawks S Bud Clark was asked what teams he's most looking forward to playing: "Just being able to play the '9ers and the Rams, I feel like it's a big rivalry here and I love rivalries." "I'm ready to kick their butt and keep… pic.twitter.com/Iu57M8aZe1 — Seahawks Wired (@seahawks_wired_) August 4, 2026 Clark is a second-round pick out of TCU and he’s tasked with replacing free agent departure Coby Bryant, who led Seattle’s defense in snaps last year. However, the Seahawks may not have Clark start right away. In the meantime, Seattle still has Pro Bowl safety Julian Love, as well as Ty Okada, a player who had a breakout season last year when Love missed nine games. Of course, the Seahawks also have Nick Emmanwori, their rookie safety last year who finished second in Rookie of the Year voting, but Emmanwori actually plays more nickel than safety. Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald is working on how to best use his stable of players between those four and others. Clark, lauded for versatility, could have a bit part in Week 1, but a major role when the Rams face the Seahawks twice in the last three weeks of the season. By then, maybe Clark will decide which team he hates the most. But the Rams already know how to feel about Bud Clark. They must not like him either.
