title: What are the best and worst Rams trades under Sean McVay?
summary: Since Sean McVay arrived in Los Angeles in 2017, the Rams have never been afraid to make bold trades, but do they win more deals than they lose? After reviewing every Rams trade in the past 10 offseasons, Les Snead and McVay do have a winning record. Could Myles Garrett and Trent McDuffie end up […]
full_text: Since Sean McVay arrived in Los Angeles in 2017, the Rams have never been afraid to make bold trades, but do they win more deals than they lose? After reviewing every Rams trade in the past 10 offseasons, Les Snead and McVay do have a winning record. Could Myles Garrett and Trent McDuffie end up being the two best trades for the head coach-GM duo? Or two of the worst? Whether acquiring established stars, moving on from former first-round picks, or stockpiling draft capital, Snead and McVay have consistently treated the trade market as a tool to keep the franchise in championship contention. Some deals have become defining moments in the Rams’ recent success, while others have produced mixed results or failed to meet expectations. Looking back at the biggest player trades of the McVay era, it’s time to revisit each move and decide whether it ultimately belongs in the win, loss, or push column. Rams-Dolphins Trade Rams receive: 2017 6th round pick Dolphins receive: William Hayes + 2017 7th round pick The Rams selected fullback Sam Rogers with the pick they received from Miami. William Hayes only produced 3 sacks in his two seasons with Miami so the Rams parted with Hayes salary at the right time. Verdict: Push Rams-Lions Trade Rams receive: 2018 6th round pick Lions receive: Greg Robinson After 3 seasons, the Rams sent the 2014 second overall pick to Detroit. The move was purely to offload a draft bust. Verdict: Push Rams-Bills Trade Rams receive: Sammy Watkins + 2018 6th round pick Bills receive: EJ Gaines + 2018 2nd round pick The Rams only kept Sammy Watkins for one year but they turned the 2018 6th round pick into Sebastian Joseph-Day who proved to be instrumental in their run defense in 2020 and 2021. EJ Gaines only played 1 year in Buffalo and intercepted just one pass. Verdict: Win Rams-Commanders Trade Rams receive: Derek Carrier Commanders receive: 2018 7th round pick A pretty irrelevant trade at face value but the deeper dive shows that the Commanders turned the Rams pick into Greg Stroman. Stroman, a cornerback, played in 15 games his rookie year and started 3. He intercepted one pass, forced a fumble, and grabbed a fumble recovery. Verdict: Loss (minimal) Rams-Giants Trade Rams receive: 2018 4th round pick + 2018 6th round pick Giants receive: Alec Ogletree + 2019 7th round pick Fresh off receiving a contract extension, the Rams traded Ogletree away. It was merely a salary dump as Ogletree did not fit the new direction for the defense. Verdict: Push Rams-Broncos Trade Rams receive: Aqib Talib Broncos receive: 2018 5th round pick Aqib Talib was added to bring stability to the Rams secondary. He was injured for half of the 2018 season but was still a significant reason that LA got to Super Bowl LIII. Verdict: Win Rams-Chiefs Trade Rams receive: Marcus Peters + 2018 6th round pick Chiefs receive: 2018 4th round pick + 2019 2nd round pick Just like Aqib Talib, Marcus Peters did not last long in Los Angeles because of the defensive scheme shift. The Chiefs drafted Juan Thornhill in the 2019 draft and Armani Watts in the 2018 draft. Thornhill proved to have a successful stint with Kansas City and became a two time Super Bowl winner. Verdict: Loss Rams-Patriots Trade Rams receive: Brandin Cooks + 2018 4th round pick Patriots receive: 2018 1st round pick + 2018 6th round pick The Rams acquired Cooks and used the 4th round pick to draft Brian Allen after navigating some draft trades. Brian Allen was the starting center for the 2021 Super Bowl team. The Patriots drafted Isaiah Wynn with the first round pick they received. Even though Cooks time in LA was just two years, he did produce a 1200 yard season. Verdict: Win Rams-Jaguars Trade Rams receive: Dante Fowler Jr Jaguars receive: 2019 3rd round pick + 2020 5th round pick The Rams added to their pass rush in 2018 with the mid-season acquisition of Dante Fowler. Other than a highlight moment in the 2018 NFC Championship, Fowler was very hot and cold as a pass rusher. The Jaguars drafted Quincy Williams (linebacker) but was gone from the team within two years. Williams earned all pro honors with the Jets in 2023. Verdict: Win Rams-Browns Trade Rams receive: Austin Corbett Browns receive: 2021 5th round pick Needing offensive line help in 2019, the Rams traded for Corbett even though their initial target was Joel Bitonio. Corbett anchored a guard spot for the 2021 Super Bowl team before departing in 2022 for the Carolina Panthers in free agency. Verdict: Win Rams-Jaguars Trade Rams receive: Jalen Ramsey Jaguars receive: 2020 1st round pick + 2021 1st round pick + 2021 4th round pick The Rams dumped Aqib Talib and Marcus Peters to add superstar cornerback Jalen Ramsey who wanted out of Jacksonville. The Jaguars subsequently drafted K’Lavon Chaisson (2020), Travis Etienne (2021), and Jordan Smith (2021). Jalen Ramsey earned all pro honors with the Rams in 2020 and 2021 along with a Lombardi Trophy. Verdict: Win Rams-Ravens Trade Rams receive: Kenny Young + 2020 5th round pick Ravens receive: Marcus Peters Unfortunately, the Rams sold too early on Marcus Peters who became an all pro in 2019 with the Ravens. Verdict: Loss Rams-Dolphins Trade Rams receive: 2022 7th round pick Dolphins receive: Aqib Talib + 2020 5th round pick The move was to sell Talib’s remaining salary to the Dolphins. Verdict: Push Rams-Lions Trade Rams receive: Matthew Stafford Lions receive: Jared Goff + 2021 3rd round pick + 2022 1st round pick + 2023 1st round pick As of right now, the Rams have won this trade because of Matthew Stafford delivering a Super Bowl in 2021 and winning MVP honors in 2025. The Lions could turn this back into a push if Jared Goff, Jameson Williams (2022), and Gibbs (2023) deliver a Lombardi to Detroit soon. Verdict: Win Rams-Texans Trade Rams receive: 2020 2nd round pick Texans receive: Brandin Cooks After Brandin Cooks suffered a concussion in 2019, the Rams felt ready to part with his hefty contract. They found a suitor in the Texans. The Rams then used their 2020 2nd round pick on Van Jefferson. Cooks actually put together back to back 1000+ yard / 6 TD seasons. An argument could be made that the Rams could have gotten more out of Cooks trading him away as he was only entering his age 27 season. Verdict: Loss Rams-Patriots Trade Rams receive: Sony Michel Patriots receive: 2022 4th round pick Cam Akers went down with an achilles tear before the 2021 season; leaving the Rams thin at the running back position. They traded for former first round pick Sony Michel who produced 845 rushing yards and 4 touchdowns in the 2021 Super Bowl run. The Patriots selected Bailey Zappe. Verdict: Win Rams-Broncos Trade Rams receive: Von Miller Broncos receive: 2022 2nd round pick + 2022 3rd round pick To give Aaron Donald a running mate in 2021, the Rams went after Von Miller who was on a losing team in Denver. The addition of Von Miller was crucial on the field and off – as Miller was instrumental to extracting Donald’s leadership down the stretch. Denver did select Nik Bonitto (2022) and Drew Sanders (2023) via a secondary trade with Indianapolis. Bonitto has become one of the best pass rushers in the NFL since 2023. Regardless, the Rams got exactly what they needed with Miller’s services. Verdict: Win Rams-Steelers Trade Rams receive: 2023 7th round pick Steelers receive: Allen Robinson + 2023 7th round pick This trade was merely for the Rams to not have to pay $5 million worth of Allen Robinson’s salary. Verdict: Push Rams-Steelers Trade Rams receive: Kevin Dotson + 2024 5th round pick + 2025 6th round pick Steelers receive: 2024 4th round pick + 2025 5th round pick Kevin Dotson has become a top 5 guard in the NFL. This has become a steal for the Rams. Verdict: Win Rams-Dolphins Trade Rams receive: Hunter Long + 2023 3rd round pick Dolphins receive: Jalen Ramsey A lot of Rams fans were disappointed to depart with Ramsey for only a third round pick. In large part because of Ramsey’s salary at the time and desire for a…

title: Can Myles Garrett Lead the Rams to the NFL Sack Record?
summary: The Denver Broncos have already set the bar. This week, Broncos defensive tackle D.J. Jones boldly predicted that Denver can break the NFL record for sacks in a season. After falling four sacks shy last year, the Broncos have the record on their mind. But now that they have Myles Garrett, and possibly Aaron Donald, […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - JANUARY 04: Myles Garrett #95 of the Cleveland Browns celebrates breaking the NFL single-season sack record after the game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Denver Broncos have already set the bar. This week, Broncos defensive tackle D.J. Jones boldly predicted that Denver can break the NFL record for sacks in a season. After falling four sacks shy last year, the Broncos have the record on their mind. But now that they have Myles Garrett, and possibly Aaron Donald, can the Los Angeles Rams also challenge for the league’s all-time sack record? Currently, the Chicago Bears hold the record with 72, set one season before their legendary and historic Super Bowl run. If the Rams are going to attempt to break the record, they have an uphill climb. Denver fell four sacks shy of tying the mark, making their goal of breaking the record far more realistic in 2026. L.A. finished seventh in the NFL with 47 sacks, only 21 behind the league-leading Broncos. As far as we know, no Rams player has boasted about the team challenging the record. Even with Garrett leading the pass rush, it’s still a long shot, but not impossible. The most sacks the Rams have had in a season was 57, unsurprisingly set during the 1999 campaign . Despite all of Aaron Donald’s success with the franchise, the most sacks the defense achieved with him in the lineup was 53 in 2020. So yeah, remember when I said this was going to be an uphill climb? The ‘99 team wasn’t loaded with dominant sack masters, because several guys contributed. Thirteen players finished with a sack that season, led by All-Pro Kevin Carter’s 17. No other player on the defense had double-digit sacks. For reference, D’Marco Farr had the second-most sacks on the team with 8.5. If Los Angeles hopes to challenge for the NFL record, guys beyond Garrett must step up. The Broncos were so dangerous last season because, like that iconic Rams team, they had several contributors. Eight players had at least four sacks, including four with seven sacks or more. Looking at L.A. now, they have plenty of capable players. Byron Young led the team with 12 sacks, and Kobie Turner added seven. Swapping Jared Verse for Garrett should undoubtedly help the unit, given the Florida State product had 12 sacks in two seasons. Myles Garrett joins the Rams after setting the NFL single-season sack record with 23 sacks in 2025, despite facing a league-high 139 chip blocks. Over the last five seasons, no player has recorded more sacks (83) or generated more quick pressures (218) than Garrett. #RamsHouse https://t.co/anLo4NHKYa pic.twitter.com/DtTZpK9Yrq — Next Gen Stats (@NextGenStats) June 1, 2026 The Rams are unlikely to challenge for the NFL’s all-time sack record, but the franchise record is well within their sights. L.A. should be aiming for that goal first, and with the reigning Defensive Player of the Year on defense, potentially Aaron Donald as well, it’s perhaps inevitable that mark will fall. Should the team get enough production from several guys, not just the stars, they could finish with the best pass rushing season in franchise history.
author: Evan Craig

title: Former head coach had high praise for Rams and Sean McVay
summary: Former Buffalo Bills head coach Sean McDermott recently visited training camp for the Los Angeles Rams. He joined The Jim Rome Show to talk about his experience. McDermott was highly complimentary of Sean McVay’s operation in Los Angeles. It seemed to be an enlightening experience for someone who will likely be back in the head […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JANUARY 04: Head coach Sean McDermott of the Buffalo Bills walks off the field after the Buffalo Bills defeated the New York Jets at Highmark Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. The Bills defeated the Jets 35-8. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Former Buffalo Bills head coach Sean McDermott recently visited training camp for the Los Angeles Rams . He joined The Jim Rome Show to talk about his experience. "When you get a chance to see someone who is really good at what they do, you can just soak it in. I was a sponge, soaking it in." Sean McDermott on his recent visit with Sean McVay and the Rams. pic.twitter.com/MN3HLjw7UD — Jim Rome (@jimrome) August 5, 2026 McDermott was highly complimentary of Sean McVay’s operation in Los Angeles. It seemed to be an enlightening experience for someone who will likely be back in the head coach cycle as soon as next year. Quarterback Matthew Stafford and others have said that the team’s recent practices are as competitive as they’ve seen . The Rams are performing at a high level ahead of the regular season. Expectations are sky-high, and McVay deserves credit for helping the roster cut through media narratives and staying focused on the mission. Some notable quotes from the interview: On McVay: When you get a chance to see someone who is really good at what they do, you can just soak it in. I was a sponge—soaking it in. Did McVay try to hire McDermott? Well, you know, I thought for a second there the visit was going so well. I’m like, if he asks me to stay, I might consider it but only if I get to stay at his house. I’m done living in dorm rooms (for camp)… It was a great visit. It’s probably unlikely that McDermott would join McVay’s staff at this point of the season—or at least it would be rare for a hiring for someone of this public profile. Whether McDermott is a longer term fit for Los Angeles is the better question. Rams defensive coordinator Chris Shula garnered attention this past offseason for teams with an opening at head coach. His name is certain to be included in the rumor mill again for 2027. Bringing in a former head coach would mitigate a potential downturn if McDermott can’t find his way back to a head seat. The Rams have no shortage of big personalities on the defense, including Myles Garrett, Trent McDuffie, and others. This might not be a role well-suited for a first-time coordinator. Stay tuned at Turf Show Times for updates on all news coming out of training camp.
author: JB Scott

title: The Toughest Roster Battle on the Rams Might Be at Defensive Tackle
summary: The Los Angeles Rams may have one of the NFL’s deepest defensive tackle rooms entering 2026, even without adding Aaron Donald. Kobie Turner has already developed into one of football’s premier interior pass rushers. Poona Ford helped transform the Rams’ run defense. Braden Fiske is looking to rebound, Tyler Davis earned a larger role last […]
full_text: The L.A. Rams defensive line is ready for a lot of celebrating in 2026 (Photo by Keith Birmingham/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images The Los Angeles Rams may have one of the NFL’s deepest defensive tackle rooms entering 2026, even without adding Aaron Donald. Kobie Turner has already developed into one of football’s premier interior pass rushers. Poona Ford helped transform the Rams’ run defense. Braden Fiske is looking to rebound, Tyler Davis earned a larger role last season, and several young players are battling for what could be the final two roster spots. With training camp underway, here’s a complete look at every Rams defensive tackle, how each player fits Chris Shula’s defense, and who has the best chance to make the 53-man roster. Who’s locked into the roster? Who’s on the bubble? Which players have breakout potential? Here’s a player-by-player breakdown of the Rams’ defensive tackle room. Versatility in Defensive Linemen One reason the Rams value depth so highly is the way defensive line coach Giff Smith and defensive coordinator Chris Shula deploy their front. Rather than assigning players to fixed roles, Los Angeles asks its interior defenders to move throughout the formation, creating one of the NFL’s most versatile defensive line rotations. The Rams put a lot of weight on the shoulders of the defensive interior, gone are the days when they made due with their 5-2 base and high shell coverages. Last year, according to Sharp Football Analysis , L.A. used sub defensive packages at a 75 percent clip. The defensive front was expected to provide the pass rush pressure without a lot of blitz calls, 18 percent, second fewest in the NFL. They were also expected to hold their mud against the run, with Shula using light boxes 56 percent of the time to lure opponents into running the football. 2026 sees the return of all six of seven snap recipients from last year, only Jack Heflin (8 reps) is gone. It will be a tough room to bust into for the few newcomers. Let’s meet them all. Meat on the bone Kobie Turner – 6’2” 290 lb. 32” arms In his three pro seasons, Turner has been a steady force in the Rams interior. He’s put up consistent production numbers up and proven to be very durable, seeing action in all 51 regular season games as well as every playoff matchup. Pro Football Focus recently ranked him as the 59th best player in the NFL and 4th best defensive tackle. His 69 pressures in 2025 was second-best in the NFL. Even though Turner lacks prototypical mass and has adequate arm length, his build is stout and powerful. He’ll have problems if opposing blockers latch on to him, but he eludes them with nimble footwork, short area agility, and change of direction. Plays with low pads and a constant motor. Follows the ball in pursuit and a good tackler. Has very good hand fighting skills, a bevy of pass rush moves, and is bursty and powerful on stunts/loops/twists. Poona Ford – 6’ 314 lb. 33” arms Built like a fireplug with good arm length, Ford was brought in last season as a free agent to help re-build the Rams run defense and did exactly that. According to Pro Football Focus , the L.A. run defense improved from 27th in Expected Points Added (EPA) per play in 2024 to 8th in 2025. Ford was a huge part of the upgrade. As part of the Rams interior rotation, he was in on about 50 percent of reps, down from his past work, but that seems about right for a 31 year-old that has spent eight seasons in the middle of a gang fight. His thick build, strong lower half, and low pad level gives him leverage, as well as a strong anchor. When matched against double team’s, he engages from underneath and corkscrews his leg into the turf to hold his ground. Ford’s also sneaky quick through gaps, if not briskly squared up. A power-based pass rusher, best-suited to collapsing the pocket than chasing down quarterbacks. Poona Ford ( @PoonaF_95 ) with the swipe swim. Gets the sack to force OT! #PassRush #InteriorRusher #RamsHouse pic.twitter.com/Wluqm1LILb — DLineVids (@dlinevids1) December 19, 2025 Braden Fiske – 6’4” 294 lb. 31” arms Fiske looks to bounce back after battling the sophomore jinx in 2025. His production in snaps, tackles, and sacks were substantially down. To be fair, he got a late start after knee surgery in his rookie off-season and was hit-and-miss on the 2025 injury lists with ankle and oblique woes. He did however, play well in the playoffs. Wins with get-off, nimble feet, and effort. Strong hand fighter. Very impressive is how he keeps opposing linemen from squaring him up, he plays on their shoulders, abating their balance and power. When he has an edge, he really bursts to the ball. Conversely, his average arm length and relative lack of low mass can allow linemen to stick to him. His burst is not only evident as a pass rusher, Fiske gets through gaps or backdoors in a hurry, particularly against zone runs. His upper body strength allows him to stack/shed well. Tyler Davis 6’2” 305 lb. 31 3/8” arms Compact, blocky frame, his build starts him with good leverage. Davis plays a very disciplined game, consistently maintaining his gaps. Shows the ability to control and stack/shed or drive blockers with constantly moving feet and strength. He generally has good awareness as to what’s going on around him, reacting and flowing towards the ball. A better run defender than pass rusher, when he stays low he is very hard to move off his spot, even versus double teams. Not a lot of pass rush moves, but Davis can be explosive off the snap and strikes a powerful punch. He can pressure opposing linemen when shooting gaps Last year, Davis nearly doubled his snaps from his rookie season and stat production was commensurate. His toughness versus the run makes him one of the “dirty work” players on the interior, he’s accountable, disciplined, and tough. Roster battle: youth and exuberance vs. age and treachery Ty Hamilton – 6’3” 301 lb. 32 1/4” arms Re-watching Hamilton’s film, his work as a rookie didn’t fully match up to his college traits. He did show a quick and accurate punch and plays with low pad leverage. It was his get-off that didn’t show up. In college, his twitch and leg drive were explosive. He stacks blockers well, but lacked in shedding them. Held his ground pretty well, even on double teams. Pursues to the ball well. His pass rush is bullrush-based, didn’t show a lot of different moves, although he did hand fight well. A 2025 Round 5 draftee, Hamilton played in 14 regular season games with 138 snaps. Well-put together frame and tested quite well for athleticism, strength, and explosiveness. Big, strong hands and adequate arm length. Year 2 will be the litmus test for how much value Hamilton will offer going forward. The traits are right, he will just need to apply them. This is one play by Ty Hamilton that is pretty good. They have been playing him mostly at NT. Here in a near 4-point stance in a shade technique. He steps and fights pressure and keeps his legs at a good leverage angle step, then control step, keeping eyes up pic.twitter.com/D35XTWdvuc — Jim Youngblood 53 (@53_jim70721) August 18, 2025 Larrell Murchison – 6’3” 297 lb. 32 5/8”arms Originally a Round 5 selection (Tennessee Titans) in the 2020 NFL Draft, Murchison came to L.A. off waivers in December 2022. title: Trent McDuffie Got Mad When He Found Out He Was Traded
summary: The Los Angeles Rams were one of the busiest teams of the offseason, trading for Trent McDuffie in the spring and then Myles Garrett in the summer, and both deals had players upset that they were changing teams unexpectedly. In the case of the Garrett trade, it was Jared Verse who got caught off-guard, and […]

(Photo by Chad Salvador/Variety via Getty Images) | Variety via Getty Images The Los Angeles Rams were one of the busiest teams of the offseason, trading for Trent McDuffie in the spring and then Myles Garrett in the summer, and both deals had players upset that they were changing teams unexpectedly. In the case of the Garrett trade, it was Jared Verse who got caught off-guard, and McDuffie says that Sean McVay let the pass rusher stand up in front of the whole team to say goodbye. And honestly having that conversation with Sean McVay and our defensive backs coach Jimmy Lake, who was my DB coach at Washington, already just calmed me.” McDuffie may not have expected the Chiefs to under-value him, but he was happy that the one team that appreciated his talent was a Super Bowl favorite. title: Is Tom Brady Holding Back Fernando Mendoza The Right Move?
summary: Las Vegas Raiders part owner Tom Brady has said over and over, going all the way back to last year’s NFL postseason, that whoever gets drafted will sit. Remembering how advantageous sitting, learning and watching were to his early development. One of the key things he said was holding Mendoza off until the team was […]
full_text: HENDERSON, NEVADA - AUGUST 03: Kirk Cousins #8 and Fernando Mendoza #15 of the Las Vegas Raiders practice during the team's training camp at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on August 03, 2026 in Henderson, Nevada. (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Las Vegas Raiders part owner Tom Brady has said over and over, going all the way back to last year’s NFL postseason, that whoever gets drafted will sit. Remembering how advantageous sitting, learning and watching were to his early development. One of the key things he said was holding Mendoza off until the team was ready for him, but what did he mean? Everyone remembers Brady sat his rookie year, so did Patrick Mahomes. Many more quarterbacks didn’t; some enjoyed success early. Others learned on the job and eventually crafted themselves into champions. Some careers got ruined behind a team that couldn’t protect its best player. The case for sitting Brady’s rookie offense, led by the mighty Drew Bledsoe, was ranked 25th in points, 25th in total yards, 11th in passing attempts, 20th in passing touchdowns, 26th in rushing yards, and 25th in rushing touchdowns. Further complemented by 8th in sacks allowed, 23rd in third-down conversions and 24th in red zone percentage. Offensively, they were entering offensive coordinator Charlie Weiss first year on the job. Sitting allowed Brady and Weiss time on the sideline to sit and watch the whole game in real time and talk it out together. An experience which proved to be invaluable when Brady had to take over for Bledsoe in his second season. The amount of mental reps taken while obtaining visual reinforcements on preparation at the same time can’t be understated. He got to learn the game in real time without taking the beatings Bledsoe was and learning the ins and outs of the system next to his offensive coordinator. Patrick Mahomes was largely a surprise pick. During his rookie year, Alex Smith was playing the best football of his career, making the Pro Bowl and the Chiefs won the division. There was absolutely no need for him to do anything but sit on the bench and consume, digest and absorb what he saw. Two opposite extremes, but both solid cases for sitting Mendoza for the majority of the year and letting him get his feet wet slowly. Completely understandable, but there is another option. The case for not sitting him Today’s NFL is a passing league and coaches don’t have the luxury of sitting rookies to learn. Rookies don’t have the luxury of training camp to get up to speed; they now need to be an All-Pro by day 1. However, top draft picks have produced in their rookie seasons and turned franchises around immediately. Jayden Daniels comes to mind; the Commanders finished the 2023 season at 4-13, firing head coach Ron Rivera. Daniels, named 2024 Offensive Rookie of the Year, won 12 games in his rookie season, reaching the NFC Conference Championship. Joe Burrow was the last Heisman Trophy and National Championship-winning quarterback before Mendoza. He started his rookie season and by year two he and the Cincinnati Bengals were a score away from winning the Super Bowl. Andrew Luck is a closer overall comparison to Mendoza, who took the previously 2-14 Indianapolis Colts and led them to back-to-back 11-5 records, playoff appearances and one division title in his first two seasons. Caleb Williams had a terrible year under Matt Eberflus, but with offensive coordinator guru turned head coach Ben Johnson, he resumed looking like the world beater he was in college. He is now currently on the cover of Madden 27. Final Thoughts Whether Mendoza starts or sits, one thing is for sure: whenever head coach Klint Kubiak and the Raiders brass decide to go with Mendoza, he’s the guy. There shouldn’t be any back and forth, he needs to be the guy until he either retires or the day they let him go. What should be the largest determining factor is how well the offensive line plays in training camp. Personally, it’s my belief that Mendoza’s greatest weapon is his ability to process and make quick decisions. Grasping the concepts and intricacies of Kubiak’s offense should be easy for him. Physically, there isn’t a question of who is superior between Mendoza and heir apparent Kirk Cousins. If the Raiders are solid up front can run the football and protect the passer, then, respectfully to Brady, start the kid.

title: How does Taron Johnson playing safety impact rest of Las Vegas Raiders’ secondary?
summary: There’s an interesting development coming from the early stages of the Las Vegas Raiders’ training camp: veteran defensive back Taron Johnson has been getting reps at safety. During the offseason, the Raiders traded for Johnson to, presumptively, solve the defense’s nickelback problem. The former Buffalo Bill has almost exclusively been a slot corner, with about […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - JANUARY 17: Taron Johnson #7 of the Buffalo Bills defends in coverage during an NFL divisional playoff football game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field At Mile High on January 17, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images There’s an interesting development coming from the early stages of the Las Vegas Raiders’ training camp : veteran defensive back Taron Johnson has been getting reps at safety. During the offseason, the Raiders traded for Johnson to, presumptively, solve the defense’s nickelback problem. The former Buffalo Bill has almost exclusively been a slot corner, with about 5,100 of his roughly 6,500 career snaps coming at that spot, per Pro Football Focus . He’s recorded about another 1,000 snaps lined up in the box, but has only had 39 reps at free safety, per PFF. Granted, ESPN’s Ryan McFadden posted on X/Twitter that the Raiders are planning on using Johnson at nickel and safety this season, suggesting this is an attempt to expand the veteran’s role on the defense. McFadden also noted that TruMedia has Johnson with 67 career snaps at safety, a little less than double PFF’s figure. But the overall point is that Las Vegas’ coaching staff is asking the offseason addition to play a position he doesn’t have much experience in, and that will have a ripple effect on the rest of the depth chart in the secondary. Free Safety At least part of the reason the Raiders are trying Johnson at safety is that they have a massive hole on the backend of the defense. Isaiah Pola-Mao struggled in coverage at free safety last year, and Tristin McCollum has the most NFL experience at the position with about 250 career regular-season snaps over the last three seasons, per PFF . After the draft, the presumption was second-round pick Treydan Stukes would man the free safety spot for at least a year while Johnson handles the nickel duties. However, that could be flipped if the early training camp reports hold, where the veteran moves to the backend, and Stukes sticks at the position he played the most in college. Nickel As mentioned above, the eight-year veteran moving to free safety would create an opportunity for Stukes to play nickel. He recorded over 1,000 snaps as a slot corner (via PFF ) over the last three years at Arizona, and played pretty well in that role during the 2025 season. The former Wildcat had four interceptions and six PBUs in coverage, while allowing no touchdowns and just 213 yards in 10 games, posted a 72.5 PFF run-defense grade, and had four pressures and a batted pass on just 11 pass-rush opportunities. Additionally, Johnson playing safety creates a greater opportunity for Greedy Vance to make the roster, who generated some buzz early in camp by coming up with an interception against Fernando Mendoza. Vance, a 2025 undrafted free agent, spent the majority of last season on the practice squad and had some struggles during his limited regular season action. However, the USC product made some noise during last year’s training camp and has drawn strong early reviews from the coaching staff this summer to potentially take on a bigger role in year two. Strong Safety There shouldn’t be much impact or change at strong safety regarding Johnson’s expanded role. Jeremy Chinn held down that job in 2025 and should continue to do so since he was one of the team’s better defensive players a year ago. The biggest shift could be if Rob Leonard doesn’t want to leave Johnson as a single-high safety and opts to run more two-high coverages, rotating Chinn into the deep half of the field more frequently. Granted, in nickel personnel, that can also be accomplished by sending Stukes (or the third safety/extra defensive back) to the backend of the defense. Cornerback The Raiders have a competition for the starting outside cornerback spot opposite Eric Stokes, with Darien Porter, rookie Hezekiah Masses and Decamerion Richardson getting reps with the first-team defense so far in camp. Rookie Jermod McCoy also figures to factor into the equation. However, who lines up at free safety should have very little impact on that battle.

title: Devin Lafayette flashing for Las Vegas Raiders
summary: Recently I broke down the Las Vegas Raiders 3-3-5 defense, and their need for a big nickel. Additionally, the Raiders have shown a big emphasis on trying to fix their special teams unit that was a historically bad unit in 2025. The Raiders safety room currently features Jeremy Chinn at the strong safety/big nickel, Dalton […]
full_text: HENDERSON, NEVADA - JUNE 09: Devin Lafayette #40 of the Las Vegas Raiders looks on during mandatory minicamp at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on June 09, 2026 in Henderson, Nevada. (Photo by Louis Grasse/Getty Images) | Getty Images Recently I broke down the Las Vegas Raiders 3-3-5 defense, and their need for a big nickel. Additionally, the Raiders have shown a big emphasis on trying to fix their special teams unit that was a historically bad unit in 2025. The Raiders safety room currently features Jeremy Chinn at the strong safety/big nickel, Dalton Johnson/Treydan Stukes as a BANDIT safety and FS role, followed up by Isaiah Pola-Mao, Tristin McCollum, and undrafted free agents Devin Lafayette and Tanner Wall. 𝗗𝗘𝗩𝗜𝗡 𝗟𝗔𝗙𝗔𝗬𝗘𝗧𝗧𝗘. ▪️ 19 Tackles ▪️ 104 Passing Yards Allowed ▪️ Battle for the Belt Rivalry Win pic.twitter.com/4geYGiDf8t — Sun Belt (@SunBelt) October 6, 2025 Stukes, Johnson, Chinn, and likely Pola-Mao are set to be on the Raiders roster with Stukes playing a diverse FS, nickel, bandit, and strong safety role while Dalton Johnson should take a free safety position with Chinn/Pola-Mao playing big nickel and strong safety roles. NFL teams traditionally carry five safeties, with the fifth being a special teams standout, and/or a diverse chess piece. The Raiders currently have a battle for that spot among three players as noted above and the biggest leader seems to be UDFA Devin Lafayette. Lafayette, a 6’2/215 pound undrafted free agent primarily played a big nickel role for the Troy Trojans where he logged 114 tackles, 4 TFL, 2 INT, 9 PBU, and 2 FF in 2025 while being an honorable mention All-American and first team All Sun Belt. Lafayette spent nearly 70% of his snaps in 2025, which by far was his best season, playing in the box as a big nickel. That’s translated to the NFL, where Lafayette was a quick standout in OTA’s working his way into NFL team drills compared to just special teams. Additionally, Lafayette has also started training camp with the 2nd team defense in nickel positions playing right behind Jeremy Chinn and ahead of Isaiah Pola-Mao at the position. Lafayette is a limited athlete, but he’s able to diagnose the run exceptionally well (7% missed tackle rate in his career at NIU & Troy), and he showed a good ability to cut the top of the defense, play physical, and enjoys to defend the run. In coverage, Lafayette did a good job staying in his breaks, utilizing leverage, and finding a way to play the ball. 1Q – 1:45 | ⚔️ 0 – 🐱 0 Where you going?? Devin Lafayette comes up with a huge tackle-for-loss on a QB rush for Georgia State to force a fourth down – Troy comes up with a fourth down stop to keep it tied at zero. #BattleReady | #OneTROY ⚔️🏈 pic.twitter.com/dvdKHKJkC8 — Troy Trojans Football 8x⚔️ (@TroyTrojansFB) November 22, 2025 The best standout route for Lafayette may be on special teams, while Las Vegas does have standouts with Tommy Eichenberg, Segun Olubi, and Cody Lindenberg they lack a true gunner and/or flyer (KO gunner) on the unit. Lafayette stood out on special teams at Troy with 17 career tackles and just 3 missed tackles plus a FF. The Raiders will likely carry a 5th safety if the player can push for special teams and/or standout in diverse packages which Rob Leonard will look to run. Lafayette is an instinctive player, and he’s shown the ability to immediately make an impact early in training camp.

title: Las Vegas Raiders Summer Scouting: SAF Rankings
summary: I broke down the 2027 scouting classes in my early summer scouting series, and the room has a ton of potential with a long list of potential standout players. I broke down the offense and defense in articles and I suggest reading those for a broad aspect of the room. The Raiders do have some […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - JANUARY 01: Kewan Lacy #5 of the Ole Miss Rebels is chased by Kj Bolden #4 of the Georgia Bulldogs during the first quarter during the 2025 College Football Playoff Quarterfinal at the Allstate Sugar Bowl at Caesars Superdome on January 01, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images) | Getty Images I broke down the 2027 scouting classes in my early summer scouting series, and the room has a ton of potential with a long list of potential standout players. I broke down the offense and defense in articles and I suggest reading those for a broad aspect of the room. The Raiders do have some talent on the interior OL, and I’d expect Las Vegas to add more in 2027 as John Spytek does. The Raiders will see Jeremy Chinn possibly hit free agency, and they did add rookies Treydan Stuke & Dalton Johnson this last year, though Stukes likely will play a diverse bandit safety role leaving some holes in the FS and SS positions. The 2027 draft class is exceptional at safety, and Las Vegas could really use a rangy over the top free safety that they have lacked for a long time. These rankings are extremely early, and they will evolve over not only the summer but the next 8-10 months throughout the season, and into draft season. Some lists will feature 10, 15, 20, or more ranked prospects but I’ll include others on the list below to note. Tae Johnson, Notre Dame – 6’3/195, R-So Elite. Johnson is coming off a 2025 where in his first year as a starter he logged 51 tackles, 4 INT, and 7 PBU with another 2 TD and a FF. Johnson allowed a 51.7 QBR, is an elite tackler, and he’s an uber athlete. He has a phenomenal first step and continues to show sideline to sideline ability. Johnson plays physical, has elite hip flexibility, and he uses his full body in most reps with an ability to consistently turn and run and take away passing lanes. Johnson is smart, he has an ability to read and react well, and with his first step quickness Johnson can close passing lanes quickly to jump routes. As a run defender, Johnson is able to drive downfield, he’s shown good great tackling angles, and is just a strong tackler overall. There’s a lot of potential for Johnson to be even better than Xavier Watts, Alohi Gilman, and Kyle Hamilton. KJ Bolden, Georgia – 6’0/190, Jr KJ Bolden and Tae Johnson are going to be 1a & 1b all year long and I might end with them just tied for number one. He’s logged a career 135 tackles, 3 INT, and 7 PBU and while not elite production, Bolden just hasn’t been targeted. Bolden has elite hip flexibility to pair with strong first step explosiveness, and he’s just an elite athlete overall. Bolden is average in size, he isn’t the strongest and it does show at times with him getting boxed out by bigger tight ends and receivers in situations. Bolden shows sideline to sideline skill, elite instincts, and he pairs these with a good first step to take away passing concepts, routes, and he’s extremely knowledgably in the backend working to manipulate quarterbacks eyes. Bolden also shows good tackling ability, but the lack of strength does knock him at times, as does average tackling form where he’ll ankle bite. He’s aggressive, which can get him flagged, and he’ll bite on double moves but Bolden shows a high level recovery speed to take routes away. Bray Hubbard, Alabama – 6’2/215, R-Jr Bray Hubbard is a traditional SS but he shows some tendencies to play a FS role, though I like him a lot in a BANDIT role or box safety. Hubbard is coming off a 2025 with 79 tackles, 5 TFL, 4 interceptions, 7 PBU, and 3 FF for Alabama & his elite frame/athleticism works in his favor a lot. Hubbard is super aggressive, and playing near the line of scrimmage helps him avoid being susceptible to big plays over the top due to biting on double moves/play action. Hubbard is an elite athlete, drives on the ball well, and he’s consistently able to take away route combinations and lanes due to his length. The Alabama product also shows good tackling angles, he’s physical, and he has an ability to work off blocks but I’d like to see him clear up his form with a high missed tackle rate. Overall, Hubbard is versatile, and it’s rare to find strong safeties with his level of athletic ability and ball skills. Corey Myrick, Clemson – 6’3/205, R-So Myrick is an exceptional athlete, and he’s played at Marshall then Southern Miss before transferring to Clemson. The Junior has true sideline to sideline range, a quick first step, and elite hip flexibility. Myrick does a good job working the sideline to his advantage, and he uses his size to consistently to box out defenders. Myrick does need to improve as a tackler where he can be slow to react at times, and there’s also some inconsistent angles which will not succeed at Clemson compared to the SunBelt. Myrick’s athleticism is elite, and he pairs that with good football IQ at the position, Myrick tracks the ball well, shows an ability to break and take away route concepts, and overall projects as a long-term starting FS with an ability to play in single high coverage. In his lone year at Southern Miss, Myrick logged 92 tackles, 5 TFL, 2 INT, and 6 PBU. Tao Johnson, UCLA – 6’1/195, Sr Johnson transferred to UCLA from Utah after 51 tackles, 2 TFL, 2 INT, and 4 PBU in 2025. Johnson isn’t the best athlete, and he’s shown some issues at times in downfield coverage due to his lack of long speed and inconsistent first step. That said, Johnson is a phenomenal run defender, he takes good fluid angles, has strong hip movements, and he’s physical. Johnson isn’t an ankle biter, shows good form in his tackling, and he’ll deconstruct blocks well. Additionally, Johnson does show an ability to play the ball in space, and wins with his instincts where he’s extremely smart, able to bait quarterbacks, and understands leverage well to force defenders to the sideline. Johnson is likely going to push into the strong safety or closer to the line of scrimmage role in the NFL, and he’s a good mover in space but limited athletically overall though his instincts make up for it. Jelani McDonald, Texas – 6’2/200, Sr Koi Perich, Oregon – 6’1/200, R-Jr Perich is going to play a similar role to Dillon Thieneman as a single high safety, and the former Minneosta standout could excel in the role. Perich is instinctual, he’s a great tackler, and he drives on the ball well. There’s times he’s very aggressive and abandons his passing lanes to try and make a play on the ball, leaving a big play opportunity open. Perich does have a ton of inconsistency on his film, but the natural ball skills, aggressiveness, and instincts will get looks in the NFL. Ty Bartrum, UCF – 6’1/195, R-Sr Harvard standout, good athlete, extremely intelligent player. Shows ability to play the nickel, strong/free, and single high safety. Interested how it adapts to UCF compared from FCS Harvard. Peyton Bowen, Oklahoma – 6’0/201, Sr Amare Ferrell, Indiana – 6’2/205, Sr HIGHLY instinctual single high safety, shows good ball skills. Versatile safety, good hip flexibility, limited range at times but does a good job driving on the ball and taking away route concepts. Ferrell can rise quickly, he’s smart, a stable athlete, and does his job in the run game. There’s a lot to like, despite limitations in his lower body movement. He’s coming off back to back seasons with 50 tackles, 4 TFL, and 4 interceptions though he added 8 PBU in 2025 compared to 2 in 2024. Other Names To Watch: Adon Shuler, Notre Dame – Aggressive, physical strong safety. Needs to refine his play, likely won’t commit, can play SS/FS/Nickel. Good tackler Marcus Neal, Penn State Keon Sabb, Alabama Faletau Satulala, BYU – Sneaky riser in the class. Great size, good ball skills. Tackles well, will take over Tanner Wall’s FS role and could see a lot of production. SMART player. Ty Benefield, LSU Qua Moss, Tennessee – Athletic, 6’3 safety. That will be the case this weekend when […]
full_text: Roger Craig #22, Running Back for the Los Angeles Raiders in motion carrying the football during the American Football Conference West game against the San Francisco 49ers on 29th September 1991 at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, Los Angeles, California, United States. The Raiders won the game 16 - 13. (Photo by Ken Levine/Allsport/Getty Images) | Getty Images Once a Riader, always a Raider, right? That’s how the franchise treats their players and that is always evident when they celebrate the success of players who enter the Pro Football Hall of Fame even if they played just a brief time for the Silver and Black. That will be the case this weekend when running back Roger Craig will be inducted into the Canton, Ohio musuem as a senior committee candidate. The induction ceremony starts Saturday at 11:30 a.m. PT. Craig joined the Los Angeles Raiders in 1991 after starring for the San Francisco 49ers for eight years. He played for the Raiders for one season before spending the final two seasons of his career with the Minnesota Vikings. Craig made the Hall of Fame, of course, because of his vital role on the 49ers’ championship teams. But he did contribute for the Raiders as he was a teammate of Hall of Fame running back Marcus Allen. Craig started 13 games for the Raiders and he had 590 yards and 17 catches for the Raiders, who went 9-7. And now he will be inmortalzied in Canton forever.

(Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Miami Dolphins claimed rookie tight end Jeremiah Fanklin off waivers on Wednesday, the team accounted. To make roster space for Franklin’s, they waived edge rusher Seth Coleman-Lyles. The move joined the earlier reported addition of defensive tackle Fatorma Mulbah, who replaced injured rookie defensive tackle Rene Konga. Konga was placed on injured reserve in the moves. Franklin went undrafted out of Boston College this spring, signing with the New England Patriots two weeks ago. He was waived Tuesday by the Patriots when they claimed wide receiver Tejhaun Palmer, who was waived by the Arizona Cardinals. Franklin appeared in 44 games at Boston College, including 30 starts, catching 93 passes for 1,010 yards and six touchdowns. Coleman-Lyles signed a futures contract with the Dolphins at the end of the 2025 season, joining the team for all offseason training program activities this year. He originally entered the league as an undrafted free agent out of Illinois, signing with the Seattle Seahawks. He spent time last year on the Indianapolis Colts’ practice squad. The addition of Franklin gives the Dolphins six tight ends on the roster as they continue through the 2026 training camp period and build toward next week’s first preseason game. South Florida Sun-Sentinel reporter David Furones indicated presumptive starter Greg Dulcich returned to practice but was wearing a red no-contact jersey during Thursday’s training camp practice. Dulcich is dealing with an undisclosed injury. Head coach Jeff Hafley spoke about Dulcich’s status on Tuesday, indicating it was not a major issue, but adding, “I would say for Dulcich, just being truthful with you, probably back in that Washington timeline.” Miami faces the Washington Commanders on Friday, August 14 during the first week of the preseason.

I have no idea what KOC is looking for and if “counting stats” is going to win the day. There are daily reports from various sources where folks are trying to decipher what they are seeing, hearing, or reading. I guess it is good for clicks. I just do not see how people who are not coaches and do not know what play is being run, etc. can truly know what KOC is thinking. I mentioned his below in the thread from 08/06 … After extending O’Neill they are sitting at $21,154,099 in cap space for 2026. Right now, the team is sitting at $29,932,787 in cap space for 2027 (according to overthecap) but it does not include the 12M in cap credits they will get from Allen and Hargrave signing pretty similar deals in free agency this offseason. After adding in the 12M, the Vikings will have roughly 41.93M in cap space for 2027 before adding in any carryover from this year and doing extensions (Van Ginkel, Cashman, Mason, and maybe Hockenson) or cuts (Metellus, Fries, Theo Jackson, and Tavierre Thomas offer decent savings). … The team does have some room to do things. I wonder if they are considering extending Addison now? Brezinski made a comment in March about budgeting long-term money for O’Neill and Addison. They took care of O’Neill but the Addison extension could be tougher to complete. Our Fearless Leader wrote a piece here about it … https://www.dailynorseman.com/minnesota-vikings-news/97911/jordan-addison-just-got-even-more-expensive-zay-flowers-baltimore-ravens-minnesota-vikings Some other sites picked up on it too. Zay Flowers Just Made Jordan Addison More Expensive https://zonecoverage.com/2026/minnesota-vikings-news/zay-flowers-just-made-jordan-addison-more-expensive/ On Tuesday morning, the Ravens extended Flowers, their first-round pick of the 2023 draft, on a four-year, $140 million contract. They took Flowers one pick before Addison in 2023, and he has served as their WR1. Baltimore signed Flowers shortly after the New Orleans Saints extended their premier receiver, Chris Olave, on a four-year, $124 million deal. Some folks believe that the Flowers extension along with the Chris Olave extension somehow will affect the Addison extension. I disagree. Addison does not have as many targets or receptions as these two who are the #1 WR on their teams. Addison also benefits from having Jefferson on the other side of the field drawing all kinds of attention. How would Addison do if he was the #1 WR? No one will know which means his agent can ask for #1 WR money but is unlikely to get it. Still, Addison could be worth Devonta Smith money. When Smith signed he got 9.79% of the cap. If he received an extension this year and it was close or matched the Smith pct of cap, then he would get $29M aav. If they wait until next year then the 9.79% goes up to $32M per year. The real question is would the team want to tie up all that money on their top two receivers? Will Nolan Teasley want to go down this route? If he takes what he learned with the Seahawks then the answer is probably nyet. title: Vikings Day 7: Surprises, Standouts, and a QB Race Nearly Run
summary: The Minnesota Vikings completed Day 7 of training camp — their second day in pads at TCO Performance Center — and the quarterback battle between Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy is beginning to look less like a competition and more like a coronation. On the latest episode of The Real Forno Show, host Tyler Forness, […]
full_text: EAGAN, MINNESOTA - MAY 27: Kyler Murray #1 of the Minnesota Vikings participates in a drill during an OTA workout at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center on May 27, 2026 in Eagan, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings completed Day 7 of training camp — their second day in pads at TCO Performance Center — and the quarterback battle between Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy is beginning to look less like a competition and more like a coronation. On the latest episode of The Real Forno Show , host Tyler Forness, who was live at TCO, broke down everything Vikings fans need to know alongside co-host Dave Stefano. Key Points from This Episode: QB Battle: Murray Pulling Away — Forness, who has attended the last four practices, said Murray is separating from McCarthy in the areas that matter most: processing speed, consistency, and explosive downfield throws. Murray connected on two deep post touchdowns — a 40-yarder in 7-on-7 and a 60-yarder in team drills. “I think it’s now becoming a matter of time that Kyler Murray is going to be named the starter,” said Forness. J.J. McCarthy: Best Day, But Not Enough — McCarthy had his sharpest processing day of camp but couldn’t sustain it. “He’ll drop back, he’ll have a really clean process, and he’ll rip a 15-yard out route — but two plays later it feels like it’s unraveling,” Forness noted. Tai Felton Turning Heads — Forness compared Felton’s emergence to K.J. Osborn’s 2021 breakout. “I’m very impressed with Tai Felton. He’s showcasing a lot.” Felton hauled in a 60-yard touchdown bomb from Murray on a deep post in team drills. Chuck Demmings Is the Real Deal — The fifth-round rookie cornerback is winning reps against Justin Jefferson. “He is winning against Justin Jefferson… This dude has the perfect brain for a cornerback,” Forness said. Demmings is a legitimate steal. Demond Claiborne Struggling — The return specialist has logged multiple drops in his first two camp days and was laid out by Jamal Adams. “Very, very unimpressed so far with Demond Claiborne,” Forness said plainly. Dallas Turner Flashing — The pass rusher tallied multiple pressures and sacks during team drills. title: 5 performances of note from the Patriots’ 11th training camp practice
summary: Coming off a walkthrough on Wednesday, the New England Patriots upped the intensity again on Thursday. They tossed their bucket hats and T-shirts aside for some good old helmets and full pads. To recap the 11th session of this year’s training camp, please head over to our daily practice recap. In addition, here are the […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - AUGUST 06: Marcus Bryant #52 of the New England Patriots on the field during New England Patriots training camp on August 6, 2026 at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Coming off a walkthrough on Wednesday, the New England Patriots upped the intensity again on Thursday. They tossed their bucket hats and T-shirts aside for some good old helmets and full pads. To recap the 11th session of this year’s training camp, please head over to our daily practice recap . In addition, here are the players who caught our eye. Standout of the day CB Christian Gonzalez: The battles between Gonzalez and wide receiver A.J. Brown have been one of the main events of this year’s training camp, and on Thursday the cornerback got the better of them. Brown did beat him for one reception during a late two-minute drill — on a perfectly-thrown ball and impressive catch despite tight coverage — but the other matchups went in Gonzalez’s favor: he covered the offseason trade pickup on a downfield target during 11-on-11s that fell incomplete, and later also won both of the 2-on-2 goal line reps. All of the reps were highly contested, including a pass breakup in the end zone that led to a heated verbal exchange. The two teammates almost needed to be separated after the incident. “He’s going to face corners like that who are going to yap at him and going to try to get in his head,” Gonzalez said after practice . “And I’m going to face receivers like that who are strong and come right back at me. So it’s great work for the both of us.” Other performances of note OT Marcus Bryant: With Will Campbell again wearing a brace on his left arm and not participating in any competitive periods, the Patriots needed a new starting left tackle. They found one in fellow sophomore Marcus Bryant, who currently seems well-positioned in the race for a roster spot. The fact that he and not first-round rookie Caleb Lomu replaced Campbell speaks for itself: Bryant is the current LT2, and he looked the part as well. OT Caleb Lomu: Speaking of Lomu, he only entered the mix at left tackle with the third-stringers. He also served as the second-string right tackle behind Morgan Moses, his usual position this summer. The fact that he seems to be behind Bryant in the left tackle pecking order despite it being his college position at Utah is somewhat surprising. As for his performance, it had its ups and downs — including a bad loss to Gabe Jacas in a team period. ED Gabe Jacas: Speaking of Jacas, the rookie did not just get the better of his fellow rookie Lomu at one point, he also took another step forward. Less than a week after his practice debut in the NFL, the second-round pick saw his first reps with the starting defense. He did not necessarily stand out, but did show his size, power and even speed throughout the day (especially when lined up versus the second-stringers). Most importantly, though, the arrow keeps pointing up. CB Marcus Jones: Christian Gonzalez was not the only cornerback catching the eye on Thursday. Jones undercut a pass intended for Kayshon Boutte during the two-minute portion late in the session, registering the first of the defense’s three straight interceptions. Before that play, he also recorded a pressure on a corner blitz. It was a good day to be named Marcus. Other noteworthy performances include Drake Maye, who threw two interceptions during a two-minute period late in the session. On the plus side, guard Alijah Vera-Tucker and rookie edge Quintayvious Hutchins had their moments in 1-on-1s, while Kevin Byard and John Saunders Jr. both notched an INTs. Mike Brown, meanwhile, took some starter reps at safety on Thursday after previously repping with the backups. The Patriots will hold their 12th practice of training camp on Friday. The session is scheduled to begin at 10:15 a.m. ET, with fans allowed to be in attendance again.

title: Kayshon Boutte remains uncertain about Patriots future
summary: New England Patriots wide receiver Kayshon Boutte’s future continues to remain in limbo. With Boutte entering the final year of his rookie contract, he told reporters on Thursday there have not been any recent conversations regarding his future with the team. For now, Boutte continues to show up and make plays on the practice field. […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots wide receiver Kayshon Boutte (9) speaks to the media after minicamp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect New England Patriots wide receiver Kayshon Boutte’s future continues to remain in limbo. With Boutte entering the final year of his rookie contract, he told reporters on Thursday there have not been any recent conversations regarding his future with the team. For now, Boutte continues to show up and make plays on the practice field. “I’m a pretty positive person. I come in every day ready to work,” Boutte said. “It’s another opportunity. You could be without a job. I mean, I get to wake up every day at 7 a.m., come here, do what I do — make plays. That’s my life.” After the additions of A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs this offseason, Boutte was pushed further down the Patriots’ wide receiver depth chart. On Thursday, he said he still believes there is a role for him that makes sense in the offense. But with his first major payday on the horizon, a larger opportunity elsewhere also remains a possibility — something that factored into his trade request this spring. “Ultimately, it’s whatever’s best for me,” Boutte said. “Whether it’s here or somewhere else, I gotta do what’s best for me.” As for what that ultimately looks like, Boutte is content letting things play out for the time being. “I can’t really say today. I gotta see how things play out. I’m taking it day by day. I’m not a future teller, so I couldn’t tell you,” Boutte said. “Just keep doing what I’ve been doing. That’s really all I can do. I can’t control nothing else.” Through 11 training camp practices, Boutte has made several highlight-reel plays downfield. He has split his time between the first- and second-team offense, although he repped more with Drake Maye on Thursday with Doubs sidelined. The quarterback has appreciated Boutte’s approach throughout the uncertainty. “I think just the way Kayshon is approaching it, man. He’s here now. He’s where his feet are at, and I’m having fun throwing it to him out there in practice,” Maye said Wednesday . “He’s doing a great job, and he makes plays when the football’s in the air. And I think he can speak for that, and that speaks for itself. So, I’ve had a lot of great times with Kayshon, and I’m looking forward to us getting better each and every day.”

title: Christian Gonzalez embraces intense competition with A.J. Brown
summary: Competition between the New England Patriots offense and defense is a common theme throughout training camp this week, especially between two of New England’s biggest stars: Christian Gonzalez and A.J. Brown. During a two-on-two period with the defensive backs and wide receivers at Thursday’s practice, Maye lofted a pass to Brown in the red zone […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - JUNE 09: Christian Gonzalez #0 of the New England Patriots runs drills during a minicamp at Gillette Stadium on June 09, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Jaiden Tripi/Getty Images) | Getty Images Competition between the New England Patriots offense and defense is a common theme throughout training camp this week, especially between two of New England’s biggest stars: Christian Gonzalez and A.J. Brown. During a two-on-two period with the defensive backs and wide receivers at Thursday’s practice , Maye lofted a pass to Brown in the red zone as his receiver ran a corner route. Gonzalez, in coverage, broke up the attempt and waved his hands in the air to celebrate his victory on the rep before pointing at a nearby camera. Both players then spoke to each other as the position groups walked back to the sideline, which later escalated into a brief face-to-face confrontation. Fourth-year receiver Kayshon Boutte was among those who separated the two, pulling Brown away. “I mean, it’s good on good,” Gonzalez said after practice of his matchup with Brown. “You know, he’s a number one receiver in this league, going up against a number one corner. I mean, that’s how it’s going to go. It’s football at the end of the day. There’s never any disrespect or anything. We’re just battling and getting each other better. “He’s going to face corners like that who are going to yap at him and going to try to get in his head. And I’m going to face receivers like that who are strong and come right back at me. So it’s great work for the both of us.” The competition between Gonzalez and Brown has been a familiar sight this summer during team periods and positional one-on-ones as the teammates regularly exchange friendly banter. Media members got a close look at the competitive spirit among this Patriots roster when Monday’s practice moved into the field bubble and player conversations echoed. It’s something head coach Mike Vrabel welcomes as long as the trash talk is “authentic” and players don’t lose focus of their assignments. “I think the competitiveness has been great,” Vrabel said on Tuesday. “I want that. I think we need that. I think that’s part of building a team, but then also the line that we take [the players] to is being able to take care of each other. We’re not throwing punches. We’re not into that … But I’m all for the energy and the trash talk and the back and forth and being able to get back and then do your job.” Gonzalez, despite “everybody” thinking he’s quiet on the field, says he does talk a little and acknowledges that his competition with Brown brings some of that trash talk out of him. “Oh, for sure,” the cornerback said. “I mean, this competition is how you get better, how [Brown] can get better [and] how I can get better — the defense and team. It all comes together. [It’s] the dog days at camp … [We’re] about to start getting into [joint practices], and now we’re really into camp. So, I mean, of course tempers are going to flare. Everybody’s hot and wants to be the best.” The 24-year-old added that he hasn’t been more talkative this summer; it just depends on the day of practice. “In practice, it comes out a little more just because [you’re] getting a little more rest in a game,” Gonzalez said about whether he enjoys the trash talk or prefers to be quieter. “It’s moving a lot faster. The speed is faster. I’m a little more tired, winded in the game. But, I mean, there’s a little bit of both. “I like to figure out how to attack a receiver. Not every receiver you can talk to. Some receivers get more mad if you don’t say anything to them. So it’s a battle. You get used to going up against guys and trying to figure out how you can get an edge on them.” Entering his fourth year in the league, Gonzalez is eligible for a contract extension this offseason. Team owner Robert Kraft revealed to the media earlier this offseason that the franchise made an offer to the 2023 first-round pick that would make him the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history and the highest-paid player in Patriots history. Gonzalez repeatedly said Thursday that he wouldn’t get into the details of his contract. He’s said throughout the offseason that those conversations are between the team and his agents.

full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - NOVEMBER 02: Greg Van Roten #74 of the New York Giants is introduced against the San Francisco 49ers before their game at MetLife Stadium on November 02, 2025 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. A free agent since March, the 36-year-old Van Roten has started 105 games on the interior offensive line during his NFL run, including 51 in a row. He spent the previous two campaigns with the New York Giants, finishing both as the organization’s ironman and logging a career-high 1,150 offensive snaps in 2025. Originally entering the league as an undrafted free agent out of Penn in 2012, Van Roten has also been a member of the Green Bay Packers, Seattle Seahawks, Jacksonville Jaguars, Carolina Panthers, New York Jets, Buffalo Bills and Las Vegas Raiders. A CFL stint arrived along the way with the Toronto Argonauts. Primarily a right guard, the 6-foot-4, 295-pound former All-Ivy League offensive tackle has also eclipsed 2,000 downs between left guard and center. title: Patriots training camp recap: Defense caps day with 3 straight interceptions
summary: The New England Patriots were back in full pads on Thursday following a day of walkthrough work. With the tempo picking back up, the Patriots worked both full-field and red zone work. Here’s what went down throughout the session on the humid fields behind Gillette Stadium. Attendance Absent: WR Romeo Doubs, CB Carlton Davis III, […]
full_text: Jul 25, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots safety Kevin Byard III (31) makes a catch at training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New England Patriots were back in full pads on Thursday following a day of walkthrough work. With the tempo picking back up, the Patriots worked both full-field and red zone work. Here’s what went down throughout the session on the humid fields behind Gillette Stadium. Attendance Absent: WR Romeo Doubs, CB Carlton Davis III, TE Jack Westover, WR Cameron Dorner Injured: DL Christian Barmore, CB Charles Woods Limited: OT Will Campbell, OG Caedan Wallace PUP/NFI: ED Harold Landry III, S Brenden Schooler The Patriots attendance list largely remained the same on Thursday as Romeo Doubs and Carlton Davis again highlighted the absentees. New England saw depth offensive lineman Caedan Wallace return to the practice fields in a limited fashion. On a hot, humid day, the defense did see Christian Barmore and Charles Woods depart with head athletic trainer Jim Whalen. Takeaways Defense ending strong: It was a strong day in general for the Patriots defense, but the unit put the cherry on top with three straight interceptions in two-minute situations to end the session. With 1:20 on the clock from the 40-yard line, Drake Maye found a trio of completions — including a strong hands catch from A.J. Brown with Christian Gonzalez all over him — before a short pass to Kayshon Boutte saw Marcus Jones jump the route for the interception. Allowing Maye’s unit to then stay on the field, the quarterback’s next pass down the seam to Hunter Henry was intercepted by Kevin Byard. As Tommy DeVito’s unit then took over, a similar result follow. Facing pressure on his first drop back, DeVito moved to his left before firing an interception to safety John Saunders Jr. The defensive sideline was rightfully rowdy while Mike Vrabel ended practice. A.J. vs Gonzo: It’s been a highly competitive back-and-forth summer between cornerback Christian Gonzalez and wide receiver A.J. Brown. On Thursday, advantage Gonzalez. After a downfield target to Brown with Gonzalez in coverage fell incomplete in full-team work, the duo matched up twice against each other in 2-on-2 goal line work. Gonzalez was on the winning side of both reps, which included a pass breakup in the corner of the end zone to end the drill that sparked back-and-forth trash talk — with the two almost needing to be separated as work transitioned to a new period. Christian Gonzalez with a smile as he recalls some trash talk between him and A.J. Brown from today’s practice … where the two almost needed to be separated after one pass breakup in the end zone. pic.twitter.com/bQBeIOZTeg — Brian Hines (@iambrianhines) August 6, 2026 Campbell limited: Starting left tackle Will Campbell did not participate in any competitive periods on Thursday as he again wore a Rob Gronkowski-like arm brace on his left arm that he debuted in Wednesday’s walkthrough. Without their top left tackle, fellow second-year pro Marcus Bryant repped in his place with the top offense as first-round pick Caleb Lomu continued to train at right tackle with the second unit. That then elevated rookie Dametrious Crownover to backup left tackle. Jacas’ ramping up: Rookie pass rusher Gabe Jacas worked in with the first-team defense on Thursday as he continues to ramp up following his offseason knee procedure. While Jacas’ size and power stand out, the rookie won multiple times with speed on Thursday while working against the second unit. That first came when he dipped around Lomu to register a pressure (and a likely holding penalty) before beating Crownover in two-minute to help force an interception. Other notes: With Romeo Doubs sidelined, increased reps were split between Mack Hollins, Kayshon Boutte, and Efton Chism III. Kyle Williams worked in with all three offenses and caught a downfield corner route from Behren Morton while DeVito missed him on a goal line fade. Mack Hollins and DeMario Douglas caught touchdowns from Drake Maye in red zone work. In 2-on-2 goal line work both Hunter Henry and Eli Raridon had multiple wins while Kyle Williams smoked Kevin Byard on a slant. Efton Chism saw a pair of passes uncharacteristically hit the turf before ending with a win. The Patriots worked their QB/option run game in the red zone. Their regular run game largely continued to struggle. Terrell Jennings was the first running back up behind Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson. Morgan Moses had a false start. Quintayvious Hutchins continues to flash along the edge as he was in the backfield for a potential sack. Jesse Luketa also logged a would-be sack with the third unit. Joshua Farmer added another run stuff to his impressive summer resume. Brandon Crossley had a late pass breakup guarding Nick DeGennaro along the goal line. The Patriots will be back on the practice fields on Friday for their fifth and final practice of the week, which is set to begin at 10:15 a.m. ET. Mike Vrabel will speak beforehand.

title: Bryce Baringer aiming for more consistency entering Year 4
summary: The New England Patriots held tryouts for two punters during rookie and mandatory minicamp this offseason. Neither was signed. Instead, the team entered training camp with confidence in Bryce Baringer. The 27-year old is coming off a season in which he punted a career-low 51 times in the regular season before a busy playoff run. […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA- JUNE 11: Bryce Baringer #17 of the New England Patriots ready for the snap during New England Patriots Minicamp on June 11, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots held tryouts for two punters during rookie and mandatory minicamp this offseason. Neither was signed. Instead, the team entered training camp with confidence in Bryce Baringer. The 27-year old is coming off a season in which he punted a career-low 51 times in the regular season before a busy playoff run. Baringer continued to showcase his big leg by again eclipsing the 70-yard longest punt mark and recording a career-best 4.41-second average hang time, but remained hampered by the occasional mishit — such as a 22-yard punt in Week 13 against the Giants. That’s why Baringer’s offseason focus was centered on one thing. “I want to be more consistent,” he said. “No. 2, big emphasis was hang time and distance. Kind of having that relationship. Just knowing what I’m capable of doing, trusting myself, my process. Like I said, [Jeremy Springer], [Tom Quinn], [Mike Vrabel], they all know what I’m capable of. It’s just going out and being able to do it, and just trusting myself wholeheartedly.” In addition to slight tweaks to his mechanics, Baringer is hoping a new mental approach can help him find more consistency on a kick-to-kick basis. “Looking at it more holistically. If it was a punt that I didn’t like, rather than being upset about it — obviously I’m going to be upset about it, I’m very hard on myself — flip it to the 180. ‘Okay, what did I do wrong there? And how can I not do it again?’,” Baringer said. “Rather than coach has talked about in squad meetings, if you’re in a rut or a lull, don’t let it bleed into further reps or plays. And that’s kind of what I’m working on right now.” As Baringer enters the final year of his rookie contract, he stands without direct competition on the roster during training camp. Head coach Mike Vrabel also praised the punter for his work as a holder and the positive impact he has on kicker Andy Borregales. “Bryce is such a calming piece for Andy and does a nice job,” Vrabel said. “Really, we want our punters to be great holders and excellent at plus-50 punts. If we punt, we want them to be plus-50. That means we are moving the football and giving me a decision whether we are going to go for it on fourth down or we are going to punt. So, again, we cannot take those guys for granted, and the reason when they do their job, you never hear about them.” Through the early portion of training camp, Baringer has seemingly struck the ball well while Borregales has been nearly perfect, connecting on 28-of-30 field goal attempts. The specialists — which also includes second-year long snapper Julian Ashby — have set a high standard for themselves, and Baringer believes the coaching staff continues to push them because it knows what the group is capable of. “[The coaches] have a large amount of trust in us, they know what we’re capable of, and that’s why they’re hard on us, because they know what we’re capable of doing,” Baringer said. “Coach talked about it yesterday. He’s trying — if you squeeze an orange, you’re going to get orange juice out of it. Like, whatever you squeeze is what you are. That’s you. And so, he’s just trying to pull that out of us, which is awesome.”
