title: What we learned from attending Wednesday’s Seahawks training camp practice
summary: The Seattle Seahawks are in the middle of their second week of training camp as they gear up for another Super Bowl run. Field Gulls was on-site for Wednesday’s non-padded practice at the VMAC in Renton, plus we got to have a great chat with Emerald City Spectrum’s Corbin Smith as part of our special […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks are in the middle of their second week of training camp as they gear up for another Super Bowl run. Field Gulls was on-site for Wednesday’s non-padded practice at the VMAC in Renton, plus we got to have a great chat with Emerald City Spectrum’s Corbin Smith as part of our special Seahawks Syndicate live post-practice podcast . Thursday is a glorified walkthrough for the Seahawks, so this is essentially an “off-day” for us before Friday and Saturday practices are public. In the meantime, I’ve emptied my notebook with a deeper summary of what we saw at Wednesday’s practice, along with some extra podcast insight from Corbin as a longtime credentialed Seahawks reporter. The Sam Darnold to Rashid Shaheed connection is legit and it’s growing I would not call Wednesday’s practice a great day for the offense; Drew Lock and the second unit probably fared the best in 11-on-11s. However, we want give-and-take and for both units to sharpen each other up, so please don’t fret too much. If you want to get excited about something, it’s the Darnold to Shaheed combo. Shaheed ran an over route to the right sideline and Darnold lobbed the ball perfectly to Rashid for an explosive play. Shaheed also made a great hands-only catch along the sideline with Josh Jobe (I think, it could’ve been Nehemiah Pritchett but I didn’t write it down) draped all over him. Shaheed shouldn’t be typecast as a deep threat and he won’t be in this offense. Seattle worked on getting him the ball on a screen pass in the red zone, on intermediate-ish throws over the middle, so there’s room to grow in Shaheed’s first camp with the Super Bowl champs. It will relieve the pressure off of having Jaxon Smith-Njigba put up OPOY numbers again. Jalen Milroe is getting more put on his plate Please do not conflate the sub-headline with the idea that he’s set to even overtake Drew Lock on the depth chart this season. What I mean by that is Milroe is not predominantly parked in shotgun and throwing to guys who have no functional shot to make the roster. Brian Fleury has Milroe getting plays in with Elijah Arroyo and Jadarian Price, who have worked with the first- through third-team offense. We’ll be here for two more practices, so I’ll have a more definitive assessment on his performances after Saturday. Any thought of the Milroe package returning this year is contingent on Milroe being a threat as a passer. Brian Fleury all but hinted at that in his press conference on Tuesday. What I’m looking for in preseason is for Milroe to maybe get a few snaps with the second-team offense and to show enough for the staff to be confident that, if he has the odd snap in a regular season game, it is not an immediate tell that it’s just a QB run or option play. Pass protection is a work in progress for the non-George Holani running backs Seattle’s pass pro standouts at the running back position are George Holani (whom Corbin called ‘Furious George’ for his style) and Zach Charbonnet. One of these guys is not playing for another several weeks. Jadarian Price, Emanuel Wilson, and Velus Jones Jr collectively are not as good as either Holani or Charbonnet in pass pro. Price has a lot of time on his side to get better but I noticed how much Thomas Hammock was coaching him up during pass pro drills and having him re-do his reps. The lack of history of pass pro and pass catching at Notre Dame means Price still has a lot to learn. Velus Jones is a receiver/running back hybrid so a lot of this is new to him. Wilson is probably okay without being outstanding. I think that RB pass pro is a reasonable concern for Seattle to have entering the regular season, but I also want to see what happens the rest of this week and in preseason. Speaking of Charbonnet, by the way… Zach Charbonnet’s return timeline looks promising We saw Zach Charbonnet at practice not just walking normally, but also doing some ramp-up activities like one-legged jumping. One of Corbin’s tidbits from last night’s show was telling us that Charbonnet is both walking and running “perfectly normal” and from what he’s seen, he believes Charbonnet will be off PUP and ready to play Week 5 against the San Francisco 49ers. The important thing to note about the PUP list this year is that players can now have their practice window open up as early as the start of Week 3 instead of Week 4, so that will be the litmus test for Charbonnet’s readiness. It’s going to come down to the wire for that sixth wide receiver spot I believe the Seahawks will roster six wide receivers this season. We can checkmark Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Tory Horton, Rashid Shaheed, Cooper Kupp (who had a vet rest day and barely practiced), and Jake Bobo as the top five. For WR6? Whoo boy it’s going to be fun. Cody White is Cody White and I mean that endearingly. He’s a workmanlike player who seems to be getting better as a receiver, plus he has special teams value. Ricky White III, perhaps in part because Jake Bobo is hurt, is stepping up and earning more reps with the second-team offense and has shown smooth route-running and good hands. Montorie Foster, whose practice inauspiciously started by muffing a punt in punt return drills, had a few bright moments mostly working with the threes and Jalen Milroe. Emmanuel Henderson got involved a little bit but I think his route is realistically on special teams. This will be a battle that will go through the end of preseason. Anthony Bradford is not losing his starting job, deal with it Sorry if I sound coarse but I’m also being realistic. Beau Stephens is an awesome hype man but he’s still a fifth-round rookie who is currently running with the third-team offense. That’s right. Christian Haynes has been with the second-team offense consistently, and he has no shot to usurp Bradford. This means that for the first time in his career, Bradford doesn’t have to battle to earn his job. If he has an indefensibly bad string of regular season performances, perhaps we can revisit this convo. But for now, there is no starting RG competition for Week 1. Incidentally, Stephens had a big wrap on his left arm (thanks to Bryce Coutts for noticing that, hence he is “The Hawks Eye” podcast host ), which suggested injury, but he practiced the whole way. Corbin said it’s the first time he’s seen it so it looks to be a new issue. Rylie Mills is going to have a major role on Seattle’s defense He lines up as a big end, he lines up as a 3-technique, he lines up sometimes at nose, he is a big, strong, versatile human being whose Super Bowl sack only scratched the surface of what he’s capable of. Mills blew up pass plays on the first- and second-team units and wins with power, hand fighting, and out-leveraging his man. I can’t wait to see him in a padded practice. The one thing I’d say is I back him to be more of a pass rusher than top run defender, but that’s just instinct more than anything else. The camp hype is real. The deeper EDGE depth was underwhelming I specify “deeper” as anyone below Dante Fowler Jr on the depth chart. Aidan Hubbard, Jalan Gaines, Jared Ivey (who didn’t practice), Connor O’Toole, and Marvin Jones Jr are the bottom-end of the EDGE group. Gaines had a nice play in which he snuffed out a Drew Lock play-action and would’ve had a sack at normal game speed, and I think Marvin Jones would’ve been credited with a coverage sack on another 11-on-11 rep. That’s about it. In previous practice write-ups from beat reporters there have been scant mentions of any of the fringe edge rushers standing out and making a push to be on the 53. Corbin told us that Hubbard, “looked like he’s playing in slow motion.” Watching him in camp that looked to be the case. Seattle was fortunate enough to have none of its core edge rushers miss more than a game here and there, because anything beyond that and I’d have some concern. However, this is Mike Macdonald, and he has some ideas… Tyrice Knight, living on the “edge”? It sounds like Tyrice Knight has had a good training…

title: Why Grey Zabel’s rookie film suggests he’s one of John Schneider’s best first-round value picks
summary: The Seattle Seahawks’ first-round history under John Schneider has never been boring. Over the years, the Seahawks have used premium draft capital on prospects who divided evaluators, while other first-round picks have been moved in aggressive trades for established veterans. That willingness to trust the organization’s board over public consensus has produced both memorable successes […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - DECEMBER 07: Grey Zabel #76 of the Seattle Seahawks drops back to block during an NFL football game against the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on December 7, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks’ first-round history under John Schneider has never been boring. Over the years, the Seahawks have used premium draft capital on prospects who divided evaluators, while other first-round picks have been moved in aggressive trades for established veterans. That willingness to trust the organization’s board over public consensus has produced both memorable successes and frustrating misses. One year into Grey Zabel’s NFL career, however, it’s becoming increasingly difficult not to view him as one of the best first-round values of Schneider’s tenure. Background Coming out of North Dakota State, Zabel entered the draft process with two primary concerns attached to his scouting report. The first was his arm length. For teams projecting him as an NFL tackle, his measurements created understandable questions. Seattle, however, drafted him with the expectation that his future would likely come inside at guard, where his technical ability, leverage and movement skills matter far more than a few inches of reach. The second concern was the level of competition. Dominating FCS opponents doesn’t always translate to Sundays, making the transition from North Dakota State to the NFL one of the biggest unknowns surrounding his projection. Ironically, Zabel began answering those questions long before he ever played an NFL snap. A quick side note: I’ve become a huge believer in the value of the Senior Bowl. Maybe that’s because Seattle consistently finds contributors through the event, but I also appreciate prospects who embrace the entire process instead of leaving after one or two impressive practice sessions. Zabel embodied exactly what the Senior Bowl is supposed to showcase. Throughout the week he accepted every challenge presented to him, taking reps at multiple interior positions while competing against some of the best defensive linemen in the country. He didn’t manage his workload, didn’t leave early and finished the week by playing in the game itself. Combined with his decision to stay at North Dakota State for his final collegiate season instead of transferring to a larger program, it reinforced the type of competitor Seattle was drafting. That mentality quickly carried over into his rookie season. Despite suffering an injury against the Los Angeles Rams that initially looked serious enough to cost him time, Zabel returned remarkably quickly. He clearly wasn’t operating at full strength against the Titans the following week, but simply getting back onto the field that soon spoke volumes about both his toughness and determination. Like every rookie offensive lineman, his season wasn’t flawless. Seattle’s offensive line experienced its share of growing pains throughout the year, and Zabel had his own moments of inconsistency. Even so, his overall body of work consistently pointed toward a player whose strengths translated immediately to the NFL. What stood out on tape Elite footwork/Athletic Ability If there is one trait that consistently jumps off the tape, it’s Zabel’s footwork. Zabel's footwork consistently stands out. While many rookie OL are still working through their kick step, he's often already on his third, staying square, recovering against counters and reaching landmarks before defenders can exploit leverage. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-06T01:06:57.740Z One of the biggest differences between him and many rookie offensive linemen is how quickly he gets himself into position. While some blockers are still working through their initial kick step, Zabel is often already on his third step, allowing him to stay square, recover against counters and reach landmarks before defenders can exploit leverage. Grey Zabel's footwork is outstanding. He wastes no time climbing to the second level, takes the proper angle and removes the linebacker from the play before he has any chance to react. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-06T01:08:09.194Z Excellent footwork and nimble feet are traits that consistently show up on Grey Zabel’s tape. On this rep, he immediately climbs to the linebacker, reaches him without hesitation, and—unlike the previous snap—takes a much cleaner angle to completely erase any chance of the defender getting involved in the play. Elite mobility for an OL. Zabel locates his target at the third level, stays under control and sustains the block nearly 30 yards downfield, finishing the rep with the same intensity as the snap. PS: Amazing call from Klint Kubiak — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-06T01:09:24.214Z Outstanding mobility paired with the vision to locate and engage targets at the second and even third level. It’s rare to see an offensive lineman sustain blocks with this kind of control 30 yards downfield, but Zabel finishes the rep as if the play had just begun. Zabel's athleticism is on full display. He reaches the second level with almost no wasted movement, weaving through traffic under control. One of the cleanest and most impressive blocks on his 2025 tape. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-06T01:10:09.047Z Another example of the athleticism that makes Zabel such a unique prospect. Many offensive linemen can eventually reach the second level, but it often looks labored. Zabel gets there effortlessly, wasting virtually no movement as he flows through traffic. This was one of the most impressive blocking reps of his entire season. Promising technique Beyond his movement skills, Zabel consistently plays with refined technique. Zabel's hand usage, balance and control rarely look like those of a rookie. His tape shows steady growth throughout the season, even if inconsistency showed up at times—like allowing two sacks to Kobie Turner before bouncing back with quality reps. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-06T01:11:07.508Z His hand usage, balance and ability to stay under control rarely resemble those of a first-year player. More importantly, the tape suggests he became increasingly comfortable as the season progressed rather than maintaining the same level of play. Obviously, inconsistency will appear, like in this game where he allowed two sacks to Kobie Turner and in the same game had good snaps against him. Outstanding rep vs. the 49ers. Zabel absorbs a powerful bull rush, anchors despite the length disadvantage, then shuts down multiple counters with excellent balance, hand usage and recovery. High-level pass protection. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-06T01:11:50.813Z Outstanding rep against the 49ers. The defensive tackle attacks with power immediately off the snap, but Zabel absorbs the initial surge and anchors well. Despite giving up arm length, his hand placement and technical refinement allow him to maintain leverage and keep the pocket clean. After his initial rush stalls, the defender strings together multiple counters, but Zabel’s balance, hand usage, and recovery ability neutralize every one of them. Areas for improvement Most of Zabel’s negative plays weren’t the result of losing individual matchups. Instead, many of them reflected communication issues that affected Seattle’s offensive line throughout the season. This looks more like a protection breakdown than a physical loss. The left side slides to protect the outside gap, but Zabel loses track of his assignment, allowing No. 10 through almost untouched. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-08-06T01:13:18.861Z Several missed assignments involved double teams failing to climb properly to the second level, delayed handoffs between blockers or protection adjustments that never fully developed against stunts. The left side of the offensive line is clearly working to protect the outside gap, as shown by the center’s and left tackle’s initial…

full_text: The Seattle Seahawks held their seventh of 10 public training camp practices on Wednesday. It was another warm (and, due to the wildfire smoke, hazy) day at team headquarters in Renton, and the VMAC berm was filled to capacity yet again for what was a non-padded practice for the reigning Super Bowl champions. While the pads may not have been there, there was still a lot to take in. Field Gulls was on-site at VMAC observing what was just about a 2.5-hour long practice. Myself and fellow Field Gulls staff writer and host of The Hawks Eye podcast , Bryce Coutts, filmed a quick reaction video after practice ended (from outside The Pro Shop in Renton, we were in a hurry to get to SoDo!) with our immediate takeaways and analysis. Over a nice and tight five minutes, we discussed how well the defense performed, the Sam Darnold-Rashid Shaheed connection, an interesting name to watch at safety, Nehemiah Pritchett’s increased role with the starters, Rylie Mills’ versatility, and the work in progress that is a rebuilding running game. (Update: We’ve swapped in the video to include auto-generated and therefore not totally accurate transcription, so this should be a help!) Check out the video below, and don’t forget that at 7:30 pm PT we will be live from Fast Fashion Brewing in SoDo for more in-depth, fleshed out training camp analysis, with special guest Corbin Smith of Emerald City Spectrum joining the Seahawks Syndicate podcast! full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - AUGUST 10: Kion Smith #71 Miami Dolphins works against Jonathan Ford #64 of the Chicago Bears during an NFL preseason football game between the Miami Dolphins and the Chicago Bears at Soldier Field on August 10, 2025, in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Kara Durrette/Getty Images) | Getty Images 49ers sign former Dolphins starting guard; waive receiver “No surprise, as the 49ers made an official move to add a lineman. They signed Kion Smith. The corresponding move was to waive Colton Dowell. Smith started the first three games of the season for Miami last year at right guard. He was good for the first two games, but struggled in the third game against the Bills, based on his blown block rate.” The Good and Not So Good from Day 8 of 49ers Camp: Brock Purdy is Raising his Game “Absolutely eviscerated the starting defense today while throwing to wide receivers named Malik Turner and KhaDarel Hodge. Technically, Purdy’s No. 1 receiver on the field is Deebo Samuel, but he can’t get open, so Purdy is forced to go through his progressions and fire tight-window throws to players who may or may not make the final roster. And despite all this, he threw two deep touchdown passes today and no interceptions. In fact, he has thrown just one interception in all of camp. He’s making good, quick decisions, and he’s playing with the most confidence I’ve ever seen from him. There’s no question that he’s having the best camp of his career. Unfortunately for him, his offensive line is shaky, his running game is non-existent and his receivers mostly are injured. The 49ers need to get him some help before he gets injured like last season.” 49ers’ Mac Jones, Raheem Morris share Week 3 training camp updates “’The layer king’ has some really intensive intensity, and I like that about him. It’s really fun for me when you get a chance to get some of those call-it periods and you get a chance to go in the back with the offense and you call your play and you get a chance to just hear him operate. You’re listening to him and you’re able to hear him operate and you’re able to hear him operate in a very pro manner. How he communicates with the coaches, how he’s very up front. Today he got fired up, which was cool, which was fun, which was competitive, and I love that. When he does those things, it just makes the team go. I watch that team go out there and basically have a fight for an hour and a half, and then hug at the end of practice and cheer for each other. It’s the weirdest thing ever. It’s awesome. It was a lot of fun with that guy. He’s awesome.” Brock Purdy impresses new 49ers DC Raheem Morris with layered throws in practice “Yes, Purdy hooked up on a couple of deep passes, but the best play was what one sideline observer immediately described as, “Good on good.” There was nothing wrong with the coverage of cornerback Deommodore Lenoir and Brown. But there was nothing that could be done to prevent a completion on a deep crossing route with Purdy’s perfect throw and Deebo Samuel’s contested catch.”

(Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers held their eighth practice of training camp on Thursday, with their annual Dwight Clark celebration happening as the team doesn’t have an open practice tomorrow. San Francisco’s injury list continues to mount, as offensive lineman Nick Zakelj did not practice after suffering an elbow injury on Wednesday, according to ESPN’s Nick Wagoner. That brought the list of players out to 16, as a couple of others made their returns to the practice field. Dre Greenlaw, De’Zhaun Stribling, and Osa Odighizuwa all returned to practice, with the rookie wideout coming off a hamstring injury. In addition, Sam Okuayinonu was back and participating. While Stribling was not practicing at 100 percent, it was a good sign to see him return, and he’s gotten some strong reviews from teammates for his early performances in training camp while other receivers were injured. “I call him the Flying Hawaiian because he’s so fast,” quarterback Mac Jones said of Stribling. “But he definitely is fast. Some guys, you know, they can be really quick, but they’re not as strong. So he has both. I don’t have a comp for him yet, but I think he’ll be a really good player. Obviously got a chance to throw to him in the offseason a little bit, like when we went to Nashville and stuff. And I don’t know, just the way he got to the ball when it’s in the air was impressive. “He has like a second gear when the ball’s in the air. Some guys are really fast, but when the ball goes up, and your eyes go up, you slow down. But he doesn’t do that. So it’s pretty impressive. And we’ve got a few guys that are like that, Jordan Watkins and obviously, Mike Evans is one of the best at it. So you want to have guys like that. And speed is good, but you want ball speed where the ball’s in the air, they don’t slow down. So he has that.” On the field, the 49ers’ battle at left guard continued, as free agent addition Robert Jones got another day of reps with the first-team offense. Connor Colby, who had been getting a ton of first-team reps at left guard, instead was rotating with the backups on both the left and the right side, according to Wagoner. It seemed to be a strong day for the offense and quarterback Brock Purdy, who received some major praise from defensive coordinator Raheem Morris after practice for his energy and ability to layer throws. “The Layer King has some really intensive intensity, and I like that about him,” Morris said about Purdy. “It’s really fun for me when you get a chance to get some of those call-it periods, and you get a chance to go in the back with the offense, and you call your play, and then you get a chance to just hear him operate. You’re listening to him and you’re able to hear him operate, and you’re able to hear him operate in a very pro manner. “How he communicates with the coaches, you know, how he’s very upfront. Today he got fired up, which was cool, which is fun, which is competitive. And I love that. And like when he does those things, it just makes the team go. I watched our team go out there and basically have a fight for an hour and a half. And then I’ll hug at the end of practice and cheer for each other. It’s the weirdest thing ever. It’s awesome. But it was a lot of fun with that guy. He’s awesome.” San Francisco has a walk-through practice on Friday before returning to the practice field on Saturday. Hopefully, we continue to see more players get off the sidelines and onto the field as San Francisco’s injury bug looms.

title: How versatility is showing out in Raheem Morris’s defense during training camp
summary: Under new defensive coordinator Raheem Morris, the San Francisco 49ers defense is still expected to carry remnants of the defense under Robert Saleh, which brought them success back in the late 2010s and last season, despite injuries. However, Morris is also expected to add his own wrinkles to the defense, with versatility seemingly being a […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - MAY 28: Romello Height #94 of the San Francisco 49ers works out during a team OTA practice at SAP Performance Facility on May 28, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Under new defensive coordinator Raheem Morris, the San Francisco 49ers defense is still expected to carry remnants of the defense under Robert Saleh, which brought them success back in the late 2010s and last season, despite injuries. However, Morris is also expected to add his own wrinkles to the defense, with versatility seemingly being a key point of that. As training camp is going on, reports are suggesting we’re starting to see more of that, and Morris alluded to that on Thursday as he broke down the value of ‘fever’ linebackers in his system. “I’ve been making up a lot of terms since I’ve been here,” Morris said. “But, obviously, you know what traditional backers look like: stand-up guys that can move around. Those fever backers are kind of those guys that bring you subtle changes, subtle different things. They can do different things. They can play star for you. They can play outside edge and play, you know, sort of a big nickel. They can get at the line of scrimmage. They can use their hands, do a couple of different things. “We got a couple of different terms for what those styles look like and what they feel like in order to get guys lined up, in order to put them on paper. So, you know, those guys have been doing such a good thing with some of the spinner-type stuff that you’ve heard about. All the unique things that these guys can do, you want to find ways to use them. And we got some guys on our team that got some real unique skill sets. So being able to use those guys, whether it be a spinner situation, a fever backer, whatever the call is, getting those guys out there so you can have those names, so you can be sharp, crisp, and be able to substitute those guys the way you need to do it, I think is important.” Has that position been a staple in Morris’s defenses? “I think that depends,” the defensive coordinator said. “A lot of this stuff is based on how you can utilize guys. A lot of stuff is based on how you get through games, how you utilize those guys to be able to get through games, what you plan for, things you can’t plan for. When you get those unexpected injuries and be able to fill people in in those positions to do different things. A lot of guys on our football team have been able to show that they’re versatile, and I really love that. And that’s pretty cool.” The 49ers have been trying to get that versatility out of a couple of their young rookies, with Jaden Dugger and Romello Height being prime examples. Dugger, who was a safety-converted-linebacker, is seeing looks at both positions, while Height, primarily known for his pass-rushing ability, is being tested in a couple of different roles. “[Height is] a smart young man,” Morris added. “He’s been able to come out and been able to, you know, always the guy you’re like scared to talk about early. I’m sure for you guys, when you watch him move around in shorts, it’s not real football yet. Then you got a chance to watch him in pads and you get a chance to see his physicality and some of the things that he can do, particularly rushing the passer, setting the edge, doing all the things that he’s doing. “Then you get a chance to see a little bit of versatility out of him. So you’re excited about his learning capacity. You’re excited about his ability to go out there and play at a very high level. You’re excited about the what-if when he gets a chance to play with [Nick] Bosa and some of those other guys like Mykel [Williams] that we got coming back. It’s exciting. He’s an exciting young player, um, that we had a lot of hopes for, and hopefully we can meet them.” For Morris, his goal, especially with those younger players, is testing who can be versatile and what the strengths of each player are. That benefits him during the regular season as he tries to place players in the best roles to be successful. That versatility has also been seen in the secondary, where Morris has moved some of his cornerbacks around. “I mean, [position switching], that all depends on demeanor,” Morris said. [Upton] Stout can play whatever he wants. You know, Stout can play linebacker, Stout can play safety, Stout can play corner. Right now he is our starting star, he’s our starting nickel. And him going out there playing at a very high level with his hand usage, his ability to get after the pass rush, his ability to pass rush, his ability to use his short-space quickness, defend anything whether it be zone, whether it be man. Highly competitive young man. Stays angry every single day. I love him. Ge’s got the mindset of a football player, and he’s got the mentality of a football player, and he certainly has the movement and the skill set of a football player. “And then to just talk about being versatile with guys, I think we kind of did that a little bit, switched the corners with DeMo (Deommodore Lenoir) and Renardo [Green], made those guys go opposite, make Jack [Jones] play opposite, making those guys, whether it be Siran [Neal] playing a little bit of safety, being able to play corner, you’re creating versatility across the board because you just never know what happened in the game. DeMo playing inside a little bit for us the other day, being able to do some different things for us. When things happen in the game, something goes off through the course of the game, you want to be able to have an answer. And it’s our job as coaches to have an answer for our head coach when something goes wrong, what we’re going to do and what our plan is. It may not be the right plan, may not be the right decision, but you better have one.” Overall, it seems like the defensive coordinator will look to add his own wrinkles to the defense, be it more five-down fronts or playing guys in different roles at all levels of the defense. And that could be the key for younger guys to get on the field more, but also increase the team’s preparedness for all situations in a game.

title: 5 49ers we need to see take the next step in 2026
summary: Training camp is upon us, and with the San Francisco 49ers, that unfortunately includes injuries, which have come in bunches to start camp. Nonetheless, that provides an opportunity for younger players to step into bigger roles, and that feels like a theme for the 49ers in 2026. While we’ve seen a couple of reunions and […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JANUARY 11: Renardo Green #0 of the San Francisco 49ers defends in coverage during an NFL wild card playoff football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on January 11, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Training camp is upon us, and with the San Francisco 49ers, that unfortunately includes injuries, which have come in bunches to start camp. Nonetheless, that provides an opportunity for younger players to step into bigger roles, and that feels like a theme for the 49ers in 2026. While we’ve seen a couple of reunions and veterans being added in the offseason, there are still a ton of young players who should assume big roles in 2026 for the 49ers, with some getting a bigger opportunity than before. So, who are five 49ers we need to see take the next step in 2026? Honorable Mention: Ricky Pearsall Pearsall would’ve easily been a candidate for this list, as the potential has been there through the first two years of his career. With how the 49ers’ wide receiver core was aligned, it felt like Pearsall and his separation ability were bound for big things this season. Alas, the injury bug that has caused his career to halt several times has hit again, and the third-year pro is expected to miss the season due to surgery to repair his PCL injury . So, we move on. CB Renardo Green When it came to the 49ers’ secondary last season, many hoped to see Renardo Green trend in the right direction in Year 2 after being a second-round pick in 2024. Unfortunately, it was an up-and-down game with Green, who was benched on a few occasions and even had trade rumors this offseason. But Green is back and with a projected starting spot this year, and the early reports have been good out of training camp. The 49ers’ pass rush struggled last year, which ultimately had an effect on the secondary. But if Green can become more consistent, that solves a big issue on defense and could get the 49ers’ unit back to a Top 10 group. LB Nick Martin The 49ers added Dre Greenlaw to pair with Fred Warner at linebacker this offseason. But, as we’ve seen, injuries can happen, and they will need good depth at the position. Insert Nick Martin, who struggled with injuries as a rookie himself after being a third-round pick by the 49ers in 2026. Martin has put himself in a position to start as the No. 3 linebacker for the 49ers in base packages this offseason, which would be a great outcome for the 49ers. He’ll likely contribute on special teams, but if the 49ers can continue to get his development going into being a productive player, that’s a good sign in 2026. LG Connor Colby The 49ers’ offensive line was an above-average unit in 2026 with several above-average starters. But the one inconsistent piece was at left guard, where Ben Bartch went down early, and Connor Colby replaced him as a seventh-round rookie. Naturally, Colby struggled a ton, which led to Spencer Burford being kicked inside to play left guard, and a rotation of Burford and Bartch later in the season. Now, both the veterans are gone, and Colby is competing with free agent signees Robert Jones and Brett Toth at guard. Early on, it seems like he’s running away with the starting job, which is a good sign, but results now have to come on the field. If he can be a serviceable left guard as a seventh-round pick, that’s great value for the 49ers. Playing next to Trent Williams should help that cause. DE Mykel Williams After going down with a torn ACL midway through last season, Mykel Williams is still ramping up this offseason as he recovers back to full strength. The 49ers’ first-round pick in 2025 had some strong flashes as a rookie, showing improvements as a pass rusher while also being solid on the edge. He’s got all the physical tools and just needs reps to develop. Unfortunately, he won’t get many of those this offseason as he recovers, and the 49ers need him to play a big role this season. San Francisco didn’t make any major additions on the edge, setting up Williams for a big role opposite Nick Bosa, and the 49ers drastically need improvements with their pass rush after ranking 32nd in sacks last year. Bosa and Osa Odighizuwa should help that, but it’s clear they’ll need Williams to take the next step as they look to ascend to contender status once again. RB Jordan James On the tune of those young guys, the 49ers need second-year running back Jordan James to also take that next step this season. It’s not great that James suffered a rib injury on Day 1 of training camp, but the 49ers did not make any major additions at running back either this offseason, only adding Kaelon Black via the draft. San Francisco has repeatedly said they want to manage Christian McCaffrey’s workload more this season, but you need a capable backup in order to do that. James seems like the No. 2 for the upcoming season. Even if it’s just playing 15-25 percent of the offensive snaps, getting production from those snaps will be key for the 49ers, who saw their rush efficiency dip drastically last year.

title: 49ers trade for Falcons star in trade proposal ‘that makes too much sense’
summary: On Wednesday, the San Francisco 49ers continued to reunite defensive coordinator Raheem Morris with some of his former players, signing defensive lineman Ogbo Okoronkwo and wide receiver KhaDarel Hodge. Both veterans are coming into position groups in need of depth after the injury bug has hit the 49ers once again during training camp. Morris now […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - DECEMBER 29: Safety Jessie Bates III (3) of the Atlanta Falcons and the Falcons celebrate the pick 6 by safety Jessie Bates III (3) of the Atlanta Falcons during the first half of the Monday night NFL game between the Atlanta Falcons and the Los Angeles Rams on December 29, 2025 at the Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by David J. Griffin/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images On Wednesday, the San Francisco 49ers continued to reunite defensive coordinator Raheem Morris with some of his former players, signing defensive lineman Ogbo Okoronkwo and wide receiver KhaDarel Hodge . Both veterans are coming into position groups in need of depth after the injury bug has hit the 49ers once again during training camp. Morris now has a couple of familiar faces on defense, and ESPN’s latest trade proposal has him reuniting with another. ESPN’s Seth Walder conjured up five training camp trades that ‘make too much sense’, which include the 49ers trading a 2027 third-round pick for Atlanta Falcons star safety Jessie Bates and a 2028 sixth-round pick. Bates, 29, would provide an immediate upgrade at safety for the 49ers, who have struggled at the position in recent years with their young players being inconsistent. “The Falcons’ 2023 signing of Bates was an example of free agency gone right,” Walder wrote. “The Falcons paid sticker price — four years and $64 million — to sign Bates, who was very effective in Cincinnati and continued that quality play in Atlanta. That was particularly true in 2023, when Bates delivered six interceptions and three forced fumbles while earning second-team All-Pro honors. “He was good again in 2024, but he wasn’t quite on the same level last season. Still, the 29-year-old Bates remains one of the best safeties in the league. (He ranked fifth in this year’s survey of coaches and executives conducted by ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler).” For the Falcons, the move makes sense in a salary-shedding sense to push their chips towards the 2028 season and focus more on their younger players. “If the Falcons were expected to contend, it would make sense to keep Bates and see the original contract through,” Walder continued. “But they aren’t, and with a ton of 2027 cap space even after the Bijan Robinson extension, the Falcons will likely be spenders next offseason. They would risk losing Bates without getting a compensatory pick in return if he walks in free agency. So it’s better for Atlanta to deal him now. And while that would mean finding a replacement for Bates, the Falcons wouldn’t be lacking in safety talent thanks to emerging second-year player Xavier Watts. “It just so happens that former Falcons head coach Raheem Morris, who coached Bates the past two seasons, is now the 49ers’ defensive coordinator. And he could use an upgrade at safety alongside Ji’Ayir Brown and Malik Mustapha. The timing works, as the 49ers are contenders who could use defensive help after ranking 25th in EPA allowed per dropback last season. “San Francisco would be giving up real draft capital for a short-term player, but that’s an indicator of Bates’ skill and the fact that his contract would cost the 49ers only $13 million in 2026 — a below-market price to sign a player of his caliber.” This is the type of move we’ve seen happen at the deadline in years past, and the 49ers also haven’t invested much in the safety position. But the fit does make a lot of sense, given that Bates is still 29 and very familiar with Raheem Morris’s defense. San Francisco also still has plenty of cap space, and Bates is on the final year of his deal, set to make just over $13 million a year. If there’s a time to push the chips in, it would be now. But with the NFC South wide open in Kevin Stefanski’s first year at the helm, I’m not sure that Atlanta would trade Bates until the midseason mark.

full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 3: KhaDarel Hodge #12 of the Atlanta Falcons scores a game-winning touchdown during overtime of an NFL football game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 3, 2024 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images KhaDarel Hodge, another former Raheem Morris player, joins the 49ers “Hodge lined up primarily on the outside with the Falcons. While he’s likely nothing more than a camp body, that nugget is important as it would allow De’Zhaun Stribling, or maybe Deebo Samuel, or whichever player they want to focus on getting more slot reps. It’s going to be a critical couple of weeks for players like Jacob Cowing and Junior Bergen. Both are fighting for that final roster spot at wideout. They’ll need to show they can win inside and outside. It shouldn’t be ruled out that if both excel, Christian Kirk might be the odd man out, even if it’s because of an injury. It also helps, in Cowing’s case, that he has the upper hand at punt returner — for now, at least.” 49ers’ Dre Greenlaw opens up on lost season with Broncos: ‘Fighting demons left and right’ (paywall) “I don’t blame anything on the Broncos,” he said. “Coming off the Achilles and the calf (injuries), I just wasn’t in the shape that I needed to be to go out there with them and give it all I got. I should have taken it slow. (But) naturally, they’d just paid me, so that’s all I wanted to do — go show them what I could do. And it bit me in the ass, the second day I got there.” Similarly, Greenlaw owns his failure to master Joseph’s scheme. “I know what I could have done better, as far as being in that film,” he said. “That’s where I feel like I let myself and everybody down.” …“Dre, he grew up different, and I always felt like he thrived in San Francisco because he had the right group of people who he trusted,” Al-Shaair said. “When you’re used to doing things the same way for so long, and you’ve been exposed to that gold standard, it’s tough to break that — even if you go to a building where people are good at what they do.” 49ers interim head coach Chris Foerster shares Week 3 training camp updates “It seems like we’re very healthy. I mean, we have injuries. We have dings and bumps and bruises, and guys are missing practices. It’s yet to come up in anything I’ve heard. Doesn’t mean it hasn’t been discussed, but, shoot, I think it will be plenty. If you’re two deep at every position, you can practice. You can always adjust with the threes, one, two, threes. Threes are hard to stay healthy through the course of training camp, if you’re practicing football hard. If you’re not practicing football hard, you can get through camp easily without injuries, a couple muscles here and there. But if you’re practicing hitting, contact, style of football, whatever it is. So, yeah, that’s not come up at this point.” 49ers signing Ogbo Okoronkwo to bolster pass rush depth “Okoronkwo’s 2025 campaign was cut short after he suffered a season-ending triceps tear in Week 4. His last full season came in 2024 with the Browns, when he totaled 23 tackles, five tackles for loss, three sacks, and one forced fumble. Over two seasons in Cleveland, he recorded 7.5 sacks. His most productive season came in 2022 with the Texans, when he posted career highs with 44 tackles and five sacks. Across 81 career games (13 starts), Okoronkwo has compiled 132 tackles, 17 sacks, four forced fumbles, one fumble recovery, and four passes defensed.” The Good and Not So Good from Day 7 of 49ers Camp: Bosa and Greenlaw Miss a Day “By far the most physically gifted quarterback on the roster even though he’s the smallest quarterback on the roster. He’s just so quick and difficult to contain in the pocket, which is important for the 49ers, because they don’t provide much of a pocket. And when it’s time to throw, Purdy is making outstanding decisions with the ball. He hasn’t forced a pass into coverage in more than a week. Unfortunately for him, his best receiver remains his running back, and his best wide receiver currently is Jordan Watkins….Now that Mike Evans, Ricky Pearsall and Jacob Cowing are injured, the 49ers’ top-three healthy wide receivers on the depth chart are Demarcus Robinson, Deebo Samuel and Jordan Watkins. And today, the best of those three clearly was Watkins, who caught a deep touchdown pass from Purdy during 11-on-11s. Of these three healthy wide receivers, Watkins is the youngest, the fastest, the quickest, and the best route runner. He can beat you with a quick slant or a post over the top. The only area of the field where he struggles is over the middle, because he’s not particularly big. Still, he’s improving.” ESPN proposes 49ers trade for All-Pro safety Jessie Bates “They would risk losing Bates without getting a compensatory pick in return if he walks in free agency,” Walder added. “So it’s better for Atlanta to deal him now….San Francisco would be giving up real draft capital for a short-term player, but that’s an indicator of Bates’ skill and the fact that his contract would cost the 49ers only $13 million in 2026 — a below-market price to sign a player of his caliber,” Walder wrote.” Early 49ers training camp trends: CB, LB groups look fierce; DE already an issue (paywall) “ Thanks to newcomers Jack Jones, Nate Hobbs and rookie Ephesians Prysock, it’s a deep group. And it’s a group that’s being allowed to play to its feisty strength. The biggest critique of San Francisco’s defense in recent years is that it’s been too static and predictable. Robert Saleh, who implemented the system in 2017, preferred to keep things simple because he wanted his players to be fast and aggressive. ….A more aggressive style of cornerback play has been apparent in the first few practices. It’s a style that seems to fit starters Deommodore Lenoir, Renardo Green and Upton Stout, all of whom see themselves as “dogs” on defense. (Well, Lenoir sees himself as a hyena, which is doglike.)”

title: Cam Ward 2026 passing yards: What’s a success for Titans QB?
summary: Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward is expected to take a sizable step forward as a sophomore. After an impressive rookie season despite lackluster surroundings, the Titans bet big on Ward this offseason. They invested in his development by hiring Brian Daboll as his OC, and adding Wan’Dale Robinson and Carnell Tate at wide receiver. Ward […]
full_text: Jun 16, 2026; Nashville, TN, USA; Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward (1) talks with the media post practice during day 1 of mini-camp at Vanderbilt Health Football Center. Mandatory Credit: Steve Roberts-Imagn Images | Steve Roberts-Imagn Images Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward is expected to take a sizable step forward as a sophomore. After an impressive rookie season despite lackluster surroundings, the Titans bet big on Ward this offseason. They invested in his development by hiring Brian Daboll as his OC, and adding Wan’Dale Robinson and Carnell Tate at wide receiver. Ward finished his rookie season with 3,169 passing yards, 15 touchdowns, and seven interceptions. Ward had two head coaches (Brian Callahan and Mike McCoy) and two play callers (Callahan and Mike McCoy). His top wide receivers were fourth-round rookies Chimere Dike and Elic Ayomanor. Ward finished his rookie season ranked 17th in passing yards. The No. 1 overall pick likely would have been 16th had he not injured his shoulder on the first series of the Week 18 regular season finale. With a massive sophomore campaign looming, how many passing yards would you consider a success for Ward in 2026? The theme of OTAs and minicamp was that Ward apparently struggled . He’s learning Daboll’s offense while figuring out how to test tight throwing windows. Ward was better at minicamp than OTAs, proving he’s growing in Daboll’s scheme. We’re now underway at training camp, where he’s had mostly positive practices to date. Ward should aim for about 3,500 passing yards in 2026. That total would have placed 13th in the league last season ahead of Jordan Love and Aaron Rodgers. If Ward starts all 17 games, he’d just need to average roughly 206 passing yards per game to reach 3,500. Titans fans are hoping Ward takes a Drake Maye or Caleb Williams-like sophomore step. Maye finished fourth in passing yards last season with 4,394. Williams was seventh with 3,942. Perhaps Ward can flirt with 4,000 passing yards if he really thrives in Daboll’s system. Expectations are high for Ward as a sophomore. About 3,500+ passing yards would signal a success. Hopefully Ward establishes himself as the Titans’ franchise quarterback in 2026.

(Photo by Greg Fiume/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Daily Slop – 7 August 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Last Man Standig (paywall) What the Stefon Diggs signing says about Adam Peters in Year 3 Washington’s latest move isn’t just about adding another accomplished receiver. It suggests the Commanders’ GM has refined his approach after seeing how uncertainty can carry real football costs. All-Pro receiver Terry McLaurin. Depending on your perspective, Peters won that negotiation. Washington eventually reached an agreement on terms that, while setting up the 30-year-old McLaurin with a lucrative payday, were largely favorable to the organization. But there was another cost to that victory. McLaurin remained away from the team beginning during the spring offseason program and continuing through training camp. Tension from the standoff was felt daily in the team facility and all around the Beltway. Valuable practice time with Daniels entering his second season was lost. Then, after finally returning, McLaurin suffered an injury that sidelined him for seven games. When paired with McLaurin, Diggs provides Daniels with another proven target capable of punishing defenses that focus extra attention on Washington’s No. 1 receiver. If McLaurin misses time again, the Commanders now have someone who can approximate the responsibilities of a top option rather than forcing an entire committee into roles they may not be suited for. Should Father Time finally decide to wrestle Diggs into submission, Washington can pivot to its other viable options. For more from Ben Standig, click here The Athletic (paywall) Commanders takeaways after 6 practices Trey Amos still hasn’t returned to the field after suffering a fractured fibula in early November, which leaves him little time to get back into football shape for the season once he’s medically cleared. Washington brought in veteran Rasul Douglas for additional help, and recently signed Fabian Moreau following Ahkello Witherspoon’s abrupt retirement. But given the Commanders’ defensive shortcomings in recent years, it’s fair to wonder if that’s enough. Quinn never publicly tabbed one player to wear the green dot; he repeatedly said it would depend on the defensive package on the field and who seemed most comfortable in the role. He also said it could be a linebacker or a defensive back. After a week of camp, the primary guy has been Frankie Luvu. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders.com Hail Mail | Kaytron Allen is a bowling ball @A_Smith_FS: Will JCM operate as the “lead” back? Or will White see a 50/50 split? @FantasyTags: What do you think the running back split looks like this season if both JCM & Rachaad stay healthy? That’s an interesting question, and I think there are a few factors at play here. Jacory Croskey-Merritt has burst and the ability to make explosive plays; Rachaad White is a fun addition as a pass-catcher; Kaytron Allen is your physical battering ram that can pick up the tough yards; and Jeremy McNichols can do a little of all three. There’s also Jerome Ford and Robert Henry Jr., who have flashed, but you can only keep so many players on the roster. I think labeling any player as the lead back right now and giving them most of the carries would somewhat hamstring the position group’s potential, because all of these guys can help you in games. However, I also believe there is a chance for Croskey-Merritt to take a leading role if he keeps showing improvement. I think the Commanders have been pushing him to show that, and to his credit, he has done so over the past week. The Commanders don’t just hand jobs to people; rather, they make them earn it. Croskey-Merritt has so much potential, and if he keeps standing out, I could see a world where he is their lead back. For now, however, I think the running back room will operate as The Avengers rather than Superman and Friends. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated Winners and Losers From the Commanders’ First Week of Training Camp Winner: Luke McCaffrey Luke McCaffrey came to Commanders camp with the idea that the WR2 role was wide open and available to the player who was willing to take it. And that is just what he has done: play like he is trying to take that role. Of course, his case is built on several productive practices rather than one isolated catch or touchdown, even though he has had a few of those as well. McCaffrey has used the first week of camp to earn greater leverage and a stronger claim to more consistent offensive opportunities this season. While Stefon Diggs being signed all but killed any chance he has at WR2, his argument for WR3 is strong. Loser: The Kicking Competition Jake Moody and Drew Stevens entered camp without meaningful separation after ending minicamp 6-for-6 on the last day and initially matched one another through perfect kicking sessions the first few days of camp. The two have had some misses of late, which has left the competition without either kicker building any amount of momentum or giving Washington a clearer answer in the process. The competition has failed to deliver to this point as it sits pretty much in the same place it began a week ago. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Riggo’s Rag Commanders’ Antonio Williams quietly struck gold with the Stefon Diggs signing [T]he tide turned last season with Diggs. He reportedly emerged as a strong leader and mentor last season on the New England Patriots, emerging as the model teammate and barely putting a foot wrong. If the same player shows up in Washington, Williams would be wise to hang on his every word. Williams has the talent. He now has two top-level performers in Diggs and Terry McLaurin to lean on for advice, counsel, and some extra nuances that can help take his game to another level. Learning behind Diggs could be a blessing in disguise for Williams. It means he won’t be forced into a role beyond his present-day capabilities in his first NFL season, and he’ll be able to develop with patience and grace under Washington’s coaching staff. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders Roundtable Jayden Daniels has drawn consistent praise in training camp With a chance to quiet critics, Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels may be doing exactly that ahead of the start of the preseason slate. Redzone reps were the theme of the Commanders’ first few practices of training camp with a chance to evaluate both sides of the ball, such as rookie linebacker Sonny Styles making his presence felt with plays against running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt at the goal line in consecutive days. While new edge rusher Odafe Oweh has been hard to ignore while rookie wide receiver Antonio Williams has drawn praise for being fluid in his route tree, Daniels has remained a constant among the early takeaways. In Monday’s first padded practice of training camp, Daniels flashed his zip and accuracy inside the 20 after finding Terry McLaurin among others in the back of the end zone. Day two provided more of the same as Daniels once again connected with McLaurin on a beautiful throw that sailed just over the shoulder of cornerback Mike Sainristil, a play that drew praise. title: Analyzing storylines from first set of Commanders padded practices
summary: The addition of Stefon Diggs on Wednesday is the big news of the week, but there are still plenty of other Commanders storylines to cover. Washington players were in pads for the first time Monday, and the team responded with their best practice of camp thus far. The players went without pads on Tuesday before […]
full_text: The addition of Stefon Diggs on Wednesday is the big news of the week , but there are still plenty of other Commanders storylines to cover. Washington players were in pads for the first time Monday, and the team responded with their best practice of camp thus far. The players went without pads on Tuesday before suiting up again on a rainy Wednesday . There was a lot to cover in those three days. Key Commanders players look sharp early The 2025 season did not go according to plan for many of the Washington Commanders’ star players. Quarterback Jayden Daniels battled injuries and inconsistent play, receiver Terry McLaurin sat out a good portion of training camp while missing time in the regular season due to injury, and future Hall of Famer Bobby Wagner’s play fell off substantially. Monday’s practice was a big step towards putting last year’s disappointing season behind them and moving forward with a new attitude and energy. Daniels started the week sharp, throwing a dot to tight end Chig Okonkwo in the back of the end zone and following it up with a pinpoint fade to McLaurin. Daniels looked in control of the new offense, and before Monday’s practice, Dan Quinn said he is “ further ahead ” with the new scheme than Quinn imagined he would be at this point. Daniels stayed hot on Tuesday, slinging the ball with a quick release, and looked sharp all three days. TERRY MCLAURIN AND 1 😱 via @BleedinBnG pic.twitter.com/LN7a14t7BO — Outta Pocket with RGIII (@OuttaPocketRG3) August 3, 2026 Today is by far the best the offense has looked. Specifically Jayden. He’s processing and delivering really well #RaiseHail — Denton Day (D-Day) (@TheDentonDay) August 5, 2026 McLaurin did his part, hauling in the throw on the corner and looking like his old self. Rookie linebacker Sonny Styles also met early first-round expectations when the pads came on Monday and made a splash play of his own to start the first padded practice. He also had another to finish the session Wednesday. Just sipping coffee and watching Sonny Styles be a grown ass man This dude is going to be a stud pic.twitter.com/bqrihq31wp — Will Compton (@_willcompton) August 4, 2026 Sonny Styles closed practice with a big pop on Jacory Croskey-Merritt in a goal-line drill. Was hard to see from our vantage point so saw Jeremy Reaves in the scrum and celebrating so wondered if he made the pop. “No, that was all Sonny,” he said. — John Keim (@john_keim) August 5, 2026 Sam Cosmi was bringing it on Monday as well, driving defenders off the ball, he followed it with a rest day on Tuesday before returning Wednesday. Everyone expects these names to play well, but it is always a welcome sight for key players to perform at a high level. Many have noted that Daniels looks sharper in camp this year than the last two. How will the linebacker room shake out this season? One of the big talking points last week was the confirmation of Leo Chenal and Sonny Styles possibly playing in dual MIKE roles this season, but Frankie Luvu stepped into the linebacker conversation this week. The team started full field work, and the defense utilized some 4-3 looks with Styles as the MIKE, Luvu at WILL, and Leo on the ball as a strong side backer. So far, Luvu is having a good camp and looks like his old self in the new scheme. Frankie Luvu looks like a completely different guy… visually and physically.. he’s flying around like it’s 2024 — Bleeding Burgundy & Gold (@BleedinBnG) August 3, 2026 Of note, Luvu also appeared to be wearing the green dot during Tuesday’s session. Linebacker utilization is one of the items the team wants to keep under wraps, and while Frankie might not match his snap total from last season, coordinator Daronte Jones appears poised to use Luvu as a blitzer and disruptor where he could be more effective in less snaps. Fight is on for the last roster spot in the wide-receiver room The Diggs addition clearly changes the roster math for the wide receivers. While there has been some speculation the team could keep seven wide receivers, there will be a roster crunch for a team that plans to utilize heavy personnel groupings. McLaurin, Diggs, and Williams are all locks, and Luke McCaffrey made his case to be one this week. He had a good day of practice on Monday and a great one on Tuesday with multiple receptions and a catch-and-run for a long touchdown. He followed it up with another splash play on Wednesday. a Luke touchdown for you 🫵 @mccaffrey_luke | #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/tAIu8LcFeQ — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) August 4, 2026 Luke McCaffrey is having another good day. Just had a nice touchdown in the back of the endzone from Jayden on an over route. Got both feet down too. #Commanders — Josh Taylor (@JoshTaylorFB) August 5, 2026 It’s all about stacking good days on top of each other in camp, and McCaffrey has been the best at it so far. Dyami Brown and Jaylin Lane both had drops on key throws and need to build more consistency, but Lane should make the roster as a punt returner. Daniels singled out Treylon Burks in his wide receiver discussion on Saturday, and after recovering from foot soreness, Burks continued to take first-team reps alongside McCaffery. Van Jefferson has also looked good at times. The last wide receiver will need to be a contributor on special teams, which still gives undrafted free agent Jaden Bradley a chance at a roster spot. In Week 6 of his senior season at UNLV, Bradley blocked a punt and also returned a different blocked punt for a touchdown. Bradley also returned five kickoffs for 106 yards and one punt for 36 yards over the course of the season. When will the Commanders injured players return? Ahkello Witherspoon was placed on the reserve/retired list on Tuesday. While the team added Fabian Moreau as a reasonable depth piece, the loss of another player in the cornerback room highlighted the need to get Trey Amos back on the field. The second-year cornerback was sighted at camp this week, in good spirits and moving well, and the team will reassess his availability today. Tress Way was seen getting some punts in before practice on Wednesday and will also be evaluated at the same time. The team added a center in Trey Hill , but it was more for practice functionality than concern over Allegretti’s injury. Still, Washington needs to get Nick back sooner than later. Julian Good-Jones had another bad snap during Tuesday’s session while Matt Gulbin continues to be brought along slowly . The team also seems to have focused on developing Tim McKay at center so he can bring his versatility at all three positions along the offensive line. Guard Timothy McKay (his full name always trips me up with that other guy) is taking snaps with that group — Martenzie Johnson (@10zJohnson) August 5, 2026 As expected, there is still no timeline for Dorance Armstrong and Deatrich Wise , and it was reported earlier that tight end John Bates would be out for at least another week. The team did get linebacker Kain Medrano back on Monday, and he immediately made his presence known with an interception . Several players also missed Wednesday’s session, so we will wait for an update there. #Commanders on the active roster I don't see at practice today: – RB Jeremy McNichols (undisclosed) – C Nick Allegretti (calf) – TE John Bates (hamstring) – OLB K'Lavon Chaisson (undisclosed) – DE Drake Jackson (illness) – CB Amik Robertson (undisclosed) — Tashan Reed (@tashanreed) August 5, 2026 UDFA Watch The kicking matchup between Jake Moody and Drew Stevens looked fairly even on Monday, but Stevens pulled ahead in Tuesday’s session, going 5-for-5, including a 55-yarder with plenty of room to spare. Moody went 3-for-5, missing two field goals in the kicking session and another in the team’s 11-on-11 sessions. There is a long way to go in the competition, but right now the UDFA has the edge. Jeffrey M’ba batted down a pass to blow up a running back screen play in Tuesday’s session. The first mention of the big…

full_text: The Daily Slop – August 6, 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Day off for the players. Back at it Friday/Saturday. But today: a physical for Stefon Diggs and an evaluation of Trey Amos and Tress Way. Both on the PUP list. There is optimism regarding their return, perhaps as soon as Friday. But… have to make sure today. pic.twitter.com/eZPnAhGg1z — John Keim (@john_keim) August 6, 2026 Articles JP Finlay Stefon Diggs’ signing proves Adam Peters learned a lesson [I]n multiple conversations with sources close to the Patriots locker room – Diggs was a model citizen and leader for the young players last year. So now he’s coming to Washington. Coming home. A product of Good Counsel High School and the University of Maryland is now wearing burgundy and gold. Diggs makes the Commanders a better football team. Immediately. Breaking news on Inside Training Camp Live: Stefon Diggs is signing with the #Commanders . pic.twitter.com/gtzLxXDFCc — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) August 5, 2026 He has elite hands and runs great routes. He will be invaluable to Daniels on 3rd downs and in the red zone. Last year he was still recovering from a major knee injury suffered in 2024. This year, it’s entirely possible Diggs gets more speed back to add to his veteran savvy. The Commanders defense was awful in 2025 so Peters set out to fix it. He spent real money on the defensive line, used his 1st-round pick on LB Sonny Styles, and invested in the defensive backs. The defense already looks different, faster and possibly much better. On offense, however, questions remained at receiver. Now there’s far fewer questions. The expectation from the team is that Stefon Diggs will most likely have his first press conference after Friday's practice. — Scott Abraham (@Scott7news) August 5, 2026 It would be tremendous if somebody from the collection of Treylon Burks, Luke McCaffrey, Dyami Brown, Jaylen Lane or rookie Antonio Williams breaks out for a great year. But that happening is hardly a given, and now there’s much less of a need for that to happen. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE NOTUS The former Patriot is expected to slot in as Washington’s No. 2 receiver, answering one of the offseason’s biggest questions A source close to Diggs said the 32-year-old DMV native chose Washington because he was impressed by the entire organization, from the front office to the coaches to the players. Diggs, a four-time Pro Bowler, wanted a “chance to play with one of best young [quarterbacks] and opposite one of [the] best receivers — and to do it all at home,” the source said. His 9,032 receiving yards since 2018 is the third-most in that time period behind only Davante Adams (9,822) and Tyreek Hill (9,587). Putting a player with 942 career receptions, 11,504 yards and 74 touchdowns alongside Terry McLaurin (498 receptions, 6,961 yards and 41 touchdowns) makes the receiving unit deep and dangerous. The two veterans will be grouped with promising rookie Antonio Williams, who has had breakout moments during training camp. Diggs has also garnered headlines away from the field. In May, he was found not guilty of assaulting his private chef. He is currently suing a social media influencer who has accused him of sexual assault and facing a civil lawsuit for accusing a former concierge of stealing his Ferrari. The conversation has gone from "who is the Commanders' WR-2?" to "can they keep a 7th WR so that Dyami Brown or Van Jefferson hangs around?" This move completely changes the room and the feeling about the talent around Daniels in a huge season. — Grant Paulsen (@GrantPaulsen) August 5, 2026 To read more of this article, CLICK HERE ESPN Will WR Stefon Diggs be a fit with the Washington Commanders? Why Diggs and not other WR options? It was either Diggs or bust for Washington — nobody used those words, but one team source said he was the only free agent they were interested in signing at this time. Washington lost out on other possibilities in the offseason. It had wanted to sign Alec Pierce, but he opted to re-sign with Indianapolis before free agency; one league source said Pierce would have signed with the Commanders — had he come free. They also tried, but failed, to sign Romeo Doubs. And Carnell Tate would have been an option had he been available with the seventh pick. In other words, they had kept searching for more at the position. Why did the Commanders wait so long to sign him? And does his delayed start hurt his chances to make an early impact? There were multiple reasons. At one point, Brandon Aiyuk appeared to be a possibility — Washington was just waiting for him to be released from the 49ers. The Commanders would have been interested, according to multiple team sources. But he has yet to be cut. So that likelihood diminished this summer, putting them more on a path to Diggs, who was always going to be the more expensive option. Also, with Diggs not in camp, others — notably rookie Williams — have gotten more reps — and a better chance for Washington to see what it had in its receiving corps. Williams in particular will play a key role, and there are similarities in how he’d be used along with Diggs. It’s also possible that Diggs wanted to see what other opportunities arose — or the money just wasn’t right. But he had made it known that he would like to play in Washington. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) What WR Stefon Diggs brings to the Washington Commanders So what does Diggs bring to Washington? In a word; production. He’s had over 1000 receiving yards in seven of his last eight seasons. The only time he didn’t break 1000 yards during that eight year span was in 2024, where he tore his ACL after eight games, but even then he was on target to hit 1000 yards. Last year he bounced back from that ACL and had another 1000 yard season with the Patriots, becoming their top receiver on their way to the Super Bowl. But what makes him so productive and can he continue to be that productive at age 32? Let’s take a closer look. One of the first things that stood out to me when watching Diggs film from last year wasn’t the route running or the catching ability. I’ll certainly get to those things in this post, but the thing that jumped out to me most was his ability to make himself available. Diggs consistently showed the awareness to know when his route was dead and how to adjust or go off-script to make himself available. It’s a veteran savviness that made Zach Ertz such a great target for Jayden Daniels the past two years. Diggs does this consistently on film. Sometimes it’s making small adjustments like sitting a route down in a hole in coverage, sometimes it’s going off-script when a play breaks down to make himself available. He’s been around multiple teams and multiple quarterbacks and always managed to build up a rapport with them quickly, likely due to this ability. It means when things break down and the quarterback is in trouble, they typically look to him to bail them out of it. What are the Commanders getting in WR Stefon Diggs? -Savvy veteran route runner -Reliable production -QB friendly target Full breakdown: https://t.co/lVBuUmdXky pic.twitter.com/ArQIEhyaJ3 — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) August 6, 2026 Last Man Standig (paywall) Washington addressed its main offensive question with a seven-time 1000-yard receiver Having signed free agent TE Chig Okonkwo this offseason, Washington has one of its better receiving trios in several years, and certainly since drafting Daniels in 2024. An outside WR much of his career, the former University of Maryland standout split time on the perimeter and in the slot with the Patriots. Washington has slot options in rookie Antonio Williams, Luke McCaffrey and Jaylin Lane. It’s…
