title: Washington Commanders Week 2 training camp observations, standouts
summary: There is a lot going on in Ashburn, VA, as the Commanders are now over a full week into training camp. Unlike previous camps run by head coach Dan Quinn, this one seems a lot different in everything from access to vet rest days. What has been an entertaining start is expected to ramp up […]
full_text: There is a lot going on in Ashburn, VA, as the Commanders are now over a full week into training camp. Unlike previous camps run by head coach Dan Quinn , this one seems a lot different in everything from access to vet rest days. What has been an entertaining start is expected to ramp up even more as we head towards joint practices next week against the Dolphins. That’s especially true after Wednesday afternoon’s once-year pact with receiver Stefon Diggs . Before we look forward to all that on a Thursday off date on the training-camp calendar, let’s look back at my observations as we get into Week 2. Who has been running with the first team? Camp is a time to mix things up and see what guys can do when they are in certain situations. There is certainly a LOT of rotation going on, but from a first-team glance, this appears to be the way things have played out very early in camp, though the receiver should change with Diggs coming aboard. Offense: QB: Jayden Daniels RB: Bill Croskey-Merritt WR: Terry McLaurin WR: Treylon Burks WR: Luke McCaffrey TE: Chig Okonkwo TE 2 (12 personnel): Ben Sinnott LT: Laremy Tunsil LG: Chris Paul C: Julian Good-Jones (while Nick Allegretti has been out) RG: Sam Cosmi RT: Josh Conerly *Antonio Williams and Brandon Coleman have also gotten some work with the first team. Defense: EDGE: Odafe Oweh DT: Daron Payne DT: Javon Kinlaw DT 3 (when in an odd front): Tim Settle EDGE: K’Lavon Chaisson ILB: Frankie Luvu ILB: Sonny Styles SAM (walked-up): Leo Chenal CB: Mike Sainristil CB: Amik Robertson S: Nick Cross S: Jeremy Reaves S: Will Harris *Sainristil has been seeing time on the outside and in the slot. Before his abrupt retirement, Witherspoon was the other outside corner when Mikey was in the slot, with Rasul Douglas seeing some time mixed in with the first team on the outside. The Green Dot There was talk that rookie Sonny Styles or free agent signing Leo Chenal would get the green dot for defensive communication. After a week of camp, however, it appears Frankie Luvu is directing the defense. As The Athletic reporter Nicki Jhabvala says below, it’s still early and things can change once live action is upon us in September, but as of now, this is where things stand. For the “green dot” crowd … it’s still early, but Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw have both said that Frankie Luvu has been that guy getting everyone set. — Nicki Jhabvala (@NickiJhabvala) August 4, 2026 Camp standouts: Luke McCaffrey: The third-year wideout continues to stack good practices. He was a beast on Tuesday , having arguably the best practice of all the Commanders, and scored again Wednesday in team work on a dime from quarterback Jayden. He’s working both inside and outside and has been said to look good wherever he’s lining up. Ben Sinnott: The increased playing time is certainly benefitting Sinnott. He’s working with the ones in 12 personnel and coordinator David Blough is using him in a variety of different ways, including in-line and as an H-back. Bill Croskey-Merritt: Bill is noticeably bigger and is bringing that physicality with him during runs, however, it’s his hands out of the backfield that have stood out early on. Odafe Oweh/K’Lavon Chaisson: The EDGE duo have been as advertised, and MORE! Camp observers have spoken of the explosion to which both players get off the ball and there have been plays every day where the whistle needs to be blown to protect the quarterbacks. Sonny Styles: The way he triggers is just different! He’s a true sideline-to-sideline defender who brought the wood a few times during padded practice . Teammates have raved about his preparation, fluidity and overall athleticism. Frankie Luvu: Observers have stated that Luvu looks like the 2024 version, not the one we saw struggle last season. He’s been looking great on timely blitzes. Sam Cosmi: Fully healthy now, Cosmi is said to be bullying guys out there, especially during Monday’s padded practice one-on-one session. Nick Cross: Cross has been all over the field, and there were many times when observers said if it was live action, he would have blown the play up. He’s going to have a big role for this new defense. Colson Yankoff: Yankoff, who has seen more time with the first and second groups with John Bates out, has made the most of his opportunities. That’s especially true in the passing game; hauling in a few really impressive catches in traffic. Josh Josephs: The rookie has impressed with his length, get-off and even coverage ability working primarily with the second group. Antonio Williams: Observers have commented on how smooth Williams is and how quickly he can uncover. He’s been with the second group a lot and backup quarterback Marcus Mariota has missed him on a few occasions where he’s been wide open. On Wednesday, during the second padded practice, he absolutely TOASTED the third- and fourth-string defense for an easy touchdown. Rasul Douglas: Douglas showed up the first two days of camp, when observers said he was all around the ball. He had a pick-six on Day 2 and supposedly looked pretty good during padded practice. Mike Sainristil: It’s been a mixed bag for Sainristil in coverage, but observers have said he’s constantly working, and it seems when he gets beat, he comes back and makes some plays. His leadership has been lauded by some of the coaches. Jeremy Reaves: Coaches have praised his effort and communication in this new defense. Who has struggled? There is a lot of praise early in camp, so the observations on who has struggled have been limited. Below is some of what I have heard early on. Marcus Mariota: Observers have said he’s not seeing things as quickly and hasn’t pulled the trigger on some throws he should have made. Quan Martin: Martin has been running with the second team after being a starter the previous two seasons. I’m not hearing that he’s been particularly bad, but he may have lost his starting job early on. He did get stiff-armed into another galaxy today by Fatman Allen. Jaylin Lane: Lane had some early drop issues, but it seems he has cleared those up over the past few sessions. Consistency will be key for the second-year pro. Car’lin Vigers: The young corner made some plays during the first day of camp, but recent reports are that he’s struggled staying with receivers in his zone. Josh Conerly: I don’t know how much struggling Conerly has actually done considering Washington has been in pads just two days, but MANY reports out of practice cite both Oweh and Chaisson getting into the backfield quickly, and I don’t believe Tunsil’s name was mentioned as someone who has been blowing a lot of pass sets. Competition between Blough and Jones We knew this would be a theme all camp, but it’s so refreshing to hear that coordinators David Blough and Daronte Jones are out here playing 3D chess against one another during sessions. Iron shapes iron, so this is absolutely music to my ears, especially after putting up with two very predictable offenses and defenses over the past two seasons. Blough has also been getting into his bag of tricks, as he looks for ways to slow down Jones’ furious rush. Wednesday he had, by all accounts, three trick plays, including a pretty hook-and-ladder between Jayden, Terry and Burks.

title: From ball boy to HOFer, inside Larry Fitzgerald's unique path
summary: After firing him, the Vikings rehired Fitzgerald as a ball boy and assigned him to the receivers, a move that shaped his career.
full_text:
A WEEK INTO the Minnesota Vikings ' 1999 training camp, the person in charge of checking media parking passes was fired. He had broken curfew, and then-coach Dennis Green wasn't having it.

 Neither was the young man's father. After all, Larry Fitzgerald Sr.'s relationship with Green was one of the reasons Larry Jr. got the gig.

 A week later, Green rehired Fitzgerald, but instead of parking lot attendant, Fitzgerald became the ball boy for the wide receivers. That episode played a significant role in the trajectory of Fitzgerald's career, which culminates Saturday when he's enshrined into the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

 "That's when," said Larry's brother, Marcus, "the true story of Larry Fitzgerald actually happened as far as the wide receiver, the phenom, the person we see today.

 "Had to wake him up, because my dad was pissed. My dad was like, 'What are you doing?'...my mom and my dad. You saw him take [the job] way more serious, and he was way more dedicated. I really think that shook him up enough to know that you don't have too many chances in life to keep screwing up."

 Fitzgerald wasn't a ball boy to just any receivers. The Vikings were led by a pair of future Hall of Fame receivers in Randy Moss and Cris Carter, who brought Minnesota to the brink of Super Bowl XXXIII after a 15-1 season. Over the next three seasons, Fitzgerald received a Ph.D.-level education in being a wide receiver and a professional football player. Without those relationships, without those hours of watching Carter and Moss, among others, Fitzgerald might never have been measured for a gold jacket.

 

 "No, I don't think so," Fitzgerald told ESPN when asked if he would be going into the Hall without those three years as a ball boy. "And I say that because I think me being around those guys and seeing players coming and going, guys blowing their money, getting hurt, just the underbelly of the league, I don't know if I would've been as focused on the big picture, stayed away from the distractions, not drink, not use drugs. All of the decisions you have to make as a young person that determine the trajectory.

 "I don't know if I would've had the insight or foresight to avoid those types of things."

 But he didn't avoid every temptation.

 

 CARTER REMEMBERS A TIME  when Fitzgerald took his "tricked-out Denali" to a car wash and it came back a little light.

 "Stole all the change out the ashtray," Carter said. "I said I hope he's good at football, because you're not going to be a good thief."

 Fitzgerald got close to Carter through Marcus, who used to babysit Carter's kids. Larry spent a couple of spring breaks at Carter's home in Florida to train. He still talks to Carter and his ex-wife Melanie Morgan -- "Aunt Mel" -- all the time.

 "They were just a really great family," Fitzgerald said. "And obviously he's a Hall of Fame talent, so to be able to pick his mind and learn from him was something that meant a great deal to me.

 "And to be able to have that type of knowledge with that proximity was not something that most people were able to have."

 The search for knowledge is what most impressed Carter.

 "Larry is a student of information," Carter said. "Everything he's into, he is deeply into it to an addictive level, and the lifestyle, the fanfare, playing the position, he could see as a youngster, 'Man, I know what I want to do.'"

 However, Carter, like a number of other Vikings, quickly noticed that Fitzgerald had the natural ability to merge his hard work and his thirst for knowledge.

 "We got hundreds of ball boys," Carter said. "Only one became a Hall of Famer because he's the only one that had the DNA."

 The impressions Carter and Moss made on Fitzgerald weren't limited to the football field.

 

 "And I'll never forget, one of the first camp practices, I always knew [Moss] played basketball," Fitzgerald said. "We were all shooting in the gym before practice started, and they had to walk through the gym to get to the locker rooms. And I remember him just grabbing the basketball and taking a few steps and just dunking it as he's walking through in flip-flops.

 "And I'm like, Jesus Christ, this dude is just so athletic. And so I think some of the freaky things that he would do every day at practice, they weren't things that you could really ... you could watch it in awe, but you know you never could do it."

 But there was one Moss trait Fitzgerald could emulate.

 "He's one of the few guys that I saw with that level of talent that had that work ethic," he said. "His work ethic was really good for a guy that was that talented."

 The admiration wasn't a one-way street.

 

 A GROUP OF about 10 Vikings that often included Moss, Carter, seventh-round pick Matthew Hatchette and quarterback Daunte Culpepper would attend Fitzgerald's high school games. They'd go to dinner after and made it a weekly thing during home-game weekends.

 Korey Stringer, who was a Vikings tackle at the time, once went to one of Fitzgerald's practices. When he saw Fitzgerald standing on the outside of a huddle at the end of practice, he yelled down from the stands for Fitzgerald to get in the middle of it.

 "It became that 'Hey, we got to help him out' type of attitude for us as a receiver group," Hatchette said.

 "He was one of the crew, basically," former Vikings running back Leroy Hoard said.

 

 It helped that Larry Sr. was a longtime Vikings beat reporter for the Minnesota Spokesman-Recorder, and was very close to Green. Fitzgerald Sr. died June 1 at the age of 71.

 "[Larry Jr.] was part of the family a little bit with his dad being the beat writer and Denny's main guy he talked to about the Vikings," former Vikings receiver Chris Walsh said.

 "He was our kid," Carter added.

 As Fitzgerald got more comfortable and as the receivers embraced him, he began asking questions. Lots of questions.

 "He was asking very specific questions like, 'OK, why'd you turn your hands over on the way you caught it like this, Cris, compared to turning your pinkies together?'" Hatchette recalled. "Stuff like that. 'How did you keep the defender on your backside when you were attacking the football?'

 "Little questions like that were way different questions that a kid would ask at that point."

 The receivers let Fitzgerald sit in on their position meetings, where he'd watch Carter reveal how  Detroit Lions  defenders would bang their fists together when they were about to check into a different play. It was in those meetings that he learned a valuable lesson from his time as a ball boy: how to read and recognize defenses.

 "I think you can be as good as you want, but if you don't know what the f--- is going on in the football field, you're not going to have very much success. You got to know what's going on," Fitzgerald said.

 "So, all of those things, I would recognize that just being able to sit in those meetings."

 After practice, after the receivers got their extra work in, Fitzgerald would catch passes from the Jugs machine, often with Hatchette. Walsh remembered Fitzgerald doing the same Jugs drills as the receivers, such as turning to catch the ball as it quickly approached or working the sideline. Fitzgerald would also run routes for quarterbacks who wanted to get in a few more reps. At one point, Carter told him to put on gloves and Fitzgerald was the only ball boy wearing gloves.

 "Well, I just thought you're going to get what you put in in terms of the work," Fitzgerald said. "And I saw those guys putting a lot of effort into getting better. And I knew that if I wanted to do that, then that was what was going to be required.

 "I was going to have to do the same thing, and I just learned the work ethic. I learned the detail. I learned the focus. And those are the things that really stood out to me."

 It was when Fitzgerald would catch balls that the Vikings started to realize his potential.

title: Super Bowl LXI odds: All 32 teams' odds to win the championship
summary: Every NFL team's win total, as well as odds to win their division, the conference and Super Bowl LXI.
full_text:
June of the NFL offseason arrived with a bang. First, the Los Angeles Rams pulled off an absolute blockbuster of a trade by acquiring two-time and reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett from the Cleveland Browns . Los Angeles had already been the Super Bowl favorite, but the transaction pushed them from +800 to +650, then further to +600. Now in August, they sit at +550. That's well ahead of the second tier consisting of the Baltimore Ravens and Buffalo Bills at 10-1, as well as the reigning champion Seattle Seahawks at 11-1.

 

 IN the other big transaction, the New England Patriots made a long-expected move for wide receiver A.J. Brown . Because the trade had been anticipated for some time, the Pats' Super Bowl odds remained at 16-1, tied for sixth on the odds board with the Philadelphia Eagles  (Brown's former team) and the Kansas City Chiefs , while the Los Angeles Chargers  and  Green Bay Packers  both lengthened, from 16-1 in mid-May to 17-1 and 18-1, respectively.

 The 2026 season will open with a Super Bowl rematch and the Seahawks listed as 3.5-point favorites over the Patriots. Caesars Sportsbook head of football Joey Feazel told ESPN, "With Seattle's recent win still fresh in bettors' minds, the public is likely to show strong interest in them again."

 Meanwhile, the Chargers are 11.5-point favorites over the Arizona Cardinals , the largest spread for a Week 1 game since 2012, according to ESPN Research. Arizona is dead last on the Super Bowl odds board at 500-1 and is thus far an underdog in every one of its 2026 games.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings Sportsbook   and subject to change.

title: Tracking 2026 NFL hold-ins: Vea and Tuipulotu
summary: Here is the latest on the Bucs' Vita Vea and the Chargers' Tuli Tuipulotu and where they stand with their deals.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL preseason kicked off with the Pro Football Hall of Game Thursday , with three weeks of action to follow, but there are two players who are waiting for their contract situations to sort out.

 The start of NFL training camps brought these negotiations to a head. Players can hold out and stay away from camp until their financial situations are addressed, or they can hold in, where they report to camp to avoid fines but skip practice while waiting for a new contract. We're tracking the important hold-ins across the league, with updates from our NFL Nation writers on each situation.

 The list of stars not practicing includes Tampa Bay Buccaneers defensive tackle Vita Vea  and  Los Angeles Chargers outside linebacker  Tuli Tuipulotu . 

 Which player will be next in resolving his contract dispute? Are any of these four willing to miss games once the season begins? Let's examine each situation.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Gibbs | Robinson | Vea | Tuipulotu 

 
 

 

 Vita Vea , DT, Tampa Bay Buccaneers 
 Status: Holding in, requesting a trade 

 Aug. 6: The Buccaneers have "no plans" to trade Vea, according to general manager Jason Licht when asked Thursday about Vea's hold-in. Collin Roberts, Vea's agent, told the Tampa Bay Times this week that he "doesn't see it ending in anything but a trade."

 "We love Vita," Licht added. "We've been engaged with his agent recently. I don't know how it's gonna end, but we've been engaged and that's at least some progress." Vea has been present at the Bucs' facility, taking part in classroom instruction and observing practice from the sideline. He has also been seen helping coach teammates up during positional drills, but he isn't physically participating.

 Aug. 2 update: The star defensive tackle remains sidelined with a back injury, as well as his contract hold-in. Coach Todd Bowles said there is "nothing new" to report on his injury, and he is unsure if Vea will make the trip to the  New York Jets  for a pair of joint practices starting Aug. 11.

 July 31 update: Vea, who stayed indoors to receive treatment Thursday, was back out on the practice field Friday with teammates but was still sidelined with a back injury sustained during the team's conditioning test. Bowles said he does not have a timetable yet for Vea's back.

 July 30 update: While Vea was on the sidelines during Wednesday's first training camp practice and was standing alongside teammates during positional drills, he was not on the practice field Thursday. Bowles said Vea tweaked his back in the team's conditioning test Tuesday and he was getting treatment. Vea did, however, participate in an interview on the "Up & Adams Show," but he did not discuss his contract. Vea is set to earn $17 million this season, but none of it is guaranteed, along with a per-game roster bonus that is capped at $1 million total. Bowles said they are preparing for the season as if Vea will play. 

 -- Jenna Laine, Bucs reporter 

 

 
 

 Tuli Tuipulotu , OLB, Los Angeles Chargers 
 

 Status: Practicing, but still seeking a new contract

 Aug. 6 update:  Tuipulotu participated in team drills during Wednesday's padded practice, his second day in a row after not participating in team drills for the first six days of training camp.

 Tuipulotu looked like himself, bursting by the line of scrimmage to shut down running back Omarion Hampton on one of his first snaps and generating pressure throughout practice.

 Coach Jim Harbaugh originally said that Tuipulotu's absence was being "handled internally," then later said it was a "ramp up." Neither Tuipulotu, his representatives or the Chargers have acknowledged a contract-related absence, but his return to the field signals that whatever matter was being handled internally is resolved.

 Aug. 5 update:  Tuipulotu, who has been a limited participant in practice this training camp amid ongoing contract negotiations, was a full participant in Wednesday's practice. The caveat is that the practice was a walkthrough, so Tuipulotu and the other Chargers players were going at half speed. He still has yet to participate in a non-walkthrough practice 11-on-11 period, but his participation could be a sign that things could be headed toward a resolution.

 Aug. 4 update:  Coach Jim Harbaugh said Tuesday that Tuipulotu's absence from team drills remains part of "his ramp up." Harbaugh stopped short, however, of explaining any further, saying, "I don't know for sure where it's at. If I knew for sure, then I would say for sure."

 After noticing a reporter's facial expression, Harbaugh went on to explain he doesn't know exactly what's happening with Tuipulotu because he is not a medical professional.

 "Am I in somebody's body? A doctor? he said. "A lot of things that hang on my wall, but a medical degree is not one of them."

 Tuipulotu participated in one 7-on-7 rep but did not take part in the remainder of team drills on Tuesday, marking his sixth straight practice with limited participation as his contract situation remains unresolved.

 Aug. 3 update: Tuipulotu again did not participate in team drills, continuing his limited participation as his contract situation remains unresolved. The Chargers, Tuipulotu, and his representation remain mum about Tuipulotu's absence from practice, though it appears to be contract-related. Tuipulotu remains in good spirits and engaged throughout practice. His routine has been the same each day: he participates in individual drills, jokes with teammates, works with a trainer briefly, then watches practice with the team.

 Aug. 1 update:  Coach Jim Harbaugh declined to say whether outside linebacker Tuli Tuipulotu's absence from team drills at practice is contract-related, saying only the situation is being "handled internally" and repeatedly describing Tuipulotu as "ramping up."

 July 31 update:  Tuipulotu continued not to practice amid ongoing contract negotiations Friday. He went through individual drills, worked off to the side with a trainer and watched practice.

 July 30 update: The Chargers outside linebacker did not practice Thursday for the second straight day amid ongoing contract negotiations, but he did more on-field work with teammates than on the opening day of camp. Tuipulotu wore a helmet and jersey Thursday and went through individual drills with the team before working off to the side with a trainer. On Wednesday, he was in a T-shirt and shorts and worked off to the side with a trainer.

 -- Kris Rhim, Chargers reporter 

 

 
 

 Bijan Robinson , RB, Atlanta Falcons 
 

 Status: Signed a new deal 

 Aug. 4 update:  The two-time Pro Bowler and the Falcons reached agreement on a three-year extension worth up to $75 million that now will make him the highest-paid running back in NFL history, sources told ESPN's Adam Schefter and NFL Network's Ian Rapoport.

 Aug. 1 update:  Robinson was again at practice, though not practicing, for the fourth straight day. Robinson left the field at one point during the media video shooting period and then came back when the cameras were off. Otherwise, he was with his teammates on the sidelines like he has been since camp started on Wednesday.

 July 31 update : Falcons coach Kevin Stefanski addressed Robinson's hold-in for the first time Friday morning. He said he was confident the contract situation will be resolved amiably.

 

 On how he is approaching the conflict, Stefanski said: "Just coach the football team."

 "Understand that there's a business side to everything we do and there's the football side and sometimes you're living in both worlds, if you will," Stefanski said. "But just going to continue to coach the football team."

 Robinson was once again in a jersey with no helmet or cleats for a third straight day. He was on the sideline encouraging teammates after plays. At the end of practice, he did pushups with his teammates who lost a drill.

title: 2026 NFL season: Future Hall of Famers from all 32 teams
summary: We went roster by roster to pick out the NFL players who are on track to make the Hall of Fame one day -- and those who still have some work to do.
full_text:
How many Hall of Famers are playing in the NFL right now?

 It depends on when you're evaluating, of course. There are veterans near the end of their careers who have already proved themselves as locks to receive the game's highest honor one day, such as  Aaron Rodgers and Derrick Henry . There are players in their prime who are well on their way, such as  Justin Jefferson and Pat Surtain II . And then there are young players who haven't yet proved themselves to be Hall of Famers but could break out in the years to come, such as  Caleb Downs or Arvell Reese from the 2026 draft.

 Go back to 2002, the first year with 32 teams. There are 54 players who suited up for at least one game that season enshrined in the Hall of Fame. That list doesn't include Tom Brady (who becomes eligible in 2028) or borderline candidates such as Steve Smith and Reggie Wayne, who could earn enough votes to cross the threshold in the future. At the very least, we can use 55 Hall of Famers as our gauge, which is just under 3% of the 1,839 players who suited up for at least one game that season.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 Today, I'm going through each of the league's 32 teams and attempting to identify the players who either are on track or have a realistic hope of earning gold jackets one day. This will be my estimate of who is likely to make it using historical comparables as opposed to my opinion of who should or should not be enshrined at some point. Naturally, that includes positional preferences; voters have historically loved to honor quarterbacks, running backs and receivers, but the bar is higher for linemen. I won't attempt to pick among the rookies, whom we haven't yet seen line up for an NFL snap, but I'll work with everybody else and split the most notable candidates into one of five categories:

 
 Players listed as "in" have already done enough to earn enshrinement given their existing résumé. They could retire tomorrow and make it into the Hall of Fame after they become eligible. 
 Those "on the cusp" have already done the vast majority of the work required and need only another season or two of solid play to get over the hump. As it stands, their résumé might already be enough to get in, but another successful season could push them into lock territory. 
 The "keep it up" category is for players who are performing at a Hall of Fame level but haven't done so for a long enough time to guarantee their path to enshrinement. They need to play at or near their existing level for several more seasons to have a shot. 
 Guys who have "work to do" aren't on track to make it to the Hall of Fame with their existing résumé and/or their most recent level of play. In some cases, that could be because injuries slowed their progress in 2025, or because they haven't played at a Hall-caliber level for long enough. They still have a shot, but something has to change. 
 Finally, the "missing out" category is for veterans who are at the point where they don't have the existing résumé to make it to the Hall nor the time to reestablish themselves as viable candidates. Though anything's possible, it will be a serious surprise if any of these players end up in Canton one day. They're far more likely to end up in the Hall of Very Good. 
 
 I usually start these all-32 columns with teams on the East Coast, so let's mix things up and begin out west.

 

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LV | LAC | LAR | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 
 

 NFC West 
 

 Arizona Cardinals 
 On the cusp: S Budda Baker 

 Baker has been stuck on some bad teams -- the Cardinals have one winning season across his nine years in the league -- but Pro Bowl voters have consistently seen him as an impactful and rangy difference-making safety. He has made eight Pro Bowls across that span. Every eligible player with at least 10 Pro Bowl appearances has been enshrined in Canton, so if Baker can earn two more, he should be a lock. One more might even be enough for the 30-year-old.

 Keep it up: TE Trey McBride 

 The invisible force field that had kept McBride out of the end zone early in his career finally lifted in 2025, as he scored 11 touchdowns, nearly doubling his total over the prior three seasons combined (six). He's not quite as explosive or elusive after the catch as Travis Kelce was in his prime or Brock Bowers has been so far as a pro, but McBride makes up that for with great hands and massive target shares.

 

 
 

 Los Angeles Rams 
 In: WR Davante Adams , Edge Myles Garrett , QB Matthew Stafford 

 I don't think I need to do much convincing here. Garrett is one of the best defenders in league history, and Adams had a five-year peak as arguably the top wide receiver in football. The case against Stafford would have been that nobody had ever really seen him as the best QB in the NFL (or close to it) in any of his first 16 years ... but after winning MVP last season, that one's out the window. He's already in the top seven for career passing yards and touchdowns, and with an MVP and a Super Bowl victory, Stafford will waltz in.

 Keep it up: WR Puka Nacua 

 Nacua already has 1,486- and 1,715-receiving yard seasons to his name by the end of his third pro campaign, which is remarkable, even given that those years are part of the 17-game era. Just for fun, the 2023 fifth-round pick is also one of the league's best blocking wideouts. The only questions are whether Nacua can stay on the field for full seasons at a time and whether there's any drop-off once Stafford is ultimately replaced by Ty Simpson .

 

 Work to do: CB Trent McDuffie , DT Kobie Turner , Edge Byron Young 

 The talented young linemen the Rams already had up front should get a boost from playing alongside Garrett. I thought Turner was the best of the bunch last season, but Young was devastating at times and parlayed his 12-sack, 29-knockdown campaign into his first Pro Bowl. I'm intrigued to see whether the Rams can afford to keep their DL standouts -- both of whom are pending free agents -- alongside Garrett for years to come.

 

 
 

 San Francisco 49ers 
 In: WR Mike Evans , RB Christian McCaffrey , OT Trent Williams 

 Evans and Williams are easy first-ballot selections. McCaffrey has struggled with injuries, but he has had multiple seasons as the best RB in the league and plays a position that the Hall is always looking to appreciate.

 On the cusp: TE George Kittle , LB Fred Warner 

 Kittle is right on the borderline of being a lock, having made seven Pro Bowls over his past eight pro campaigns before he  tore his right Achilles last postseason. I'd vote for Kittle given his dominance as a blocker and four 1,000-yard seasons, but tight ends can go underappreciated by the Hall at times. One more substantial season would push Kittle, 32, to the "lock" side of things. I'd argue the same for Warner, who had four first-team All-Pro nods over a five-year span before his own serious injury a year ago.

 Work to do: Edge Nick Bosa , QB Brock Purdy 

 Bosa has a Defensive Player of the Year award to his name, but a pair of September ACL tears have essentially cost the 2019 first-round pick two of his seven pro seasons. full_text:

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Ravens camp. We will update this file often. Can new coach Jesse Minter get  Lamar Jackson  and the Ravens to the Super Bowl? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Ravens camp 
 
 Zay Flowers, Ravens agree to four-year, $140M extension 
 Derrick Henry, entering 11th year, not thinking about retirement 
 Ravens waive rookie Diego Pavia to make room for Ethan Pocic 
 Ravens' Madubuike (neck) practices for 1st time in 10 months 
 
 
 Thursday, Aug. 6 
 The Ravens' third practice of the week in full pads was also their chippiest.

 The first dust-up of camp came when outside linebacker Tavius Robinson shoved offensive tackle Carson Vinson after the play. This caused the offensive and defensive players to converge in the middle of the field before they were quickly separated.

 There were no punches thrown, but coach Jesse Minter huddled the team together shortly afterward.

 "It was just a reminder of [how] the whole reason we are out here is to make each other better [and] help us get ready to play when we are playing against somebody else," Minter said.

 In what was the longest practice of camp at 2 1/2 hours, Minter intentionally scripted long drives of eight and nine plays, which can take a toll on a day when the heat index reached 92 degrees.

 "You want to be able to do all that with a high, high level of physicality and also keep your wits about you," Minter said.

 Other observations: 

 
 Ferran Torres, the star of the World Cup, watched practice and spoke to the players afterward. Torres came off the bench to score the winning goal in Spain's World Cup triumph. "Talk about just being ready when your number is called [and] being at your best when your best is needed -- that is like the ultimate," Minter said. 
 Kyle Hamilton showed why he is one of the best -- and most versatile -- safeties in the league. During team drills, Hamilton was constantly in the backfield and even recorded a sack of Lamar Jackson . Then, in one-on-ones, Hamilton intercepted Jackson after blanketing Elijah Sarratt on a fade route. 
 In one of the most hands-on drills the Ravens have ever had, Baltimore had its defensive backs work on tackling by hitting coaching interns. As Minter pointed out, the coaches were holding a pad and landed on a pad. "I think coaches will do anything to make players better, and we have a great group of coaches," Minter said. "All [of] those guys are willing to do whatever it takes." 
 T.J. Tampa made an impressive play by getting off a block and ripping the ball away from running back Rasheen Ali . Tampa has used camp to solidify himself as the team's No. 4 cornerback behind Nate Wiggins , Marlon Humphrey and Chidobe Awuzie . 
 Kicker Tyler Loop was a perfect 7-of-7, including ones from 53 yards and 61 yards. Last season, Loop was 1-of-4 on kicks beyond 50 yards. 
 
 
 Wednesday, Aug. 5 
 Rookie wide receiver Ja'Kobi Lane continues to be the talk of Baltimore Ravens training camp after another highlight reel catch.

 During red-zone drills, Lane leapt high in the back of the end zone to grab a Lamar Jackson throw for a touchdown. The way Lane is consistently pulling in passes has drawn lofty comparisons.

 "The guy that I was around that his hands remind me of is [former NFL great] Mike Thomas ," Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle said. "Mike Thomas had these strong hands where he could pull it down in a way. You threw it in the vicinity, and you felt like he was going to go get it. There is a lot of that feeling. He is a very friendly guy to throw to."

 Doyle was in New Orleans with Thomas from 2019 to 2022 as an offensive assistant. Thomas led the NFL in receptions in 2018 and 2019.

 Now, in his first season as the play-caller in Baltimore, Doyle has been impressed with the Thomas-like catch radius of Lane, who has been the headliner through the first seven practices of camp. He made a leaping, 30-yard reception over the middle last week and then wowed fans with a one-handed catch on Tuesday.

 When Doyle left the field Wednesday, Lane approached him to say he wasn't pleased with how he messed up at practice.

 Doyle told him, "Hey, you recognized what you made a mistake on. Now, the next step is let's fix it before that happens."

 Other observations:  

 
 After watching the Ravens not practice well in the rain during the spring, Doyle was pleased with how the players performed during the steady downpour on Wednesday. "We play in the AFC North," Doyle said. "In order to win games late in the year, you are going to play in some weather games." 
 Middle linebacker Roquan Smith is reacting to the ball better than he did a year ago. Smith ended the first team drill by picking off Lamar Jackson and then lateraling the ball on the return. 
 Wide receiver Zay Flowers added 8 pounds this offseason and is up to 186 pounds. What was the reason for the added weight? "Everybody gets mad at me when I'm running sideways," Flowers said. "So [now I can] run through some more tackles." 
 

 
 Tuesday, Aug. 4 
 Rookie wide receiver Ja'Kobi Lane has become the star of Ravens training camp.

 Early in team drills, Lane made an unbelievable one-handed grab along the sideline, which will go down as one of the best receptions in Ravens' camp history. After running a route to the right sideline, Lane had to reach back to catch Lamar Jackson 's 20-yard pass with his extended right hand while falling backward to the ground.

 "That was a great play by Ja'Kobi," Ravens coach Jesse Minter said. "He's continued to flash and make those type of plays. As [for] anybody, you're always searching for consistency down after down. Again, the more he shows Lamar that he's making those types of plays, the more trust they build, and that's really what training camp and what practice is all about."

 

 Later, in one-on-one drills, Lane showed his playmaking ability again, using a double move to get behind cornerback T.J. Tampa and catching a long touchdown pass from Jackson.

 This has been an outstanding start to camp for Lane, a third-round pick from USC who has become the team's No. 3 wide receiver behind Zay Flowers and Rashod Bateman . On Thursday, Lane first electrified the crowd by elevating over two defenders for a leaping, 30-yard catch over the middle.

 Other observations:  

 
 There was a brief scare when No. 1 cornerback Nate Wiggins leapt high to pick off Jackson and then landed hard on his back after safety Jaylinn Hawkins accidentally collided with him. Wiggins didn't move for a few minutes as trainers looked at him on the field. But Wiggins got back to his feet and continued to practice, saying he got the wind knocked out of him. 
 In one of the more unusual plays of camp, Jackson was intercepted by 310-pound defensive lineman David Olajiga , who had dropped back into coverage. But right tackle Roger Rosengarten made a heads-up play by knocking the ball away from Olajiga and forcing a fumble. 
 Reserve cornerback Amani Oruwariye picked off No. 3 quarterback Skylar Thompson with aggressive play. Oruwariye closed on tight end Ty Pezza and ripped the ball away. 
 
 
 Monday, Aug. 3

He went 5-of-7, with both misses coming from 45-plus yards. Bass had kicked once in a practice open to the media in the spring.

 Special teams coordinator Jeff Rodgers said earlier in the week that Bass had been kicking outside of open practices and that it was not planned for him to kick in practice until this point.

 "Just the whole organization, I think, Joe [Brady], Jeff ... have done a great job of just integrating me at the right pace," Bass said. "And just letting me be the best version of myself, and that's where I'm seeing a lot of growth in."

 Other observations: 

 
 Safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson (calf) and defensive tackle Deone Walker (left elbow) participated in the individual and team periods of practice. Walker is wearing a brace on his left arm. 
 WR Keon Coleman had an up-and-down day with a nice catch on a pass from quarterback Josh Allen  but also a drop later that left him vocalizing frustration. 
 The splash play of the day came from Allen with a deep pass to recently acquired WR Dante Pettis . If the play had taken place during a game, it would have drawn flags and a review. 
 ILBs Dorian Williams and Terrel Bernard are back participating in 11-on-11 drills, and defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard made it clear there would be roles on the defense during the season for both of those players and rookie Kaleb Elarms-Orr , who has taken advantage of significant practice time due to other injuries. "The physical skill set of those three guys, I think it's going be a lot of fun to work with." 
 
 

 Tuesday, Aug. 4 
 The Bills wore full pads during 11-on-11 drills for the first time in training camp. And with the pads came the fighting.

 Players had to be separated several times, with the back-and-forth talk starting between the offensive and defensive lines even before the team periods. One big altercation came when rookie inside linebacker Kaleb Elarms-Orr didn't realize the play was over and made contact with tight end Dalton Kincaid . The offense did not appreciate the late hit, and coach Joe Brady even had some words after the things calmed.

 One player who was consistently in the middle of the fighting and got involved in that one is offensive lineman Alec Anderson .

 "Well, I didn't enjoy hitting our guy after the whistle, but I enjoyed punching him in the face a couple times and choking him out," Anderson said. "So, that's always enjoyable."

 Veteran edge rusher  Bradley Chubb said that he loved the physicality the team brought.

 "You'd rather say chill than sic 'em," Chubb said. "So, when you got a team full of sic 'ems, that's a good thing. But at the end of the day, we got to make sure we channel our energy in the right place."

 More observations: 

 
 Quarterback Josh Allen and wide receiver DJ Moore connected for arguably the most eye-popping play of camp thus far. Allen found Moore deep downfield with three defenders -- cornerbacks Christian Benford and Maxwell Hairston and safety Cole Bishop -- trailing Moore. After it initially appeared Moore wouldn't catch up to the pass from Allen, the ball landed in the right spot for Moore to stretch out his arms midstride to bring it in. Fellow wide receiver Khalil Shakir said, "[Moore and Allen's] connection has been unreal" and that the play was so beautiful, it feels "fake." 
 
 

 
 Rookie edge rusher  TJ Parker was involved in the beginning of a skirmish. 
 Safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson (right calf strain) worked to the side early in practice.

 The top training camp battles continued to see rotations, including left guard (Anderson/ Austin Corbett ).﻿

 The rain poured down at St. John Fisher University for the third time in the Bills' four training camp practices. The difficult weather lasted the entirety of the team's first practice wearing pads -- which was short-lived.

 The team took off the pads before 11-on-11 drills got underway, another noticeable Joe Brady change.

 "Coming out the first day of pads, and everyone's just adjusting and kind of thinking about all the pads," Brady said. 
 
"Today's more of the intentionality of ... we're coming off an off day. Let's wake up with the mentality that we got to put our pads on. Let's get used to it."

 Tight end Dawson Knox said he appreciates Brady trying to see things from the player perspective.

 There was a hint of risk due to slippery grass. The concrete track surrounding the field wasn't far from where the players were working in the red zone. The team appeared to avoid any major injury.

 "It kind of brings you back to just kind of being a kid ... playing football with your friends in the rain," tight end Dalton Kincaid said. 
 
"Hoping for some sunshine ahead."

 Brady did not offer a timeline for safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson , who suffered a lower calf strain Saturday, to return but said the Bills were "fortunate" it was not a more severe injury. Gardner-Johnson was not present at Monday's practice.

 Inside linebacker Dorian Williams took part in team drills for the first time during camp.

 Despite  the injury suffered Saturday  to projected starting safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson , the Bills' defense showed it can still come together in the face of adversity.

 Inside linebacker Terrel Bernard made his camp debut Saturday in 11-on-11 drills, pairing with rookie linebacker Kaleb Elarms-Orr . Linebacker Dorian Williams has not progressed yet to 11-on-11 work but was alongside Bernard in 7-on-7 drills. Elarms-Orr has seen opportunities with the absences, but Bernard getting more reps is a sign the unit is moving forward.

full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The  Chicago Bears ' camp is taking place in Lake Forest, Illinois, and Bears reporter Courtney Cronin has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Bears camp. We will update this file often. Will the defense step up and lead the Bears back to the NFC North title? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest Bears news 
 
 Darnell Wright agrees to record deal 
 New Bears safety Coby Bryant out 8-10 weeks with injury 
 Bears CB Johnson views 2026 as 'definitely a contract year' 
 Ben Johnson: Bears motivated to spurn 'regression' label 
 
 
 

 Thursday, Aug. 6 
 The longest practice of training camp to date was also the most physical. The Bears were in pads Thursday for 130 minutes and commenced team periods with old-school 9-on-7 and 9-on-9 running drills. With music blasting across the practice fields closest to Halas Hall, the physical, downhill running session turned up the temperature in practice between the offense and defense with a handful of shoving matches after plays were blown dead.

 "Shoot, we love it," defensive end Austin Booker said. "That's our mentality this year: We're getting off the ball, we're being aggressive and getting in the backfield."

 The intensity carried over to one-on-ones between the offensive and defensive lines. Two days after becoming the highest-paid right tackle in NFL history ( four years, $116 million ), Darnell Wright won all three of his reps taken against defensive end Montez Sweat .

 Braxton Jones , who began practice at left tackle with the first-team offensive line for a fourth straight day, sustained an injury during his second one-on-one rep with Booker. Jones threw his helmet and was visibly upset as he tried to walk it off before heading inside with a trainer. The initial belief is that Jones didn't suffer a long-term injury.

 Caleb Williams finished practice on a high note after the offense struggled with operation issues in 11-on-11. There were multiple false starts, and when Rome Odunze slipped on a route, the ball headed in his direction landed in cornerback  Tyrique Stevenson 's hands for an interception.

 The Bears closed out practice with a two-minute drill. Williams marched the offense 65 yards downfield in 1:41 and went 6-of-6 while connecting with Odunze, Colston Loveland , Kalif Raymond ,  D'Andre Swift and Luther Burden III . Despite having time left on the scoreboard, practice ended immediately after Burden's touchdown in the back of the end zone given the session was right at the 2 hour, 10 minute mark.

 
 Multiple players exited early with injuries including Sweat, who was seen walking into the building under his own power. Defensive backs Dallis Flowers and Gervarrius Owens sustained significant leg injuries. 
 Cairo Santos went 6-for-6 during the field goal period and connected on kicks from 56, 50, 40 and 33 yards. 
 Defensive lineman Shemar Turner , who is on PUP while recovering from ACL surgery, appeared at practice for the first time in training camp and worked with a strength and conditioning staffer off to the side. 
 Kaden Davis continues to impress with his opportunities. The former Division II receiver had several big catches, including a touchdown in the corner of the end zone from QB Case Keenum . Davis punted the ball in celebration and was immediately flagged. 
 Rookie corner Malik Muhammad played nickel during the two-minute drill. He had several reps with the first-team defense. 
 Raymond, a 10-year veteran, believes  Zavion Thomas ' work habits reflect that of an older player. Two nights ago, the rookie wide receiver sent Raymond a series of ankle mobility exercises to help strengthen the muscles in his lower leg and foot. "It's a vet-type mindset to be disciplined and do something like that," Raymond said. "And when he showed me that video, I was just happy to know that that's who he is." 
 Ben Johnson said there is no update on Kyler Gordon (calf), who is on PUP, and when he might return to practice. "We're just continuing to rehab," Johnson said. 
 

 

 Wednesday, Aug. 5 
 One day after becoming the highest-paid right tackle in NFL history, Darnell Wright got ribbed by coach Ben Johnson, who congratulated Wright on his four-year, $116 million extension ($93 million guaranteed) in front of the team before practice.

 Johnson joked that Wright "owed" offensive line coach Dan Roushar a loan. Wright agreed with Johnson's assessment and credited his position coach for helping him reach the point of his career where he's played his way into earning life-changing money.

 "[Roushar's] consistent every day in what he does and what he says," Wright said. "He's consistent in what he's telling you. ... Some coaches I've had in the past or some coaches in the league, they're not very good teachers. They see a guy with talent and blah, blah, blah, but they can't really convey what it is and teach you. You still need to be taught. So I think he is such a good teacher and he does it with such good -- he's not yelling at you, he's not screaming at you, he's not demeaning you, he's telling you what's good about the rep and he's telling you what's bad about the rep so you can see both sides.

 "If you have a coach that tells you just what you did was wrong with the rep so maybe the next rep, you just change everything. Now, you have a different result and you have no consistency to stack on top of each other, where as Dan he shows you what you did good with the rep so you can, you know, keep doing the good things and fix the bad things he tells you."

 During training camp in 2025, Roushar told reporters that he didn't see Wright playing with a consistently high motor. Wright said he appreciated the honesty and path Roushar laid for the right tackle to improve. That constructive criticism paid off as Wright earned second-team All-Pro honors while playing through an elbow injury.

 Wright was the inaugural first-round draft pick by general manager Ryan Poles in 2023. The Bears traded back one spot, from No. 9 to No. 10, which allowed the Philadelphia Eagles to draft defensive tackle Jalen Carter , while Chicago snagged its franchise right tackle.

 Proving to Poles that he made the right decision is something Wright internalized over the first three seasons of his career. Seeing how the investment made by the GM went far beyond a financial commitment motivates Wright to continue to progress.

 "[Poles] really invested in me [by] helping me get more one-on-one time with the coaches, one-on-one time more with the strength staff, one-on-one time more with [assistant strength and conditioning coach] Mark [Phillipi] in there doing core strength," Wright said. "...Even when I was a young player, it's hard for you to go up to a coach and want to demand their time. I know you're a first-round pick and blah, blah, blah, so they would probably be obliged, but sometimes it's hard for a player to approach a coach and want to take all their time when they've got stuff to do ... but he was invested in me at a really early age, beyond what you'd think a GM would do."

full_text:

 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest Bengals stories 
 
 Joe Burrow, Bengals find camaraderie on unusual battlefield 
 Bengals DE Stewart out multiple weeks with hyperextended knee 
 Bengals' top storylines at training camp 
 
 
 

 Thursday, Aug. 6 
 The offensive tinkering continued on Thursday as the Bengals try to find different ways to put pressure on opposing defenses. Throughout training camp, Cincinnati has had a ton of reps with QB Joe Burrow under center, which is not typically how the Bengals like to operate. But it's clear that finding ways to mix up the offensive formations is a strategy that will be critical to creating a more explosive offense. And offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher is OK with any lumps that are taken during the process.

 "We just wanna have a lot of tools at our disposal," Pitcher said on Thursday. "And that's what we're developing right now."

 
 The offense and defense traded pre-snap victories during an unscripted 11-on-11 drill. First, the defense forced a delay of game. But the offense responded by drawing the defense offsides. 
 Rookie defensive end Cashius Howell continues to turn heads. Howell took reps with the first team and created pressure off the edge. The second-round pick has been one of the camp's biggest stars. 
 Cincinnati appears to be experimenting with its back-up offensive tackles. Cody Ford and Andrew Coker swapped between the left and right sides during second-team reps. Cincinnati is looking to solidify the swing tackle spot behind starters Orlando Brown Jr . and Amarius Mims . 
 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 4 
 The defense continues its strong start to training camp. That was punctuated by a two-play exchange that started with a pass deflection by CB  DJ Turner  on a deep ball intended for WR Ja'Marr Chase , before safety S Bryan Cook had a pick-six off QB Joe Burrow during a team drill. Coordinator Al Golden's group has looked nothing like the team that has struggled in each of the past two seasons.

 "I think as a defense, we have an edge," Golden said. "We gotta continue to have that edge. We haven't done anything."

 
 Bengals CB DJ Ivey took first-team reps with Dax Hill sidelined. Hill was dealing with a bit of tightness and was limited for precautionary reasons. 
 DT Jonathan Allen was not at practice in what appeared to be a vet rest day. Allen also missed a day last week before quickly returning. 
 Cincinnati released S Isaiah Nwokobia on Tuesday. He had not practiced in back-to-back days. 
 

 

 Monday, Aug. 3 
 The first day of pads belonged to the Bengals' defense. And in what has become a recurring theme, the defensive line was able to bring some good pressure. Boye Mafe continued to affect the quarterback and rookie Cashius Howell had a clean win off the edge against the second-team defense.

 The defense isn't letting any camp success get to their heads. "We haven't scratched the surface, which is the encouraging thing," said linebacker Barrett Carter . "Our floor right now is high. I'm not trying to jinx us or put expectations on us, but we're stacking days, and we just have to keep doing that. We're nowhere near where we can be."

 More observations: 

 
 Dalton Risner and  Orlando Brown Jr . spent a good amount of time decompressing in the locker room talking about how the day went for them. It was a detailed conversation, which Risner said was an example of the group being dialed in this early in camp. 
 Rookie wide receiver Colbie Young made a couple of good catches. The coaching staff has been adamant that the fourth-round pick out of Georgia can carve out a role on this year's offense. 
 

 

 Saturday, Aug. 1 
 Have a day, Boye Mafe . The recent Super Bowl winner was disruptive throughout Saturday's practice. He consistently produced pressure against Joe Burrow and the first-team offense, including getting into a passing lane and forcing an interception .

 It has continued a good first week for the defense. But Mafe, who helped the Seahawks win the Lombardi Trophy in February with the Seahawks, knows Cincinnati has a long way to go.

 "I feel like we're really just setting our standard," Mafe said. "You can't mistake activity for achievement." 

 More observations: 

 
 WR Tee Higgins did not practice today but was a close observer. The team has made it a point to limit his workload to avoid any major soft-tissue injuries, a strategy that worked last season. 
 Former Bengals defensive end Sam Hubbard, who retired after the 2024 season, stopped by Saturday's practice to see his old teammates. 
 Practice started indoors because of rain but eventually moved to the outdoor fields. 
 Cornerback DJ Turner had a good pass deflection on a deep ball intended for Ja'Marr Chase . But was notable was the defensive backs making sure to yell "Ball!" to let Turner know the passes was about to arrive. It was an example of the communication the secondary has displayed during the first week of camp. 
 WR Mitchell Tinsley made a diving catch during a red zone drill that appeared to knock the wind out of him. While he was shaken up a touch, his efforts didn't go unnoticed. Offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher made it a point to give Tinsley props for the effort. 
 

 

 

 Friday, July 31 
 Typically, the Bengals don't practice three days in a row during training camp, but this year, Cincinnati is opening camp with four straight practices. So to break things up, Friday was more of a walk-through as the team managed the workload and tried to avoid major injuries. The Bengals didn't even bring helmets out as they slowed the pace down for a private practice. The team spent a couple of team periods working on red zone drills, which is typically what they do on Fridays during the season.

 More observations: 

 
 Bengals defensive tackle Jonathan Allen returned to practice after a day off on Thursday.  
 Dexter Lawrence II  didn't participate in Friday's walk-through. But the Pro Bowler has had sterling attendance since the Bengals traded for him ahead of April's draft. 
 

 

 Thursday, July 30 
 Bengals TE Erick All Jr . is still limited as he comes off an ACL injury that kept him out for all of the 2025 season. But he's already been tested.

 Over the offseason, he was hit by a moped in Greece that launched him into the air and scraped his face. But that was the jolt he needed as he looks to return from the injury he sustained during his rookie season.

 "It was huge for my confidence," All said. "That did a lot of good things for the mental [health]."

 If All is healthy, he could be a big chess piece for a Cincinnati offense looking to be creative in its personnel usage.

 Other observations: 

 
 Thursday featured a couple of big catches, including one from undrafted rookie Noah Thomas , who leaped and took the ball off cornerback DJ Ivey 's back as they wrestled to the ground. It impressed Ja'Marr Chase , who is pleased to have Thomas and Colbie Young , another rookie receiver out of Georgia.

title: What are the Browns looking for in their QB competition?
summary: Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders have spent seven camp practices focused on pre-snap and post-snap techniques.
full_text:
BEREA, Ohio -- A late practice sequence on Monday encapsulated the highs and lows that can occur in the Cleveland Browns ' quarterback competition on a given day.

 Shedeur Sanders was leading Cleveland's No. 2 offense in an end-of-game situational drill: down 2, near the goal line, with about a dozen seconds remaining and no timeouts left. The objective for Sanders was to attempt a pass into the end zone but leave enough time for a field goal in case of an incompletion. Sanders held the ball too long and finally threw a pass out of the back of the end zone with no time remaining, drawing the ire of coach Todd Monken.

 About 10 minutes later, Sanders displayed his growth before the snap. Leading a two-minute drill, Sanders signaled a tight end to motion inside and block, properly setting his protection to block the defense's blitz before delivering a deep touchdown pass to wide receiver Gage Larvadain .

 The quarterback competition between Sanders and Deshaun Watson has delivered plenty of highlights and lowlights in a week-plus of practices. But most importantly to Monken, it has brought teaching moments as he installs a new offense and evaluates each passer, focusing on pre-snap operation and post-snap execution.

 

 "I think to say who's ahead is a little extreme," Monken said before Wednesday's practice, the team's seventh camp session. "But we evaluate every day where our roster is, who's where. We try not to knee-jerk react on the one day; that's hard to do. We want every day to go as smooth as it can, and it doesn't, so you have to fight that part of it. We also have to fight; we're in install. We see what you see, and we see a little more in-depth because of the film. But the reality is we're always talking about personnel and the roster; the quarterbacks just happen to be part of that."

 Sanders and Watson have been alternating first-team reps every practice since the Browns opened training camp on July 29. Each session has consisted of 7-on-7s and 11-on-11s, in addition to various situational drills. Monken said the first eight (including Thursday's) practices will center around installing the offense, adding various portions of the scheme each day. Cleveland opened with zone runs and its short passing game before expanding to longer-developing pass concepts and gap scheme runs once padded practices began Monday.

 Monken said the installation will end Thursday, and he'll then start calling plays catering to each quarterback's strengths.

 Beyond how each quarterback looks throwing the ball, Monken has also prioritized perfecting the pre-snap operation. Multiple players have said Monken's scheme heaps plenty of responsibility on the quarterback before the ball is snapped, whether it be audibling into more favorable plays or executing various cadences. Through three practices, Monken had already incorporated 10 different cadences. With those have come a bevy of pre-snap infractions, but in the eyes of the first-year head coach, it's all a part of the learning curve for a new offense.

 The pre-snap operation has been one of the biggest points of emphasis for Sanders, who in his second season has continued to display a penchant for throwing an accurate deep ball.

 "Reviewing all the film from last year and the mistakes I made, and just being able to recognize, have a better pre-snap, be able to recognize things better and post-snap, also," Sanders said of his growth. "The fact that our defense gives us a lot of different looks and everything is truly great that we're able to get that in practice."

 Monken said he has been "highly impressed" by Sanders, dating back to his performance in the offseason workout program.

 "There's a lot to take in when you're installing," Monken said. "We got through the spring, then we were gone for six weeks, and then you start back up again in a new system. I think you'll continue to see his operation and mechanics improve, and I think that's the biggest part right now is in and out of the huddle, getting to the line of scrimmage, eliminating that anxiety, his anxiety and my anxiety."

 

 Watson, who did not play in 2025 after a pair of Achilles surgeries, got off to a slow start in training camp, throwing six interceptions in the first couple of practices. But he delivered his best session to date on Wednesday, throwing multiple touchdowns during 7-on-7 red zone drills. Monken previously downplayed Watson's spate of turnovers, saying they can be positive lessons, so long as the same mistakes aren't repeated.

 "The biggest thing for me is just letting my instincts take over -- not doing anything extra, not doing anything less, just staying balanced and letting it come," Watson said. "Day to day it's getting better, and honestly, I think the biggest thing is just playing football. Whenever the preseason games come up and we're out there playing, I think that's where we can learn. Each game is just an opportunity to get better at it."

 Monken said he'll continue to alternate first-team reps between Watson and Sanders until a starter is named. For the time being, the expectation is that both passers will start one of the first two preseason games, with the Browns' preseason opener against the Chicago Bears looming on Aug. 15.

 "I don't think you're really going to know until you get through all the installs, because we're not game-planning against our own defense," Monken said. "Each day has been a different part of the pass game, so it's hard to really [tell]. And one day you go with the 1s, the other day you go with the 2s; certainly that matchup is going to be different depending on who you're going against.

 "The most important thing is, from a process standpoint, how are we operating at the line of scrimmage, where are their eyes, have they taken command of one, the huddle, and then cadence, and then understanding the concepts. I think they're all doing good, they're all fine. All of our players are working through mistakes and fighting like hell to get better."

 Thursday, Aug. 6 
 With the Cowboys holding their Military Appreciation Day at training camp Thursday, Dak Prescott was presented with a gift from a fan.

 It was a Cowboys hat with a picture of his brother Jace on the side. At first, Prescott said he just thought it was a normal hat until he saw Jace, who died in 2020 . Prescott's Faith Fight Finish Foundation, which honors his brother as well as his mother, addresses mental health and suicide prevention.

 "That actually means a lot," Prescott said. "I wish I knew who did it because I would've said thank you. I just thought it was a hat. I didn't see it until I go with my daughters [after practice]. 
 
"It's badass."

 

 More observations: 

 
 Coach Brian Schottenheimer wanted to clarify the state of the left tackle competition. Tyler Guyton hasn't been named the starter yet, but Nate Thomas needs to up his level to make sure there is a competition. Guyton took part in Thursday's work with his right elbow taped after he didn't finish Tuesday's practice. Guyton and Thomas had false-start penalties leading to their departures for a play. 
 Tight end  Jake Ferguson is off to a strong start in camp. He and Prescott have had a clear connection on the intermediate and seam throws, and they connected four times Thursday with one completion coming on a "free" play when the defense jumped early that led to a decent gain. 
 Rookie LB Jaishawn Barham did not finish practice because of a groin injury. A source said it wasn't believed to be serious, and Barham was able to return to the field to watch the final parts of the workout. 
 It did not rise to the level of the Donovan Ezeiruaku punch, but cornerback Caelen Carson and rookie receiver Anthony Smith got into a tug-of-war and needed to be separated by teammates. It was brewing with both players after a particularly physical play early in team drills. 
 LB Curtis Robinson had a near interception of a Sam Howell pass down the seam to tight end Brevyn Spann-Ford , reaching high with his right hand to knock it down. The ball nearly fell into Robinson's lap as he landed on the ground. 
 

 

 Wednesday, Aug. 5 
 A year ago at this time, the Cowboys were learning about how  Javonte Williams  fit into their run game. They found out what he did well, as he rushed for 1,201 yards in 2025. Then they rewarded him with a three-year, $24 million contract in the offseason.

 As Williams enters his second season with the Cowboys, offensive coordinator Klayton Adams is looking to expand the list of what Williams does best.

 "Obviously the guy's pretty good on direct runs and he's hard to get down behind the line of scrimmage, but I think that he is a more diverse runner than he probably gets credit for," Adams said. "I think the guy does a really nice job with some of the outside zone stuff, particularly the weak side.

 "He's got really quick feet. He's able to get in and out of cuts really well. And he's one of those dudes that's not scared to run through the smoke, and that's what you're going to have to do on some of the time. I think he's good at a lot of things."

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 4 
 Sometimes coaches can be inventive when it comes to putting players through drills. On Tuesday, wide receivers coach Junior Adams had CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens catching passes off the Jugs machine during a special teams portion of practice while wearing what looked like a mosquito net or beekeeper's hat.

 The goal is to limit the receiver's vision and force him to concentrate longer on the catch. Lamb dropped one pass but figured it out. The first pass went through Pickens' hands, and he was finished.

 Longtime tight ends coach Mike Pope, who had a stint with the Cowboys, said he had 478 different drills for his tight ends. He would throw ice water at shirtless players while wearing a helmet. He had them wear swim goggles to limit their peripheral vision.

 Let's see if Adams has more tricks in his bag.

 Defensive end  Donovan Ezeiruaku was tossed from practice for fighting. Brian Schottenheimer abhors fighting in practice because if a player throws a punch in a game, he gets ejected. A lesson to be learned for Ezeiruaku. 
 With linebacker  DeMarvion Overshown battling a sore leg (a source said it was nothing to do with his surgically repaired knee), rookie Jaishawn Barham worked with the first-team defense next to Dee Winters . 
 Quarterback  Dak Prescott went 13-of-17 in team drills and would have been better if not for drops by Lamb and tight end  Jake Ferguson . He tried to stretch the field once with a throwback down the field to Pickens, who drew a flag on cornerback  Shavon Revel  at the goal line for pass interference. 
 Ferguson had two excellent catches, however, adjusting on a slightly underthrown seam ball from Prescott and later securing a lower pass with one hand before getting it under control. 
 Cornerback  Cobie Durant came up with the defensive play of the day, knocking away a deep ball from Prescott to wideout  Marquez Valdes-Scantling . Safety Alijah Clark was tangled up on the play and limped off to the medical tent and did not return. 
 

 

 

 Monday, Aug. 3 
 No, there is not going to be a playcaller controversy when it comes to the Cowboys this season, but coach Brian Schottenheimer gave the controls to coordinator Klayton Adams for two periods in Monday's practice, including red zone work.

 The result? Four touchdowns in a six-play span, including one to Ryan Flournoy where the receiver wrestled the ball away from cornerback  DaRon Bland for the score from Dak Prescott .

 "[Bland] actually guarded it great," Flournoy said. "I just had to win on that. I dropped slant before that so I had to make it up. Yeah, definitely great defense by DB. I just had to show strong hands."

 

 More observations from the day: 

 
 Second-year CB Shavon Revel Jr.  had a solid day, breaking up Prescott throws to CeeDee Lamb  and Flournoy, and blanketing George Pickens on a fade in the end zone. He had a pass interference penalty, reaching too early on a throw to Pickens, but it might have been the best practice Revel has had. 
 CB Cobie Durant picked off Prescott, undercutting a throw to Lamb near the goal line in which he dropped off another receiver and came up with the interception. 
 TE Jake Ferguson was back at practice after missing Saturday for personal reasons. He displayed strong hands on a TD catch in the back of the end zone while being covered by S Markquese Bell . 
 NFL officials were on hand for practice, but backup QB Joe Milton III took it into his own hands when an official did not throw a flag on rookie CB Devin Moore on a contested throw to Lamb in the end zone. The pass came on the defensive sideline, so perhaps there was some influence there, but Moore was aggressive on the play in…

 Thursday, Aug. 6 
 Wide receiver Jaylen Waddle , who left practice Wednesday with what appeared to be a left leg injury, did not practice Thursday and moved gingerly between drills as he watched practice.  Courtland Sutton , who had been held out the previous two days for rest, participated on a limited basis and is expected to practice fully Friday. Sutton said the team's training staff showed him tracking data from practices late in the season last year to talk to him about trying to pace him better through the season. "Last year I kind of got ran into the ground going into the end part of the season ... just trying to make sure the body stays as fresh as possible as late in the season as possible," he said. 
 Former Broncos coach Mike Shanahan, the franchise's winningest coach, including back-to-back Super Bowl wins to close out the 1997 and 1998 seasons, was at practice Thursday and received a tour of the team's new $178 million facility. 
 

 

 Wednesday, Aug. 5 
 Wide receiver Jaylen Waddle left Wednesday's practice and did not return. The Broncos' main offseason addition slowed down during a play in a team period and walked off to the locker room. He did not return to practice. Coach Sean Payton said after the workout that Waddle would be "fine" after the initial exam by the team's medical staff. "But we'll evaluate him ... he had some muscle tightness," he added.

 

 Payton has said repeatedly "we'll be smart" about returning players to practice after injuries. With the Broncos still nine days away from their preseason opener, Waddle could be held out of some practice time in the remainder of the week. Courtland Sutton was also given his second consecutive off day, so Marvin Mims Jr ., Troy Franklin and Pat Bryant got the bulk of the work with the starters after Waddle left the field.  Franklin and Bryant each had explosive plays in team drills Wednesday and Franklin might have had his best day of camp overall. The receiver combination of Sutton, Waddle, Mims, Franklin and Bryant -- if healthy -- looks like it will be the top five, so the Broncos would have to keep six receivers for another wideout to make the 53-player roster at the end of the preseason. 
 The Broncos again showed their cornerback depth, as Kris Abrams-Draine intercepted Bo Nix in an 11-on-11 period. 
 Sam Ehlinger took snaps with the second-team offense during multiple practice periods Wednesday and continues to push Jarrett Stidham for the backup quarterback job.  Tuesday, Aug. 4 

 Edge rusher Nik Bonitto limped off the practice field Tuesday after he suffered what appeared to be a lower left leg injury in a 9-on-7 run-game drill. Bonitto left the field with a trainer as well as one of the team doctors and did not return. After practice, Broncos coach Sean Payton would say only "he'll be fine, no updates."

 Bonitto has led the team in sacks in each of the past two seasons -- 13.5 in 2024 and 14.0 in 2025 - helping the Broncos lead the league and establish single-season franchise records in each campaign. Jonah Elliss and Jonathon Cooper took most of the snaps with the starters at the edge spots after Bonitto left practice, with second-year man Que Robinson getting more work throughout the day as well.

 Wide receiver Courtland Sutton was held out of practice Tuesday for rest, as Payton had said this week he would begin to give some of the veteran players scheduled days off.
