summary: Follow our daily updates from Dolphins training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The  Miami Dolphins  camp is taking place in Miami Gardens, and Dolphins reporter Marcel Louis-Jacques has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Dolphins camp. We will update this file often. Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Dolphins camp 
 
 Dolphins top pick Proctor embracing NFL learning curve 
 Miami, All-Pro LB Jordyn Brooks reach 3-year, $51.3M extension 
 Dolphins, Aaron Brewer reach 3-year, $52.5 million extension 
 Why Miami's rookies can thrive 
 
 

 Thursday, Aug. 6 

 Pressure, pressure and more pressure was the key word for the Dolphins in Thursday's practice. The team shed its shoulder pads, looking to ease back into work following Wednesday's off day, but it didn't stop coach Jeff Hafley's defense from attacking its offensive counterparts throughout team drills.

 Linebacker Jackson Woodard was a constant presence around the ball, while defensive end Chop Robinson continued his strong camp -- albeit against a banged up right side of the Dolphins' offensive line. Thursday also marked another strong performance from rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez ; defensive coordinator Sean Duggan said he could tell the game is starting to slow down for Rodriguez and the other rookie linebackers, Kyle Louis and Trey Moore .

 More conversations: 

 
 Running back Jaylen Wright broke of a couple strong runs during team drills. Speaking to the media earlier this week, he sounded calm and at peace with his career to date and ready to attack the best opportunity he's had for regular playing time since entering the league in 2024. 
 Linebacker Willie Gay Jr . intercepted quarterback Cam Miller and returned it for a long gain. We've seen Gay stand out at training camp before, the Dolphins are hoping his momentum carries into game day this preseason, and the regular season. 
 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 4 
 If you were building a basketball team out of Dolphins players, defensive tackle Zach Sieler -- all 6-foot-6, 300 pounds of him -- might be a choice at power forward. But coach Jeff Hafley said the nine-year veteran is actually more of a point guard on the team's defensive line.

 Despite his 25.5 sacks over the past three seasons, Hafley said Sieler's ability and willingness to take on blockers and open rush lanes for his teammates really pops on tape.

 When asked about the comparison after Tuesday's practice, Sieler said it all comes down to being selfless and a team player.

 "You've got to be a leader, you've got to be vocal -- but you can't be selfish," he said. "The better we do as a unit, the better we'll do as a team ... If someone's making plays one day and you're not, the plays will come. Don't stress, because when you stress and try to force a play, that's when bad things happen."

 More observations: 

 
 Defensive end Chop Robinson goes through stretches where he's simply unblockable -- his speed off the line of scrimmage has given the Dolphins' offensive tackles fits all summer, and continued to do so Tuesday. Fellow defensive end Josh Uche also had a pair of sacks in team drills. 
 Right tackle Austin Jackson , tight end Greg Dulcich and safety Lonnie Johnson Jr . did not participate in Tuesday's practice because of what Hafley described as "day to day" injuries. Neither player is expected to miss much time, but rookie UDFA DT Rene Konga will miss the entire season with an undisclosed injury suffered Monday. 
 Quarterback Malik Willis threw an interception to Zayne Anderson on the first play of the team's red-zone drill, but followed it up the next play with a touchdown pass to running back De'Von Achane . 
 

 

 
 Monday, Aug. 3 
 Malik Willis still isn't scrambling in team drills as the Dolphins want him to focus on making plays from the pocket in training camp, but he's displaying a keen ability to evade pressure and keep his eyes downfield.

 On multiple occasions during Monday's practice, Willis kept a play alive and found a receiver downfield. He spun away from pressure and found a wide open Malik Washington over the middle for an explosive gain, and lofted another off-platform throw to rookie tight end Seydou Traore -- who came down with a one-handed catch for a first down.

 Willis did throw an interception off a tipped pass, but the ball placement certainly could've been better. He also missed a throw to a wide open Caleb Douglas , who got hands on the ball but couldn't come down with it. But Willis has flashed some touch over the past few practices.

 More observations: 

 
 Linebacker Tyrel Dodson returned an interception for a touchdown in team drills, tracking the ball after it deflected off tight end Cole Turner 's hands. In Turner's defense, the ball from Willis was far too low. 
 Cornerback Ethan Bonner intercepted Quinn Ewers ' first pass of the team's game-winning drive drill, again off a deflected pass. 
 Both Willis and Ewers led their groups into field goal range during game-winning drive drills, and both kickers attempted field goals with each unit. Riley Patterson was good from 50 yards before missing from 43 yards, while Zane Gonzalez made both kicks. Both kickers were good from 52 yards on their third attempt. 
 Safety Lonnie Johnson Jr. appeared to suffer a lower body injury after thudding running back Jaylen Wright in team drills. He was attended to on the sideline and didn't return. 
 Tight end Greg Dulcich did not practice Monday for an unspecified reason, and the group's production tapered off without him. 
 Defensive end Chop Robinson blew by right tackle Charlie Heck on back-to-back plays to start the game-winning drill. The first one was credited as a sack, but Willis got the ball off just in time on the second play, hitting tight end Ben Sims over the middle for a first down. 
 

 
 Sunday, Aug. 2 
 The Dolphins' offense woke up in a major way in an exciting practice in front of fans Sunday morning. Running back De'Von Achane kicked things off with an explosive run on the first play of team drill, while wide receivers Tutu Atwell , Kevin Coleman Jr ., and AJ Henning each had receptions of at least 50 yards.

 Coach Jeff Hafley has introduced "competitive" practice segments in which the "loser" endures some sort of punishment; Sunday, that meant the defense owed Hafley 20 pushups after practice.

 "(Last practice) we beat the offense, today they got us back," rookie cornerback Chris Johnson said. "So we're looking forward to taking the lead back tomorrow."

 

 More observations: 

 
 Johnson turned in yet another strong performance, intercepting a Quinn Ewers pass early on in team drills. The 2026 first-round pick out of San Diego State has trained at both cornerback spots this summer and is destined for a big role this season. 
 Henning turned in his best practice in a Dolphins uniform, dating back to last season. He was the intended receiver on Johnson's interception, but made up for it with 50-plus yard receptions from both Ewers and Cam Miller -- the latter being an over-the-shoulder grab in stride on the final play of practice. 
 Despite the explosive passing plays, arguably the best throw of the day might have been a 10-yard pass from Malik Willis , where he perfectly lofted the ball to tight end Cole Turner just over linebacker Jordyn Brooks ' reach. Impressive touch from Willis, especially while on the move. 
 

 

 Friday, July 31 
 Wide receiver Caleb Douglas turned in his best day of practice yet, and it's…

title: Latest buzz on Vikings' Kyler Murray-J.J. McCarthy QB1 battle
summary: Here is the latest buzz on how  Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy have performed in their competition to lead Minnesota's offense.
full_text:
EAGAN, Minn. -- As promised, the Minnesota Vikings have split snaps between quarterbacks Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy through the first seven practices of training camp as part of a declared competition. Beneath the surface, however, daily observers have seen plenty of indications that Murray remains the heavy favorite to win the job. 

 Both quarterbacks have produced strong and weak moments over roughly 300 snaps during 7-on-7 and 11-on-11 drills, and each has spent time with the first and second teams. In theory, there is enough time for McCarthy to launch a late run. There have been only two padded practices so far and there will be six more days of on-field work before the Vikings' first preseason game.

 

 But the Vikings have given Murray roughly two-thirds of the snaps with the first-team offense in 11-on-11 drills, a rate that might not carry much meaning for a single practice but is a clear pattern over the course of a week, and he has used them productively. The imbalance can partially be explained by Murray's relative inexperience in the offense, and the need to get him up to speed. But unless it reverses in the coming week, it is hard to imagine McCarthy -- or any player at any position -- winning the job while spending the majority of the most important snaps of camp with the second team. 

 Instead, McCarthy has spent a significant portion of his summer working with the No. 2 offense but against the No. 1 defense. It is a challenging spot but one that NFL coaches have long used to spur development from young players. His passes have skewed more toward the short-range and midrange variety, with less frequent deep attempts than Murray.

 And coincidentally or otherwise, the Vikings have been experimenting with more shotgun and pistol handoffs than they have used in the recent past, particularly in the run game. The Vikings have been the NFL's third-heaviest under-center team in the NFL (47%) during coach Kevin O'Connell's tenure, while Murray's Arizona Cardinals used it at the league's third-lowest rate (18.3%) over his previous seven seasons. 

 During a recent visit with reporters, O'Connell praised both quarterbacks and cautioned against a search for tendencies to their deployment. He did, however, say Murray has "shown improvement every single day" and said it was clear that Murray worked hard to study the offense during his summer break. O'Connell said he was encouraged that Murray has hit some downfield throws but added: "We're just trying to implement our offense. We're trying to really focus on some foundational things that the quarterbacks play a big role in, but it's an all-11 thing right now for sure, regardless of what personnel grouping we're in."

 Let's take a closer look. 

 

 

 Kyler Murray 

 Two factors prompted the initial assessment that Murray was the favorite to win the job. 

 First, Murray was a top-15 quarterback in the NFL during his time with the Cardinals, based on combined QBR of players with enough action plays to qualify. He was not a superstar, but he had established a clear baseline performance, even if he hadn't played in the exact offense O'Connell runs. The amount of ground that McCarthy would have to make up to match Murray's baseline, based on McCarthy's performance in 2025, was substantial.

 Second, the Vikings had already fired general manager Kwesi Adofo-Mensah, who drafted McCarthy. That meant Murray would not need to overcome any organizational inertia that might have favored McCarthy, whom the Vikings used the No. 10 draft pick to select in 2024. 

 Both factors have featured prominently this summer.

 Murray has had his share of the kind of miscommunications that would be expected for a quarterback in a new offense, including several throws that didn't match with the receivers' route. One of them, at the end of a rough two-minute drill Monday, prompted O'Connell to end the practice early. 

 But there have been no indications that Murray is fundamentally uncomfortable with or incapable of what the Vikings have asked him to do, either to the naked eye or in discussions behind the scenes. 

 He has found receiver Justin Jefferson on a series of deep crossing routes, while Jauan Jennings and Tai Felton have caught touchdowns on deep posts, and he has demonstrated a level of touch, arc and accuracy that McCarthy is still working to master. 

 Some might have winced at the jump ball Murray threw toward Jefferson and into double coverage during a two-minute drill Wednesday. But Jefferson jumped over cornerback Isaiah Rodgers and safety Theo Jackson to make the catch, a reminder that some receivers merit riskier throws than others. 

 

 In short, Murray has performed at the level to be expected from a quarterback with his performance profile, within the context of adapting to an entirely new offense. That assessment matches the expectations he expressed when camp first began.

 "I feel great," Murray said July 29. "Really helped me going through OTAs for sure. Having done it once now, obviously this time it's about to be real, but I truly believe that going through OTAs has prepared me for what's to come."

 

 J.J. McCarthy 

 McCarthy has not appeared as frenetic as he did during his worst moments of last season and clearly has a full understanding of the offense. In retrospect, however, the expectation he set out during his own July 29 meeting with reporters has proved prescient.

 Speaking about his pre-camp discussions with O'Connell, McCarthy said: "Conversations were great. Just all about doing my job and doing it to the best of my ability, taking completions, taking what the defense is giving me, making smart decisions, and at the end of the day, just doing my job. Very simple."

 McCarthy's time in full team drills has been notable for the number of occasions that appear designed to get him into a rhythm with a bootleg or another quick, short-range pass. They represent many of his completions over the first week, although one of his interceptions came when linebacker Jake Golday tipped a short pass McCarthy threw while on the run.

 

 McCarthy has thrown some well-placed deep-corner or out routes to receivers Dontae Fleming and Myles Price , but overall his accuracy has been inconsistent. 

 Some of his passes over the middle have appeared late or slightly off target and resulted in incompletions. Earlier in the two-minute drill that O'Connell eventually ended early, cornerback Byron Murphy Jr . stepped in front of a pass to Jefferson on a crossing route for an interception.

 Tuesday, he overthrew three consecutive passes during a red zone period against air -- with no defenders in the drill. On the first, veteran running back Aaron Jones Sr . launched himself into a full-body dive to get closer to the ball but could not make the catch. 

 Reasonable people can argue about exactly where McCarthy is on his developmental timeline. But no objective observer to training camp could say that he has made up the ground necessary to truly challenge Murray. 

 

 Scheme 

 Murray began his time as an NFL quarterback in a shotgun-based Air Raid offense similar to what he used in college. His relative inexperience beginning a play under center, which O'Connell has used in part to build play-action concepts that set up downfield throws, has been cited as one of Murray's potential roadblocks to success in Minnesota. 

 

 But Murray is not the only newcomer to the Vikings' offense. O'Connell hired assistant head coach Frank Smith in part to help diversify his running game, and the frequency with which the Vikings have at least practiced running out of spread formations has been notable. Murray has displayed no observable difficulties under center, and offensive coordinator Wes Phillips said this week that Murray has proved to be "very comfortable playing any which way you want him to play football."

 Phillips, however, did acknowledge the diversification of formations the Vikings are…

title: 2026 Minnesota Vikings training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Vikings training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The Minnesota Vikings ' camp is taking place in Eagan, Minnesota, and Vikings reporter Kevin Seifert has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Vikings camp. We will update this file often. Who will win the starting quarterback battle between incumbent J.J. McCarthy and free agent addition Kyler Murray ? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest Vikings stories 

 
 What McCarthy-Murray QB battle means for Vikings' locker room 
 Vikings, O'Neill reach $96M extension 
 Top Vikings storylines after minicamp, from QBs to new GM 
 Will Vikings start Caleb Banks, other rookies on defense? 
 Jefferson says decision on Vikings starting QB 'coach's call' 
 
 

 Wednesday, Aug.5 

 The Vikings haven't won a playoff game since 2019 and have three playoff victories in the past 25 seasons. So during his annual training camp meeting with reporters, co-owner/president Mark Wilf was asked about the patience his family has exhibited during its tenure as owners.

 "We try to be patient as an ownership, and that we know [leads to] ultimate success," he said. "But of course, patience isn't infinite. We understand that, but I feel really good about the direction of this football club and we're going to get to those benchmarks."

 Mark and Zygi Wilf hired general manager Nolan Teasley this spring to work with fifth-year coach Kevin O'Connell. Of their early interactions, Mark Wilf said: "I just think they work well together. I had an opportunity to watch them interact, and I just see how comfortable they are with each other. They have different characteristics but from my perspective, it's working well. And I think coach can focus on what he has to focus on. Nolan can focus on what he focuses on and they share and they collaborate and everyone in the building feels that."

 

 More observations: 

 
 Facing pressure during a two-minute drill, quarterback Kyler Murray made a smart decision: He lofted a jump ball for receiver Justin Jefferson . Predictably, Jefferson extended over cornerback Isaiah Rodgers and safety Theo Jackson to make the catch and scoot into the end zone. Murray also had a key scramble during the drill, keeping the drive alive. 
 Receiver Jordan Addison jammed his thumb Tuesday. O'Connell said tests revealed no serious injury. During practice, Addison was in full pads and ran routes during individual drills. But he did not have a pass thrown in his direction, and he worked out on a side field during team drills. 
 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 4 

 As members of the 2023 draft class begin getting contract extensions, Vikings receiver Jordan Addison  said Tuesday that he is focused on "being where my feet are."

 Four receivers were drafted between picks No. 20-23 that year, and two of them -- Seattle's Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Baltimore's Zay Flowers -- have agreed to new deals. Addison and the Vikings have had to navigate two arrests and one citation during his time in the NFL, and Addison said: "I'm just putting in the work in right now, going through camp, making sure I'm becoming a better receiver, and I feel like everything is going to take care of itself."

 Addison leads the 2023 class with 22 career touchdown receptions. He ranks eighth with 175 receptions and fourth with 2,396 receiving yards.

 "He loves football," Vikings coach Kevin O'Connell said. "He's a great teammate. Clearly he was a young player when he came into the NFL. I think he's learned, matured and he knows exactly what's out in front of him. He knows what's important to him. I'm proud of his growth and development in that phase as well and I think there's a lot of folks in this building that deeply, deeply care about Jordan and what's best for him on and off the field moving forward, and you can count me as one of them."﻿

 More observations: 

 
 The Vikings had a relatively light practice Tuesday in shells, one day after their first full-pads practice of summer. Quarterback J.J. McCarthy elicited murmurs from fans in the stands after overthrowing three consecutive passes in the red zone against no defense, but he came back later with two strong throws on deep outs to receivers  Myles Price  and Dontae Fleming . 
 

 

 Monday, Aug. 3 
 Neither Kyler Murray nor J.J. McCarthy took a step forward Monday during the fifth practice -- and first in full pads -- of their competition to win the Minnesota Vikings ' starting quarterback job. The pair roughly split first-team snaps during 11-on-11 team drills, with Murray getting 10 and McCarthy eight.

 Murray found Justin Jefferson crossing across the field after evading the pass rush, but he also threw high over the middle to receiver Jordan Addison . On the play, Addison and cornerback Isaiah Rodgers collided in the air, flipping Anderson and sending Rodgers sprawling.

 The practice ended with a rough two-minute sequence for both quarterbacks. In five snaps, McCarthy went 0-for-3 with two tipped passes and an interception on a throw to Jefferson that cornerback Byron Murphy Jr . stepped in front of. Murray took over for two snaps with the second team, going 0-for-2 with a pass behind tight end Josh Oliver on the first and a miscommunication on the second.

 More observations from the day: 

 
 
 Receiver Tai Felton , a third-round draft pick in 2025, made the catch of camp in 7-on-7 drills, leaping high to grab a Murray pass in the back corner of the end zone. Felton has been working as the No. 4 receiver behind Justin Jefferson, Jordan Addison and Jauan Jennings .

 
 
 Cornerback James Pierre returned to practice after sitting out at the end of last week. Rookie running back Demond Claiborne was in full pads but worked out on a side field for players who are rehabilitating injuries."

 
 

 

 Saturday, Aug. 1 
 Quarterback Kyler Murray had by far his best day of training camp Saturday, pinpointing a series of downfield throws in traffic while taking the majority of the Vikings' first-team reps as his competition with J.J. McCarthy continues.

 Murray was on the field for 16 of the first-team offense's 22 snaps in 11-on-11 team drills. McCarthy took the other six. Murray hit receiver Justin Jefferson on a deep dig route over the middle and he threw another perfectly placed pass on his next series that receiver Myles Price dropped. All three of Murray's passes to Jefferson were complete, and Price's drop was Murray's only incompletion among seven passes in team drills.

 McCarthy did not find similar success while working mostly with the second team against the first-team defense. He threw one pass on the run that rookie linebacker Jake Golday tipped, and was intercepted by linebacker Blake Cashman . McCarthy's best throw of the day came during a stint with the first team, but tight end T.J. Hockenson was unable to come up with the ball in traffic in the end zone.

 

 More observations from the day: 

 
 At one point Saturday, the Vikings had three rookies working in the same package on their first-team defense: defensive linemen Caleb Banks and Domonique Orange , along with Golday. 
 Cornerback James Pierre was not in uniform for Saturday's practice. Rookie running back Demond Claiborne was not seen in team drills.

title: 2026 New England Patriots training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Patriots training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The New England Patriots ' camp is taking place in Foxborough, Massachusetts, and Patriots reporter Mike Reiss has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Patriots camp. We will update this file often. Will Drake Maye  start another MVP-like campaign in Year 3? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive into all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Patriots camp 
 
 A.J. Brown on injury: 'Thumb out of place, you keep going' 
 Patriots' Brown knows Vrabel's rip comes from 'great place' 
 Kraft: Patriots' Gonzalez has offer to be 'highest-paid' CB ever 
 Too many receivers? A look at the Patriots' crowded WR room 
 
 
 

 Thursday, Aug. 6 
 Cornerback Christian Gonzalez and receiver A.J. Brown needed to be separated at one point of Thursday's practice, as the competitive one-on-one matchup between them that has been a highlight of Patriots training camp nearly boiled over.

 The fireworks seemed to be sparked by Gonzalez's trash talk following a red zone drill in which his tight coverage held Brown without a catch. As the Patriots transitioned to a different period of practice, Gonzalez appeared to be chirping in Brown's direction. At first, Brown was walking away, but something appeared to spark him to turn back in Gonzalez's direction.

 Receiver Kayshon Boutte also came over to that area of the sideline and said he was trying to pull Brown away from Gonzalez. Boutte said he heard someone say, "You're a grown man!"

 The battle between Gonzalez and Brown seemed to build throughout the full-pads practice, with Gonzalez gesturing in Brown's direction after covering him tightly in 11-on-11 drills as a long pass from quarterback Drake Maye in that direction was incomplete.

 In the final drill, Brown caught a comeback route on Gonzalez.

 "It's good on good. He's a No. 1 receiver in this league going up against a No. 1 corner. That's how it's going to go," Gonzalez said after practice. "It's football at the end of the day. There's never no disrespect or anything. We're just battling to make each other better.

 "He's going to face corners like that, that are going to yap at him and try to get in his head. And I'm going to face receivers like that, that are strong and are going to come right back at me. It's great work for the both of us."

 

 More observations: 

 
 The practice ended with three straight interceptions as the offense was in a game-ending situation running the two-minute offense. CB Marcus Jones and S Kevin Byard picked off Maye, while S John Saunders Jr. picked off backup QB Tommy DeVito . Coach Mike Vrabel called the team together at that point and ended practice. 
 Starting LT Will Campbell didn't participate in team drills, which thrust 2025 seventh-round pick Marcus Bryant into the top unit over 2026 first-round pick Caleb Lomu . That is due, in part, to Lomu mostly having worked at right tackle. 
 Rookie OLB Gabe Jacas (second round, Illinois) received his first reps with the top defense. 
 With no wind, high humidity and temperatures in the 90s, this was the hottest day of the Patriots' 11 training camp practices. 
 CB Carlton Davis III , WR Cameron Dorner , WR Romeo Doubs and FB Jack Westover did not practice, while starting DT Christian Barmore , top reserve CB Charles Woods and rookie OLB Quintayvious Hutchins left early. 
 Rookie QB Behren Morton (seventh round, Texas Tech) had a surprise waiting for him upon his arrival at practice, as his parents James and Suni made the trip to town from Texas. 
 Third-unit G Caedan Wallace returned to practice. 
 The Patriots had free agent guard Greg Van Roten in for a workout. Guard depth is thin/unproven with Andrew Rupcich (left) and James Hudson III (right) the top backups in practice, while backup C Ben Brown would likely get the first call in the event of injury. 
 

 

 

 
 Wednesday, Aug. 5 
 If the Patriots are indeed considering the possibility of trading wide receiver Kayshon Boutte , their walk-through practice Wednesday was a reminder about why they should reconsider. An unexpected absence can change the receiver outlook quickly.

 Big-bucks free agent signing Romeo Doubs was not present Wednesday, opening the door further for Boutte -- who has had a strong training camp -- to carve out a larger niche as a "comforting" option for quarterback Drake Maye .

 Doubs' absence likely isn't anything serious. He appeared slightly hobbled in recent days, so it simply might be a much-needed rest day. But as Maye recently pointed out, the Patriots are going to need all their receivers, and no one has made more plays down the field than Boutte through 10 practices.

 Maye described him as a "comforting receiver to throw to" and noted his quiet demeanor and how he's "going to be in the right spot and make a play on the football."

 Maye was asked about how Boutte after Wednesday's walk-through, saluting his professionalism despite being mentioned in media-based trade rumors on a regular basis.

 "I think the way Kayshon has approached it -- he's here now, he's where his feet are at. I'm having fun throwing to him out there in practice. He's doing a great job. He makes plays when the football is in the air, and I think that speaks for itself. I've had a lot of great times with Kayshon and I'm looking forward to keep getting better each and every day."

 More observations: 

 
 TE CJ Dippre , who opened training camp on the physically unable to perform list, was in uniform for the first time. He could face an uphill climb for the TE3 role behind Hunter Henry and Eli Raridon , as undrafted free agent Tanner Arkin has been one of the surprise stories of training camp. 
 With RB Terrell Jennings returning to practice Monday, he has quickly established himself as the leading candidate for the RB3 role behind Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson , in part due to his special teams presence. At running back, Jennings is competing against 2025 undrafted free agent Lan Larison , 2026 seventh-round pick Jam Miller and 2026 undrafted free agent Myles Montgomery . 
 There continues to be notable movement at linebacker, where Chad Muma has consistently been the top backup in training camp, and rookies Khalil Jacobs (more of a middle linebacker) and Namdi Obiazor (weakside linebacker) are pushing veteran free agent signing K.J. Britt for reps on defense and special teams. 
 The slower-paced walk-through provided further context on health/injury-based situations, as CB Carlton Davis III remained out of practice since appearing to injure his hamstring July 28. In addition to Davis and Doubs, the other players not present were WR Cameron Dorner , G Caedan Wallace and FB/TE Jack Westover . Meanwhile, ST captain Brenden Schooler remains on the non-football injury list and OLB Harold Landry III remains on the PUP list. 
 

 

 
 Tuesday, Aug. 4 
 Rookie outside linebacker Gabe Jacas answered questions from reporters Tuesday for the first time since missing the entire spring and signing a contract two days into training camp, saying he wasn't looking back.

 "First and foremost, I just want to say how grateful I am to be here," the second-round pick from Illinois told the assembled media after the ninth practice of training camp. "It was a long journey, but I'm just glad to be part of this organization. It's a blessing to be at practice and run around."

 Jacas underwent a procedure on his left knee in May, which led to his absence and contract impasse. His contract includes…

title: 2026 New Orleans Saints training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Saints training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The  New Orleans Saints ' camp is taking place in Metairie, Louisiana, and Saints reporter Katherine Terrell has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Saints camp. We will update this file often. Kellen Moore enters his second season as head coach, and expectations are higher after  Tyler Shough  impressed while starting the final nine games of the 2025 campaign. Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest Saints news 
 
 Drew Brees' greatness, as seen through eyes of teammates, coaches 
 Saints place WR Ja'Lynn Polk, 24, on reserve/retired list 
 Saints starting DT Bryan Bresee to have season-ending ACL surgery 
 The legacy of Taysom Hill in New Orleans: 'There's only one' 
 WR Chris Olave signing four-year extension 
 
 
 Thursday, Aug. 6 
 Rookie wide receiver Barion Brown continues to be the rising star of camp after he concluded Thursday's practice with a 46-yard touchdown from Spencer Rattler to finish out the two-minute drill.

 "Spencer got out of it -- we'll watch the film to see if there's a sack. There's always a debate of sack/no sack, it's never ending. So we let it play out and Barion did a great job adjusting to that ball, tracking it, those are deep balls and the ball usually tails one way or another because the QB is running, so awesome job making a play," coach Kellen Moore said.

 While Brown has mostly been with the second team to start camp, he's starting to get more opportunities, including some snaps with the first team in the two-minute drill, where he caught a pass from Tyler Shough for about a 15-yard gain.

 

 More observations: 

 
 Chris Rumph (ankle), Devin Neal (hamstring) did not finish practice. Christen Miller (toe), Jeremiah Wright (shoulder) and Kendre Miller (back) are day-to-day and did not participate Thursday. 
 Alvin Kamara was not at practice, which Moore said was due to a rest day. 
 It was a rough day for kicker Charlie Smyth , who went 3-for-6 and missed three straight field goals in the indoor facility. Smyth missed from 39, 45 and 51 yards, so the team backed things up to 39 yards again. When he made that, they attempted another 51-yarder, which was good. He is now 17-of-22 for camp. 
 The first-team two-minute drill was won by the defense after a sack (pressure from Cameron Jordan ) and an interception of Shough by Quincy Riley (pressure from Carl Granderson ) as time expired. The offense was moving the ball well prior to that, with Shough completing two passes to Juwan Johnson and then passes to Travis Etienne Jr ., Chris Olave and Brown before spiking the ball to stop the clock. 
 Shough was also picked off by Kool-Aid McKinstry in the previous set of team drills in the end zone. Moore said it looked like the pass came up short in a throwaway situation. Etienne had the ball four plays in a row prior to the interception. 
 
 
 Wednesday, Aug. 5 
 Wide receiver Barion Brown , a sixth-round pick in April's draft, has seemed to find his stride since the pads came on. Brown has taken advantage of the one-on-one drills vs. defensive backs and made several nice catches during that period Wednesday. He also had a 36-yard catch-and-run from Spencer Rattler over safety Jordan Howden in the two-minute drill to end practice. That play helped the Saints get into field goal range.

 Brown was the third receiver the Saints drafted this year and he came in with the potential to make the team as a kick returner. Saints coach Kellen Moore said they saw more than that when they drafted Brown, who played at Kentucky and LSU.

 "We watched a lot of evidence of him playing receiver and playing impactful plays in the SEC for a number of years, not just the LSU year, but the Kentucky years. And when you watch all that exposure and get to know Barion, you're really fired up to have this guy," Moore said.

 

 More observations: 

 
 Cesar Ruiz was back at practice following the birth of his son, which he described as the best experience of his life. 
 Running back Kendre Miller is dealing with a back issue that has kept him limited in the past two practices. Christen Miller has a toe issue and Jeremiah Wright left early with a shoulder ailment. 
 The Saints worked the two-minute drill to end practice. The scenario was that the offense was down 3 with less than two minutes and one timeout. Both the first- and second-team offenses kicked a field goal to tie. 
 Tanner Brown  made 5 of 6 field goals, with a miss from 39 yards. He also kicked the two-minute field goals. Charlie Smyth is now 15-for-16 in camp and Brown is 17-for-19. 
 Linebacker Kaden Elliss , who is sometimes used as a pass rusher, worked in one-on-one drills against the OL. That drill is usually OL vs. DL but Moore said Elliss wanted to do the drill to get more reps. 
 

 
 Monday, Aug. 3 
 The Saints' offense bounced back in the team's first day in pads. It was a run-focused day featuring some usage of 12 and 13 personnel (sets with two and three tight ends).

 Saints quarterback Tyler Shough and the offensive unit had a solid end to practice when he completed a pass to Alvin Kamara , hit Travis Etienne Jr . near the sideline and connected again with Etienne, who found running room thanks to a hole opened up by Erik McCoy .

 Shough also had completions to Jordyn Tyson and Juwan Johnson (the last one coming with pressure from several defensive linemen). Rookie wideout Barion Brown had what might have been the play of the day, catching a deep pass down the sideline from Spencer Rattler while going against cornerback Martin Emerson Jr. 

 

 More observations from the day: 

 
 Charlie Smyth made five of six field goal attempts, missing his first kick of camp (wide right from 55 yards). Smyth kicked a 44-yarder again after his miss and made it. 
 Quincy Riley and Isaac Yiadom  substituted in with the first team at outside cornerback. Linebacker Danny Stutsman also got first-team reps. 
 The Saints practiced one-on-one individual drills for the first time. Tyson did not participate in those to limit his overall reps for the day, but Bub Means had a few solid reps. 
 Cesar Ruiz had another excused absence after the recent birth of his child. 
 Coach Kellen Moore did not say whether the Saints planned to bring in another receiver after the unexpected retirement of Ja'Lynn Polk . 
 

 
 Sunday, Aug. 2 
 The Saints' defense had a solid showing in a day that involved a lot of 11-on-11 red zone work. It specifically shined in the final period of the day. Linebacker Pete Werner punched the ball out of running back  Travis Etienne Jr .'s hands after he caught a pass from Tyler Shough ; safety Jonas Sanker blitzed and had a pressure to force an incompletion; and Chase Young had a pressure on an end zone interception from Shough that was caught by Julian Blackmon .

 On the first play of team drills, Shough made a nice downfield throw from the Saints' 35-yard line to Chris Olave in the end zone, but it was hard to tell if Olave, working against Quincy Riley , came down with the ball in bounds.

 More observations from the day: 

 
 The Saints practiced in their indoor facility because of a rainstorm, so practice was closed to fans. 
 Saints coach Kellen Moore said defensive tackle Bryan Bresee will have surgery for a torn ACL . 
 Tanner Brown rotated in as kicker and went 5-for-5 in field goals. So far he has missed one field goal in camp and Charlie Smyth has missed none. 
 Shough was knocked to the ground…

title: 2026 New York Giants training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Giants training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The New York Giants camp is taking place at The Greenbrier in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia, and Giants reporter Jordan Raanan has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Giants camp. We will update this file often. How will the Giants handle increased expectations and a new coach? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Giants camp 
 
 Cam Skattebo admits doing 'dumb things,' will save backflips for TDs 
 Nabers 'looked good' in 1st practice since knee injury 
 Giants have spoken with Skattebo after Fanatics Fest flip 
 2026 New York Giants training camp preview 
 
 
 Thursday, Aug. 6 
 The Giants shed the pads after three straight days of full contact. Coach John Harbaugh ran a 2½-hour walk-through to give his players' bodies some rest.

 They'll be back at it Friday and Saturday with full padded practices before leaving West Virginia.

 Harbaugh has run a hard training camp to date. The Giants ran over 100 live plays in the heat Wednesday. It has been in stark contrast to the training camps they had under Brian Daboll.

 But the Giants knew this was going to be the case. Harbaugh is known to run a tough camp. Even his practices in the spring don't waste time and have a lot of live periods.

 "Man, it's tough, gritty," cornerback Greg Newsome II said. "We're going to work, and I like that. There's no off days for us in terms of not competing. He's going to make sure we compete. We're always doing situational football and things like that. So, it's been super fun to play. He's a great coach. We're always talking all the time and I'm super excited to play for him."

 Other observations: 

 
 CB Dru Phillips has a mild knee sprain and will miss some time. CB Jarrick Bernard-Converse also didn't practice again and is dealing with an "ongoing" knee problem. Harbaugh said the Giants might sign another cornerback. 
 Jaxson Dart doesn't seem too worried about the offense despite the early inconsistency. "We're taking steps each day," he said. "Obviously there are thing that you go out there and maybe it's our first time running something and you have things to talk through. A lot of times we'll have the opportunity the next day to go out there and try to fix it and run it again. So I think the really good thing I'm seeing about our offense is the communication after practices to be able to fix the adjustments the next day. That's really encouraging to see." 
 
 

 

 Wednesday, Aug. 5 

 It was another up and down day for the Giants' offense. It really has been the story of training camp in West Virginia.

 Quarterback Jaxson Dart and Co. were pedestrian again on Wednesday, even against the second-team defense. He threw a pair of interceptions early, before tossing three touchdown passes and rushing for two more in red-zone drills.

 Coach John Harbaugh thought it was a good response after Dart let the frustration get the best of him one day earlier.

 "The football response absolutely was there. Yeah, he stepped up," Harbaugh said. "A lot of third down stuff we did. Fourth down stuff, fourth down in the red zone to win the game, things like that.

 "Yeah, he had a heck of a practice. It was impressive."

 Dart and the first-team offense have yet to fully hit their stride this summer. And there are some built-in excuses. Dart is learning a new offense. He's also without his No. 1 receiver in Malik Nabers , who still isn't taking part in team drills as he recovers from a knee injury. Still, it would be nice to see them put together a complete practice before leaving West Virginia.

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 4 

 In his quest to make the roster, Tuesday was an important practice for Odell Beckham Jr . For the first time this summer he worked with the first-team offense for most of the day.

 Beckham caught a pair of passes and had another would've-been touchdown grab in a strong performance.

 Beckham worked alongside Darnell Mooney and Braxton Berrios on a day when Darius Slayton and Malachi Fields seemed to have their workloads limited. Malik Nabers continues to participate in individual drills but mostly stands around and watches when the team breaks into live periods.

 "Just probably worked out that way [Tuesday]," coach John Harbaugh said of Beckham working with the first team. "He ... I don't know, worked out that way."

 Regardless, Beckham continues to get open consistently. He might not look like Prime Odell, but he still can play and create separation.

 More observations: 

 

 

 Monday, Aug. 3 

 It was a rough day for the Giants' offense in pouring rain on the first day in full pads. The performance was really an extension of the early part of training camp for Jaxson Dart  & Co.

 A lot of penalties. Too many mental mistakes. Not enough positive plays. 
 
Dart threw an interception into the hands of safety Jevon Holland when the ball slipped out of the quarterback's hand while throwing. The Giants failed to score a touchdown on any of their drives and committed nine offensive penalties, everything from delay of games to endless false starts to holding by a wide receiver.

 "I think two things," coach John Harbaugh said. "I mean, I think you've got the elements a little bit, and you've got the first day in pads. So, it's not really unexpected, but we'll be working on it."

 Harbaugh added that he generally believes the offense is ahead of the defense early in camp. That seems not to be the case with his sloppy Giants as they digest new schemes.

 Other observations:  

 
 Saturday, Aug. 1 
 It has been a quiet start to training camp from Odell Beckham Jr .

 Until Saturday.

 On the day when the Giants had their largest crowd of the summer at The Greenbrier in West Virginia, Beckham made the biggest play of the day. And received the biggest ovation of the summer to date.

 The veteran receiver made a leaping grab over a defender in the back of the end zone for a touchdown from quarterback Jameis Winston during 11-on-11 drills. It sent the crowd of approximately 2,000 fans into a frenzy and served as a reminder of what used to be.

 It was a big play for Beckham, who is battling for a roster spot with several other veterans. Braxton Berrios has stood out the most of the group this camp, until Saturday.

 "There's a lot of really good football players in our room right now," wide receiver Darius Slayton said. "From a competition-level standpoint, it's ... raised the competition level."

 Other observations: 

 

 Friday, July 31 

 Second-year linebacker Abdul Carter has enjoyed a strong start to training camp. It has him thinking big.

 His goal: "Be Defensive Player of the Year, for sure."

 Can it be this year?

 "Absolutely," he said.

 Why?

 "Just my process. I know who I can be and the belief in myself. I know what I'm capable of and I know if I put the work in and believe in myself, trust in myself, trust in my teammates, trust in my coaches, I can be whoever I want to be."

 Lofty goal after 4.0 sacks as a rookie. But Carter feels he learned a lot from last year, when he was benched twice for missing and being late to meetings. He thinks he hit his stride late in the season and can carry it into the next year.

 Other observations: 

 

 Thursday, July 30 
 Pass rusher  Abdul Carter reminded everyone why he was the No. 3 overall pick last year. He was a menace in the second practice of the summer, constantly in the backfield and even getting credited with…

title: Ottis Anderson and me: A fan's quest for the meaning of the Hall of Fame
summary: One man's journey through history and psychology to make an impassioned case for his favorite Super Bowl MVP.
full_text:
I TRY NOT to feel slighted when the MVP of Super Bowl XXV doesn't hug me on a chilly December afternoon at MetLife Stadium, but it isn't easy.

 Ottis "O.J." Anderson, you see, is not stingy with hugs: former teammates, stadium buffet station chefs,  New York Giants  executives, fans too young to have seen him play, fans old enough to never forget seeing him play -- if there's reasonable justification, the 69-year-old Anderson will wrap his still oak-tree-strong arms around you.

 But not me, not yet anyway. I'm at MetLife for a game against the  Minnesota Vikings , there to hang out with Anderson. Not long after he shakes my hand upon arrival, we're sitting at a high table in the Giants Legacy Club with another retired Giant, Rodney Hampton.

 Hampton was a rookie in 1990, Anderson's 12th season in the league, and he explains that the veteran running back was asked by head coach Bill Parcells to inform him when Hampton was "ready." Taking that mandate as seriously as he did everything in his long career, Anderson mentored the player destined to replace him as a starter through a very productive campaign. "To most people that was the season he helped us win a Super Bowl," Hampton says. "But for me that was the season he taught me how to be a pro. He was everything to all of us in the [running backs] room: dad, uncle, big brother, mentor -- call him anything you want."

 Well, anything except Hall of Famer.

 

 Hampton and Anderson are sometime ambassadors for the Giants, paid to turn up at games to shmooze with fans, especially the kind who tend to watch the action from suites. Both men are naturals, quick with a selfie smile, game memory or insight about the current squad. They hug it out before departing to make their rounds, me trailing Anderson as he runs into another longtime acquaintance.

 "My man," Roger Goodell says as he and Anderson clap backs in the Commissioner's Club, another of MetLife's many exclusive seating areas. After a brief chat, Anderson moves on to greet other patrons, but I hang around to explain to the commissioner why I'm there. It's a longish story -- and fingers crossed you'll finish! -- but the tl;dr version is that I persuaded ESPN to let me write a "Trojan Horse story": In theory, I tell Goodell, I'm using my sports world connections to make a case that Anderson, a hero of my youth, deserves to be voted in as a senior candidate to the Pro Football Hall of Fame in Canton, Ohio.

 "That would make a lot of people happy," the commissioner says.

 But hidden inside that familiar sports writing trope, I continue, is a desire to answer a more profound question: Why, exactly, as a 64-year-old supposedly well-adjusted human, do I care so much about this?

 "Maybe you want to be rewarded for your loyalty," Goodell suggests.

 I respond by saying that I believe it might run deeper than that, and Goodell nods while looking at me with what seems like concern, before shaking my hand and walking away.

 So, yeah, this is a story about the Canton-worthiness of Ottis Jerome Anderson -- not to mention the psychological underpinnings of sports fandom.

 I will also be discussing "The Wizard of Oz."

 

 

 WE SHOULD PROBABLY deal with this quickly: The Hall of Fame case for Ottis Anderson is comically easy to make.

 Start with the numbers. When Anderson retired, after the 1992 season, he ranked among the NFL's all-time leaders in rushing yards (eighth), rushing touchdowns (seventh) and yards from scrimmage (ninth). He remains, somewhat astonishingly, outside Canton despite sitting squarely among -- and often ahead of -- players who are comfortably inside.

 And that's before we get to context, which is where Anderson's résumé becomes even more compelling. He wasn't just productive; he was often dominant. His rookie season in 1979 remains one of the great debuts in NFL history: 1,605 rushing yards, Offensive Rookie of the Year, first-team All-Pro. Over his first five seasons, which included the strike-shortened 1982 campaign, he amassed 6,190 rushing yards, a total that placed him among the most feared backs in the game at a time when the league was not exactly short on them. Think: Earl Campbell, Eric Dickerson, Walter Payton.

 Then there are the matters of longevity and second acts. Traded to the Giants in 1986 in what seemed like the twilight of his playing days, Anderson did not so much extend his career as reimagine it. He was named Comeback Player of the Year for the 1989 season -- the oldest running back (32) to achieve that milestone (HOF runner Marcus Allen won it four years later at 33) rushing for more than 1,000 yards. And he did so not only with a different uniform number (24), but with a completely different style.

 Early in his career, Anderson was a prototype of the modern outside back: fast, explosive, darting, capable of turning the edge and outrunning defenses. Think: Gale Sayers with size. But in New York, he became something else entirely: a punishing, between-the-tackles runner. Think: John Riggins with speed. Most players who lose a step lose their edge. Anderson changed his game and his role, and in doing so extended not just his career, but his relevance. He did not fade; he adapted.

 "I was still running a 4.5 40," he recalls, comparing that to his rookie year 4.4 time in the dash. "But Bill [Parcells] wanted me to run inside, so I ran inside."

 And then, a year after his "comeback" season -- at age 34, when most running backs are either long retired or clinging to roster spots -- Anderson delivered a steely title game performance: 102 yards, a touchdown and MVP honors in a Super Bowl XXV victory that depended greatly on his ability to grind out yards against the Buffalo Bills defense. (The Giants were starting their backup quarterback.) "The man had two totally different careers," says former Giants defensive lineman George Martin, who was a division rival and teammate of Anderson. "In one he was pretty much unstoppable -- I tried twice a year -- and in the other he was Super Bowl MVP."

 

 That performance alone should at least complicate the conversation. Hall of Fame voters have historically been susceptible to postseason moments, and few are more impressive than a Super Bowl MVP turn. When given the chance, Anderson didn't just participate in big games, he tilted them, as the kind of player coaches trusted when the game narrowed to its most consequential moments.

 And yet, for all of this -- production, longevity, postseason excellence (he also scored in Super Bowl XXI) -- Anderson remains outside the Hall, a status that becomes harder to explain the longer one looks at it. Which is why I contacted a few current and former Pro Football Hall of Fame voters, most of whom asked to speak on background. This is understandable, given the passions that HOFs can ignite, especially regarding exclusions. "Fans don't praise you for Peyton Manning getting into the Hall," says Peter King, a longtime Canton selector, now retired. "They yell at you because Roman Gabriel isn't."

 To be clear, HOF voting in professional football is now, has always been and likely always will be something of a highly subjective mess. Indeed, there's a very interesting story to write about HOF voting in pretty much every sport, in pretty much every country.

 But this is not one of those stories. Let's just all agree that members of the Canton selection committee are hamstrung by rules and procedures that can keep worthy candidates from earning enough votes. That's true for modern era players in their initial window of eligibility (19 years, beginning five years after retirement) and for seniors (25 years or more after their last season). For this reason, I didn't press any current or former voters to say if they voted for Anderson at any point over the years. But I did ask if they had any theories for his exclusion, which ranged from the specific -- "I'm not sure he was ever the best at his position in any given year" -- to the…

title: 2026 New York Jets training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our daily updates from Jets training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The  New York Jets  camp is taking place at the Atlantic Health Training Facility in Florham Park, New Jersey, and Jets reporter Rich Cimini has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Jets camp. We will update this file often. Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football, and which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Jets camp 
 
 Rookie TE Kenyon Sadiq to miss time after hernia setback 
 Jets' Smith rues being 'distraction' after dispute with girlfriend 
 2026 Jets training camp preview 
 
 
 

 Thursday, Aug. 6 

 Quarterbacks always wear a red jersey in practice. Geno Smith is taking the red thing to a new level.

 Red contact lenses.

 To reduce the glare on the field, Smith is wearing the red lenses for the first time in his career. They were quite apparent during his weekly news conference, with one reporter joking that the red-eye look was scary.

 "It's actually pretty cool," Smith said. "It blocks out the sunlight and all that, so it's actually pretty cool. It keeps the glare from the sun out of your eyes."

 Smith's former Jets teammate Santonio Holmes, a wide receiver, was known for wearing red contact lenses more than a decade ago. Smith got the idea from Holmes but didn't go red until he consulted recently with eye specialists, who signed off on the idea.

 "It's just something we're trying out, just to see what it's like," Smith said. "I like it, so we've been sticking with it."

 Even though his eyes look red, he's not seeing that way.

 "The entire room is yellow, so it's a yellow tint to everything," Smith said. "But yeah, it's pretty cool. You guys should try it."

 Smith, who threw a league-high 17 interceptions last season for the Las Vegas Raiders , is trying to reboot his career with the team that drafted him in 2013. So far, so good. Teammates and coaches have been impressed with his command of the offense and willingness to take chances downfield.

 His goal is to make opposing defenses see red.

 Other observations:  

 
 Rookie TE Kenyon Sadiq , who suffered a setback in his recovery from hernia surgery, will miss "a couple of weeks," coach Aaron Glenn said. Glenn called it "pretty good news." This was more detail than he provided Tuesday, when he said Sadiq would be sidelined for "a little bit." Glenn reiterated that Sadiq, the second of three first-round picks, will be ready for Week 1. 
 Backup RB Isaiah Davis will miss at least two weeks with a "minor" knee injury, according to Glenn. It should be more reps for Kene Nwangwu , who probably will make the team because of his kick return ability. CB Nahshon Wright has a hip strain. Rookie CB D'Angelo Ponds (calf strain) is close to returning. 
 Rookie QB Cade Klubnik was shaky on Thursday, going 1-for-5 in team drills -- most of which were in the red zone. He was intercepted by backup LB Mykal Walker . This was the second time in camp that the former Clemson star struggled in the red zone. He's been solid in the other practices. 
 One under-the-radar player is former New York Giants S Dane Belton , who made three forced fumbles and one interception last season. The coaches love his ball production. Belton, who came over on a one-year, $4 million contract, is pushing Andre Cisco for a starting job. "No matter where I'm at," Belton said, "I can make plays and help the team." 
 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 4 

 For months, the Jets have been boasting about their tight-end depth. They will get a chance to show it off in the coming weeks.

 First-round pick Kenyon Sadiq suffered a setback from May hernia surgery and will be sidelined "a little bit," according to coach Aaron Glenn.

 Translation: He probably will miss at least a chunk of the preseason, affording more opportunities for Mason Taylor , Jeremy Ruckert and Jelani Woods .

 Ruckert capitalized Tuesday, making a team-high four receptions in practice. It was a mixed day for Taylor, who had one catch and one drop. He also was the targeted receiver on a Geno Smith pass that was intercepted.

 "I see him breaking out this year," Glenn said of Taylor, a 2025 second-round pick who made a team-high 44 receptions for 369 yards last season.

 The Jets surprised the draft world when they picked Sadiq 16th overall, one year after taking Taylor. Ruckert was a 2022 third-round pick. Yes, they've invested heavily at tight end.

 This year's plan is to use more two-tight end packages, integrating Sadiq's elite speed and versatility into the offensive equation. Those plans will be on hold. While the Jets are "very confident" that Sadiq will be back for Week 1, per Glenn, they will have to adjust on the fly with Taylor, Ruckert and Woods.

 Other observations: 

 
 The starting defense made an interception for the second day in a row. This time it was CB Brandon Stephens , who snared a Smith pass that was deflected downfield. After going interception-less for the entire 2025 season, unprecedented in NFL history, it would be an understatement to say the Jets are emphasizing takeaways. 
 It was a nice day for the running backs, especially Breece Hall and Braelon Allen , both of whom busted long runs in the second padded practice. Allen, who had knee surgery last season, came to camp at 244 pounds, slightly above his ideal playing weight (240). Allen said he's been looking forward to this season from the moment he got off the operating table. 
 WR Isaiah Williams doesn't generate much fanfare for his offense -- he's known for this kick returning -- but he made the catch of the day, a falling-down, over-the-shoulder grab. "He's a dude," Glenn said. In Glenn-speak, that's a high compliment. 
 Backup MLB Kiko Mauigoa made a big downfield hit, jarring the ball loose from rookie WR Omar Cooper Jr . Mauigoa is getting a chance to solidify himself as Demario Davis ' understudy. 
 Kingsley Enagbare didn't practice -- on Monday, he got stepped on -- leaving the defense thin on the edge. They're already without Joseph Ossai (PUP list). It afforded for more reps for Will McDonald IV . Enagbare's injury isn't serious, per Glenn. 
 No practice Wednesday, their third off day out of the first eight days in camp. 
 

 

 Monday, Aug. 3 
 There was an unusual occurrence on the practice field -- an interception by the defense, the first of training camp for the starters.

 Former All-Pro safety  Minkah Fitzpatrick , one of the Jets' marquee additions, picked off Geno Smith 's first pass in 11-on-11 drills -- a noteworthy feat, considering last season's ignominy.

 You may have heard: The Jets were the first team in NFL history to go an entire season without intercepting a pass. We're talking about almost a full century; the league started tracking interceptions in 1933.

 The defensive backs, in particular, are determined to end the embarrassing slump. They dream about getting takeaways.

 "Shoot, I tell that to myself, even in my sleep," cornerback  Brandon Stephens  said after practice.

 It's one of the big reasons why they traded for Fitzpatrick and gave him a three-year, $40 million contract . Since entering the league in 2018, he's tied for ninth in interceptions (21).

 "He's extremely smart and he loves football -- and at safety, that's what you're looking for," coach Aaron Glenn said of Fitzpatrick. "Look, I've had some good safeties in my career. Early on, I like exactly where he's at."

 Fitzpatrick can line up in multiple spots. On his interception, he was in the deep middle. He got an assist from LB Demario Davis , who got…

summary: Follow our daily updates from Steelers training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The  Pittsburgh Steelers ' camp is taking place in Latrobe, Pennsylvania, and Steelers reporter Brooke Pryor has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Steelers camp. We will update this file often. How will coach Mike McCarthy shape this roster and the offense in his first year in Pittsburgh? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?
